Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 1:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-199) In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surat al-Baqarah

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. That is the Book﴾.

Allah, exalted is He, referred to the Qur'an in this verse with the demonstrative of the distant (dhalika, "that"), while in other verses He referred to it with the demonstrative of the near (hadha, "this"), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [Nuh: 9], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Naml: 76], and the verse continues.

And His saying: ﴿And this is a Book which We have sent down, blessed﴾ [al-An'am: 92].

And His saying: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories by Our revelation to you of this Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 3], and other verses besides these.

To reconcile these verses there are several aspects:

The first aspect: what some scholars of rhetoric (balaghah) have set down is that the reference to it with the demonstrative of the near present is because this Qur'an is near and present in the ears, on the tongues and in the hearts, while the reference to it with the demonstrative of the distant is due to the distance of its station and rank from resembling the speech of created beings, and from what the disbelievers claim of it, that it is sorcery, or poetry, or soothsaying, or the fables of the ancients.

The second aspect: this is what Ibn Jarir al-Tabari chose in his tafsir, that "that" refers to what is contained in His saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾, and that He referred to it with the demonstrative of the distant because the speech referred to has passed (munqadi), though in reality it is near because of the nearness of its ending. He gave as an example a man speaking to another man who sometimes says: "By Allah, indeed that is what you said," and sometimes says: "By Allah, indeed this is what you said." So the distant demonstrative is used with regard to the speech having passed and ended, and the near demonstrative with regard to the nearness of its ending.

The third aspect: the Arabs sometimes refer to the near with the demonstrative of the distant, so the verse is according to (p-200) one of the styles of the Arabic language. A parallel to this is the saying of Khufaf ibn Nudbah al-Sulami, when Malik ibn Harmalah al-Fazari was killed:

"If my horses have been struck in their core, then I have deliberately turned toward Malik over my eye,
I say to him while the spear bends its shaft: Look at Khufaf; indeed, I am that one (dhalika)."

He means: "I am this one." This last verse was related by al-Bukhari from Umar ibn al-Muthanna Abu Ubaydah, and Ibn Kathir mentioned it. In any case, the majority of the mufassirun hold that "dhalika al-Kitab" means "hadha al-Kitab."

[p. 10]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Baqarah. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is guidance for the God-fearing﴾.

In this verse He declares that this Qur'an is ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾. By the implication of the verse, namely the implication of contrast (mafhum al-mukhalafa, the reasoning from the opposite meaning, known as dalil al-khitab, the indication of the discourse), it is understood that this Qur'an is not guidance for those who are not God-fearing. He declared this implication in other verses, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, a guidance and a healing. And as for those who do not believe, there is deafness in their ears, and it is blindness for them﴾ [Fussilat: 44].

• And His saying: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾.

• And His saying: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say, "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. And as for those in whose hearts is a disease, it has added to them uncleanness upon their uncleanness, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124, 125].

• And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief﴾, and the two verses [al-Ma'idah: 64, 68].

It is known that the guidance meant in this verse is the specific guidance (al-huda al-khass), which is the bestowal of divine enablement (tawfiq) to the religion of truth, not the general guidance (al-huda al-amm), which is the clarification of the truth.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab, Removing the Appearance of Inconsistency from the Verses of the Book):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾.

This is an indefinite noun (nakira) in the context of negation, combined with "la" (no), and so it is built on the fatha.

When an indefinite noun is like this, it is explicit (nass) in generality, as is established in the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence). The "la" here, which is explicit in generality, is the one known to the grammarians (al-nahwiyyun) as "la" of generic negation (la al-lati li-nafy al-jins). As for "la" that operates like "laysa" (not), it is apparent in generality (zahir fi al-'umum) but not explicit in it. Accordingly, the verse is explicit in negating every single instance of doubt from this great Qur'an. Yet other verses indicate that doubt about it exists in some people, such as the disbelievers who are in doubt, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾ [2].

And as in His saying: ﴿And their hearts have become doubtful, so they are hesitating in their doubt﴾ [al-Tawbah: 45].

And as in His saying: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt, playing﴾ [al-Dukhan: 9].

The way to reconcile this is that the Qur'an has reached such a degree of clarity of proofs and manifestness of the miracle that it negates the entry of any doubt into it. The doubt of the disbelievers about it is only due to the blindness of their insight, as He explained with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is one who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19]. Thus He declared that whoever does not know that it is the truth, that is only because of his blindness. It is known that a blind man's failure to see the sun does not contradict its being beyond doubt because of its manifestness:

Poetry:
"When a person does not have a sound eye, it is no wonder that he doubts, while the morning is bright."

Some scholars answered: His saying, ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾, is a report (khabar) that is meant as an injunction (insha'), i.e., "Do not doubt in it." Accordingly, there is no difficulty.

**

[p. 201] His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is guidance for the God-fearing﴾.

In this verse He restricted the guidance of this Book to the God-fearing. Another verse indicates that its guidance is general for all people, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down as guidance for the people﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Baqarah: 185]. The way to reconcile the two is that guidance is used in the Qur'an in two senses: one is general, and the other is specific. As for general guidance, its meaning is the making clear of the path of truth and the clarification of the clear way, whether or not the one addressed follows it. In this sense is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them﴾ [Fussilat: 17], meaning, We made clear to them the path of truth through the tongue of our Prophet Salih, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace, although they did not follow it, as is shown by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17].

From it also is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way﴾ [al-Insan: 3], meaning, We made clear to him the paths of good and evil, as is shown by His saying: ﴿Either grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan: 3].

As for specific guidance, it is Allah's bestowal of enablement (tafadul bi al-tawfiq) upon the servant. In this sense is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided﴾, to the end of the verse [6].

And His saying: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam﴾ [al-An'am: 125].

When you know this, know that the specific guidance for the God-fearing is the specific guidance, which is the bestowal of enablement upon them, and the general guidance for people is the general guidance, which is the making clear of the way and the clarification of the clear path. By this, the difficulty also is removed between His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56], and His saying: ﴿And indeed, you invite them to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52], because the guidance negated from him ﷺ is the specific guidance, since enablement is in the hand of Allah alone: ﴿And whomever Allah intends for trial, you will not possess for him anything from Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41].

The guidance affirmed for him is the general guidance, which is the making clear of the path. He ﷺ made it clear until he left it as a white path, its night like its day: ﴿And Allah invites to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus: 25].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from what We have provided for them they spend﴾

In this noble verse He used "min" (ِمن) of partitive sense (التبعيض), indicating that the believer spends for the sake of Allah only part of his wealth, not all of it. Here He did not specify the amount that should be spent and the amount that should be retained. But He explained in other places that the amount that should be spent is what exceeds one's need and the meeting of the necessities one cannot do without, such as His saying: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: "The excess"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. The meaning of "al-'afw" (العفو, the excess) is what exceeds the amount of need that one cannot do without, according to the most correct of the interpretations, and it is the view of the majority (الجمهور).

From it is His saying: ﴿until they grew in number﴾ [al-A'raf: 95], i.e., they multiplied, and their wealth and children increased.

Some scholars said: "al-'afw" is the opposite of "al-jahd" (الجهد, exertion), and it means that one spends what, in spending it, does not reach the level of exertion and the exhaustion of one's capacity. From it is the saying of the poet: [Al-Tawil]

"Take the excess from me, so that my affection may endure, and do not speak in my anger when I am furious."

This saying is close to what we have mentioned, and the remaining sayings are weak.

And His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely outstretched﴾ [al-Isra: 29]. Here He forbade stinginess by His saying "do not make your hand chained to your neck," and forbade extravagance by His saying "nor extend it completely outstretched." Thus the middle course between the two matters is determined, as He explained it by His saying: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are between that a justly balanced course﴾ [al-Furqan: 67]. Therefore the spender must distinguish between generosity (الجود) and squandering (التبذير), and between stinginess (البخل) and moderation (الاقتصاد). Generosity is not squandering, and moderation is not stinginess. Withholding where giving is called for is blameworthy, and Allah forbade it to His Prophet ﷺ by His saying: ﴿do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾. Giving where withholding is called for is also blameworthy, and Allah forbade it to His Prophet ﷺ by His saying: ﴿nor extend it completely outstretched﴾. The poet said: [Al-Basit]

"Do not praise the son of 'Abbad, even if his hands pour forth like the rain cloud, until the downpour is put to shame. For they are slips from his whisperings: he gives and withholds, neither from stinginess nor from generosity."

Allah, exalted is He, has explained in other places that praiseworthy spending is not of this kind unless its channel of disbursement is something that pleases Allah. As in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Whatever good you spend is for parents and relatives"﴾ and the verse [al-Baqarah: 215], and He stated explicitly that spending on what does not please Allah is a regret for its doer, in His saying: ﴿They will spend it, then it will be a regret for them﴾ and the verse [al-Anfal: 36]. The poet said:

"Indeed a favour is not counted a favour until the way to the one who makes it is struck by it."

If it is said: what you have established implies that praiseworthy spending is spending on what exceeds the necessary need, yet Allah, exalted is He, praised a people for spending while they themselves were in need of what they spent. That is in His saying: ﴿They prefer others over themselves, even though they are in poverty. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾ [al-Hashr: 9].

(p-١٢) The apparent answer—and Allah knows best—is what some scholars mentioned: that every situation has its own speech. In some circumstances preferring others is forbidden. This is like when the spender has obligatory expenses, such as the maintenance of wives and the like, and he gives voluntarily in what is not obligatory while abandoning the obligation, because of his saying ﷺ: "Begin with those you are responsible for." Or like when he has no patience against asking people, so he spends his wealth and then goes back to people asking them for their money; this is not permitted for him. Preferring others is permitted when he has not neglected an obligatory expense and he is confident in himself about patience, restraint and not asking.

As for the view that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from what We have provided for them they spend﴾ refers to zakat, then the matter is clear, and knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

The author said in (Dafʿ Iham al-Idtirab ʿan Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾

(p-202) This verse, by its apparent meaning, indicates that the disbelievers will not believe. Yet other verses have come indicating that some of the disbelievers do believe in Allah and His Messenger, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38], and His saying: ﴿Thus you were before, but Allah bestowed His favor upon you﴾ [al-Nisa: 94], and His saying: ﴿And among these are those who will believe in it﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 47].

The way to reconcile them is clear: this verse belongs to the general (ʿamm) that has been specified (makhsus), because it refers specifically to the wretched whose wretchedness was predetermined in Allah's knowledge, indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe﴾ and ﴿even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 96-97]. This specification is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has sealed over their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7].

Some have answered that the meaning is "they will not believe" as long as the seal is upon their hearts and their hearing, and the covering is upon their sight; but if Allah removes that from them by His bounty, they will believe.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering﴾, etc. It is not hidden that the particle "wa" (and) in His saying:

﴿and upon their hearing and upon their eyes﴾ is open, in both instances, to being a conjunction with what precedes it, or to being a resumptive (isti'nafiyya, introducing a new clause). He did not clarify this here, but He clarified in another place that His saying ﴿and upon their hearing﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿upon their hearts﴾, and that His saying ﴿and upon their eyes﴾ is a resumptive clause, the prepositional phrase being the predicate of the subject, which is ﴿a covering﴾. What permitted beginning with an indefinite noun here is that it is preceded by the prepositional phrase that comes before it. For this reason this predicate must be placed first, since it is what permitted the beginning with the subject, as he set it down in the [Alfiyya] (al-Khulasa) with his saying, [in rajaz metre]:

"And like 'indi dirhamun wa-li wat' (there is a dirham with me, and for me there is a need), where the predicate is obligatorily placed first."

Thus it is established that the sealing is upon the hearts and the hearing, and that the covering is upon the eyes. This is in His exalted saying: ﴿Have you seen him who takes as his god his own desire, and Allah has sent him astray knowingly, and has set a seal upon his hearing and his heart, and placed over his sight a covering?﴾ [al-Jathiya: 23]. The "khatm" (sealing) means securing a thing so that nothing inside it comes out and nothing outside it enters. The "ghishawa" (covering) is a veil over the eye that prevents sight, and from this is the saying of al-Harith ibn Khalid ibn al-As, [in tawil metre]:

"I loved you when a covering was over my eye, / but when it was lifted I cut my breath blaming it."

As for the reading of the one who put "ghishawa" in the accusative, it is then governed by a verb omitted, meaning ﴿and He placed over his sight a covering﴾ [al-Jathiya: 23], as in the surah of al-Jathiya. It is like his saying, [in rajaz metre]:

"I fed them straw and cold water, until their eyes streamed with tears."

And the saying of another, [in mursal al-kamil metre]:

"I saw your husband in the battle, girding on a sword and a spear."

And the saying of another, [in wafir metre]:

"When the adorned women come forth one day, and they have darkened their eyebrows and their eyes."

As is well known in grammar. Some have permitted it to be conjoined to the position (mahall) of the genitive noun. If it is said: the setting (tab') may also be upon the eyes, as in His saying in the surah of al-Nahl: ﴿Those are the ones upon whose hearts and hearing and sight Allah has set a seal﴾ [al-Nahl: 108].

The answer: the sealing upon the eyes mentioned in the verse of al-Nahl is the covering mentioned in the surahs of al-Baqara and al-Jathiya. And Allah knows best.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing﴾, etc.

This verse, by its apparent meaning, indicates that they are compelled, for whoever has a seal upon his heart and a covering placed over his sight has been stripped of the capacity to believe. Yet other verses have come indicating that their disbelief occurs by their own will and choice, such as His saying: ﴿So they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17].

And His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance and punishment in exchange for forgiveness﴾ [al-Baqara: 175].

And His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾, etc. [al-Kahf: 29], and His saying: ﴿That is because of what your hands have sent forth﴾, etc. [Al 'Imran: 182].

And His saying: ﴿Evil is what their souls have sent forth for them﴾, etc. [al-Ma'ida: 80].

The answer is that the sealing, the setting, and the covering placed upon their hearing, their sight, and their hearts are all a punishment from Allah upon them for their hastening to disbelief and their denial of the messengers by their own choice and will. So Allah punished them by withholding success, as a fitting recompense, as He explained by His saying: ﴿Rather, Allah has set a seal upon them because of their disbelief﴾ [al-Nisa: 155].

(p-203) And His saying: ﴿That is because they believed, then disbelieved, so their hearts were sealed﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 3].

And by His saying: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights, as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [al-An'am: 110].

And His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5].

And His saying: ﴿In their hearts is a sickness, so Allah increased their sickness﴾, etc. [al-Baqara: 10].

And His saying: ﴿Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 14], and other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 8:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾. He did not give an explanation here about these hypocrites (munafiqun), but He explicitly mentioned some of them in His saying: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 101].

Allah says: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾. Here He does not explain any of the form His mockery of them takes, but He mentioned part of it in Surah al-Hadid, in His saying: ﴿It will be said, "Return behind you and seek light."﴾ [al-Hadid: 13].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 17:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their likeness is like the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾ — the verse.

In this verse he made the pronoun singular in His saying "istawqada" (kindled) and in what surrounds it, and he made the pronoun plural in His saying: ﴿Allah took away their light and left them in darknesses, not seeing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], although the referent of all these pronouns is one thing, namely the word "alladhi" (the one who) in His saying: "Their likeness is like the likeness of alladhi."

The answer to this is that the word "alladhi" is singular in form, but its meaning is general, covering everything that its relative clause includes. It has been established in the science of usul al-fiqh (legal theory) that all relative pronouns (al-asma' al-mawsulah) are among the forms of generality. When you have verified this, know that the singular pronoun is used with regard to the word "alladhi," and the plural with regard to its meaning. On this basis, the scholars have stated that "alladhi" comes with the meaning of "alladhina" (those who). Among the examples of this in the Qur'an is this noble verse. So His saying: ﴿like the likeness of alladhi istawqada﴾ means like the likeness of those who kindled, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Allah took away their light and left them﴾ — the verse [al-Baqarah: 17].

And His saying: ﴿And the one who brought the truth and confirmed it, those are the God-fearing﴾ — the verse [al-Zumar: 33]. And His saying: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury, like the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264], meaning like those who spend, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿they have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264].

And His saying: ﴿and you plunged in as those who plunged did﴾ [al-Tawbah: 9], based on the correct view that "alladhi" there is a relative pronoun and not a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah).

A parallel to this from the speech of the Arabs is the words of the rajaz poet:

O Lord of 'Abs, do not bless anyone, whether standing among them or sitting,
except those who stood at the edges of the rope-stretch (al-masad).

(p-204) And the saying of the poet Ashhab ibn Rumaylah, which Sibawayh cited to illustrate the use of "alladhi" to mean "alladhina":

And indeed those whose blood was spilled at Faluj — they are the people, all of the people, O Umm Khalid.

Ibn al-Anbari claimed that the word "alladhi" in the verse of Ashhab is a plural of "alladh" with a sukun, and that "alladhi" in the verse is singular but intended as plural. Sibawayh's statement refutes him. And the saying of 'Udayl ibn al-Farkh al-'Ijli:

I spent the night giving drink to the people, my brothers, those whose error is my error and whose right guidance is my guidance.

Some of them said: the one who kindled is singular while the group with him is plural, but its weakness is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 18:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾, the verse. The apparent meaning of this verse is that the hypocrites are characterized by deafness, dumbness, and blindness. However, He, exalted is He, explained in another place that the meaning of their deafness, their dumbness, and their blindness is that they do not benefit from their hearing, their hearts, and their sight. This is in His saying, majestic and exalted is He: ﴿And We made for them hearing and sight and hearts, but their hearing and their sight and their hearts did not avail them anything, since they used to deny the signs of Allah; and there encompassed them what they had been mocking﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 26].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return﴾, the verse.

The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that the hypocrites do not hear, do not speak, and do not see. There have come in other verses things that indicate the contrary of that, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He could have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20].

And His saying: ﴿And if they speak, you listen to their speech﴾, the verse [al-Munafiqun: 4], meaning: because of their eloquence and the sweetness of their tongues.

And His saying: ﴿Then when fear departs, they will strike you with sharp tongues﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19], and other verses besides these. The way of reconciling them is clear: they are dumb in regard to speaking the truth, even though they speak other than it; deaf in regard to hearing the truth, even though they hear other than it; blind in regard to seeing the truth, even though they see other than it. Exalted is He has explained this reconciliation by His saying: ﴿And We made for them hearing and sight and hearts﴾, the verse [al-Ahqaf: 26], because what does not benefit anything is like the nonexistent. The Arabs sometimes apply deafness to hearing that has no effect, and from it is the saying of Qa'nab ibn Umm Sahib:

*Deaf when they hear good spoken about them, and if evil is mentioned about me in their presence, they hear it attentively.*

And the saying of the poet:

*Deaf to the matter I do not desire, and I make Allah's creatures hear whenever I desire.*

And the saying of another:

*So I made 'Amr deaf and blinded him to generosity and boasting on the day of boasting.*

(p-205) Likewise, speech in which there is no benefit is like nonexistence.

Hubayrah ibn Abi Wahb al-Makhzumi said:

*Indeed the speech of a man in other than its place is like arrows that fall with no heads upon them.*

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾ (to the end of the verse). Ṣayyib means rain. In this verse Allah has struck a parable for what Muhammad ﷺ brought of guidance and knowledge, using rain as the comparison, because by knowledge and guidance the spirits live, just as by rain the bodies live.

He pointed to the aspect of this parable's comparison in His saying, majestic and exalted is He: ﴿And the good land – its vegetation comes out by the permission of its Lord, but that which is bad does not come out except sparsely﴾ [al-A'raf: 58].

(p-14) The Prophet ﷺ has clarified this parable referred to in the two verses in the hadith of Abu Musa, agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), where he ﷺ said: "The likeness of the guidance and knowledge with which Allah has sent me is like a rain that fell upon a land. A portion of it was good; it absorbed the water and produced abundant grass and herbage. Another portion of it was hard ground that held the water, so Allah benefited people by it: they drank from it, gave drink, and cultivated. And a third portion of it was barren plains that hold no water and produce no grass. That is the likeness of one who comprehends the religion of Allah and whom Allah benefits by what He has sent me with; he knows and teaches. And the likeness of one who does not raise his head toward that and does not accept the guidance of Allah with which I have been sent."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In it are darkness﴾. In this verse Allah has struck the parable for what befalls the disbelievers and hypocrites of doubts and suspicions about the Qur'an, with the darknesses of the rain, which is struck as a parable for the Qur'an. He clarified some of the matters which are like darkness upon them, because they increase them in blindness, in other verses, by His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you were [formerly] facing except that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels. And indeed, it was [a change] difficult except for those whom Allah guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. This is because the abrogation of the qiblah leads weak-certainty people to suppose, because of it, that the Prophet ﷺ is not certain of his matter, since he faces one direction one day and another direction another day, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The foolish among the people will say: "What has turned them away from their qiblah which they were [previously] upon?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142].

He, exalted is He, declared that the abrogation of the qiblah is difficult for other than those whom Allah has guided, and strengthened their certainty with His saying: ﴿And indeed, it was [a change] difficult except for those whom Allah guided﴾, and like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people, and [like] the accursed tree in the Qur'an﴾ [al-Isra': 60]. This is because what he saw on the night of the Isra' and Mi'raj of wonders and marvels was a cause for the disbelievers to believe that he ﷺ was lying, due to their claim that what he reported could not occur. So it is a cause for increasing the misguided in their misguidance. Likewise, the accursed tree in the Qur'an, which is the tree of zaqqum, is also a cause for increasing the misguidance of the misguided among them, because when the Prophet ﷺ recited: ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that emerges from the root of Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 64], they said: "His lie has become evident, for trees do not grow in dry land, so how would it grow at the root of the fire?!"

And like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make their number except as a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31], because when he ﷺ recited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30],

(p-15) some men of Quraysh said: "This is a small number; we are capable of killing them and seizing Paradise by force, since the guardians of the Fire, which Muhammad ﷺ claims we will enter, are few." Allah, exalted is He, does that only as a test and trial, and to Him belongs the perfect wisdom in all of that, glorified is He and exalted above what they say, a great exaltation.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thunder﴾. Allah struck the parable with thunder for what is in the Qur'an of warnings that strike the ears and disturb the hearts. He mentioned some of them in other verses, such as His saying: ﴿But if they turn away, say, "I have warned you of a thunderbolt"﴾ (to the end of the verse) [Fussilat: 13], and His saying: ﴿Before We obliterate faces and turn them back on their backs﴾ (to the end of the verse) [al-Nisa': 47], and His saying: ﴿He is not but a warner to you before a severe punishment﴾ [Saba': 46].

It is established in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the tafsir of Surat al-Tur, from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im – may Allah be pleased with him – that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reciting in the Maghrib prayer with al-Tur, and when he reached this verse, ﴿Were they created of nothing, or were they the creators?﴾ [al-Tur: 35] to His saying ﴿the controllers﴾, my heart nearly flew." And besides that, of the thunderous and admonishing verses of the Qur'an which frightened the hypocrites, to the extent that Allah, exalted is He, said about them: ﴿They think every shout is against them. They are the enemy﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4]. And the verse we are concerned with, although it concerns the hypocrites, the lesson is in the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the causes.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And lightning﴾. Allah, exalted is He, struck the parable with lightning, because of the light of conclusive proofs and shining demonstrations in the Qur'an.

He has declared that the Qur'an is a light by which Allah dispels the darknesses of ignorance, doubt and polytheism, just as the darknesses of the night are uncovered by sensible light:

• as in His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾ [al-Nisa': 174],

• and His saying: ﴿But We have made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾ [al-Shura: 52],

• and His saying: ﴿And they followed the light which was sent down with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 157].

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is encompassing of the disbelievers﴾. Some scholars said: "﴿Encompassing of the disbelievers﴾ means: destroying them." What supports this view is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Unless you are surrounded [by enemies]﴾ [Yusuf: 66], meaning: you are destroyed to the last of you. It was also said: "You are overcome." The meaning is close, because the one who is destroyed is not destroyed until he is encompassed from all sides, and no escape to safety remains for him through which he can pass (p-16), and likewise the defeated one. From this is the poet's saying: [al-Tawil]

"We encompassed them until, when they were certain of what they had seen, they all inclined toward peace."

And also from it: in the sense of destruction.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed [by ruin]﴾ (to the end of the verse) [al-Kahf: 42], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they assumed that they had been encompassed﴾ (to the end of the verse) [Yunus: 22].

The Exalted said: ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight.﴾

That is, the light of the Qur'an, because of its intense brightness, nearly blinds their insights, just as a dazzling lightning-flash of intense light nearly snatches the sight of the one who looks at it, especially if the sight is weak; for the weaker the sight, the more the light removes it. As the poet said: [Kamil]

﴾Like daylight, it increases the sight of creation in light, and it blinds the eyes of the bats.﴿

And another said: [Tawil]

﴾Bats whom the day blinded with its light, *** and whom pieces of darkened night joined.﴿

The insights of the disbelievers and the hypocrites are in the utmost weakness, so the intensity of the light of the illumination increases their blindness. The Exalted has explicitly stated this blindness in His saying: ﴿Is then one who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19], and His saying: ﴿Nor are the blind and the seeing alike﴾, and other verses to this effect.

Some scholars said: "The lightning nearly snatches their sights," that is: the clear, firm verses of the Qur'an nearly expose the faults of the hypocrites.

* *

The Exalted said: ﴿Every time it lights up for them, they walk in it, and when darkness falls over them, they stand still.﴾ In this verse, Allah struck the parable of the hypocrites with the people of this rain: when it lights up for them, they walk in its light, and when it darkens, they stop. Likewise, when the Qur'an agrees with their desires and inclinations, the hypocrites act upon it, such as intermarrying with the Muslims, inheriting from them, receiving a share of the Muslims' spoils, and being protected by it from being killed despite their disbelief within. But when it does not agree with their desires, such as spending lives and wealth in jihad in the way of Allah, which is commanded in it, they stand still and hold back. The Exalted has indicated this by His saying: ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away. But if the right were with them, they would come to him in submission.﴾ [al-Nur: 48-49].

(p-17) Some scholars said: ﴿Every time it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾ means: when Allah bestows upon them wealth and well-being, they say, "This religion is true; nothing has touched us since we adhered to it but good." ﴿And when darkness falls over them, they stand still﴾ means: if poverty, illness, or the birth of daughters rather than sons befalls them, they say, "This has only befallen us because of the ill omen of this religion," and they apostatize from it. This interpretation is supported by the Exalted's saying: ﴿And among people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good touches him, he is content with it, but if trial strikes him, he turns back on his face; he has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the clear loss.﴾ [al-Hajj: 11].

Some scholars said: its illumination for them is their knowledge of some of the truth from it, and its darkening over them is the doubt that occurs to them regarding it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 21:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous﴾, ﴿who made for you the earth a bed and the sky a canopy, and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾.

In this verse He points to three proofs of resurrection after death, and He explains them in detail in other verses. The first: the creation of people at the beginning, indicated by His saying ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you﴾, because the first origination is the greatest proof of the second origination. He has clarified this in many verses:

• such as His saying: ﴿And it is He who originates creation, then repeats it﴾ (al-Rum: 27),

• and His saying: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ (al-Anbiya: 104),

• and such as His saying: ﴿They will say, "Who will restore us?" Say, "The One who originated you the first time"﴾ (Ya-Sin: 79),

• and His saying: ﴿Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time"﴾,

• and His saying: ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation? Rather, they are in confusion about a new creation﴾ (Qaf: 15),

• and such as His saying: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about resurrection, then indeed, We created you from dust﴾ (al-Hajj: 5),

• and such as His saying: ﴿And you have already known the first creation﴾ (al-Waqi'ah: 62).

For this reason He mentioned that whoever denies resurrection has forgotten the first origination, as in His saying: ﴿And he presents for Us an example and forgets his creation﴾ (Ya-Sin: 78), and His saying: ﴿And man says, "When I have died, will I really be brought forth alive?" Does man not remember that We created him before, while he was nothing?﴾ (Maryam: 66-67). Then He based the argument upon it in His saying: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾ (Maryam: 68), and other verses.

The second proof: the creation of the heavens and the earth, indicated by His saying: ﴿who made for you the earth a bed and the sky a canopy﴾ (p-18), because they are among the greatest of creatures, and whoever is able to create the greatest is more able to create what is less, a fortiori. Allah, exalted is He, has clarified this proof in many verses:

• such as His saying: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ (Ghafir: 57),

• and His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes, and He is the Knowing Creator﴾ (Ya-Sin: 81),

• and His saying: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes﴾ (al-Ahqaf: 33),

• and His saying: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the likes of them?﴾ (al-Isra': 99),

• and His saying: ﴿Are you more difficult to create or is the sky? He constructed it; He raised its height and proportioned it﴾ (al-Nazi'at: 27),

and other verses.

The third proof: the revival of the earth after its death, for it is among the greatest evidences for resurrection after death, as He indicated here by His saying: ﴿and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾, and He explained it in many verses:

• such as His saying: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth stilled, but when We send down upon it water, it stirs and swells. Indeed, He who revived it is the Reviver of the dead. Indeed, He is over all things competent﴾ (Fussilat: 39),

• and His saying: ﴿And We gave life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the emergence﴾ (Qaf: 11), meaning: your emergence from your graves alive after you were bones decayed.

• and His saying: ﴿And He brings the earth to life after its death. And thus will you be brought forth﴾ (al-Rum: 19),

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land and send down water thereby and bring forth from it all kinds of fruits. Thus do We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember﴾ (al-A'raf: 57),

and other verses.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 23:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are in doubt concerning what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾, He did not here explicitly name this noble servant, upon whom be the blessings and peace of Allah, but He named him in another place, which is His saying: ﴿And who believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad﴾ [Muhammad: 2], upon whom be the blessings and peace of Allah.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 24:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾

"The stones": many scholars said that they are stones of sulphur (kibrit). Others said that they are the idols that they used to worship. This view is clarified and supported by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾, the verse.

This verse indicates that this Fire was known to them; the evidence for this is the definite article of previous mention (al-'ahdiyyah, the article indicating a known referent). The Exalted said in Surah "at-Tahrim": ﴿Save yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾ [at-Tahrim: 6].

So the indefiniteness of "Fire" here indicates that it was not known to them with these attributes. The way to reconcile this is that they did not know that among its attributes is that men and stones are its fuel. Then the verse of "at-Tahrim" was revealed, and they came to know this attribute of the Fire from it. Then, since it was known to them, the verse of "al-Baqarah" was revealed, in which "the Fire" is made definite by the article of previous mention, because it is previously referred to for them in the verse of "at-Tahrim."

Al-Baydawi and al-Khatib mentioned this reconciliation in their tafsirs, and they claimed that the verse of "at-Tahrim" was revealed in Makkah. The apparent sense of the Qur'an indicates this reconciliation, because the definiteness of "the Fire" here by the article of previous mention indicates a prior known reference, and the relative pronoun with its clause is evidence of previous reference and not of intending the genus. This does not contradict the fact that Surah "at-Tahrim" is Madani, and that the apparent view is that it was revealed after "al-Baqarah."

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that a verse may be Makki within a Madani surah, and the reverse, as is permissible.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 25:

﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds: that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow.﴾

He does not specify here the kinds of these rivers, but he specifies them in His saying: ﴿Therein are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to drinkers, and rivers of purified honey.﴾ [Muhammad: 15].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for them therein are purified spouses.﴾

He does not specify here the attributes of those spouses, but He specifies their beautiful attributes in other verses:

- such as His saying: ﴿And with them are women limiting their glances, [with] wide, lovely eyes﴾ [al-Saffat: 48];
- and His saying: ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 58];
- and His saying: ﴿And [with them are] fair ones with wide, lovely eyes, like preserved pearls﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 22, 23];
- and His saying: ﴿And full-breasted women of equal age﴾ [al-Naba': 33].

And [there are] other verses that clarify the beauty of their attributes. The word "azwaj" (spouses) is the plural of "zawj" without the feminine "ha'" in Classical Arabic (al-lughah al-fusha), while "zawjah" (wife) with the "ha'" is also a valid usage, not a grammatical error (lahn), as some have claimed.

In the hadith of Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, she is my wife" (zawjati). Narrated by Muslim.

From its evidence is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

*Long meter (al-Tawil)*

"Indeed, whoever strives to corrupt my wife
is like one who runs to a lion of the thicket, so that he may be its prey."

And the saying of another:

*Full meter (al-Kamil)*

"My daughters wept from their grief for them, and my wife [wept],
and the travelers toward me, then they parted."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾

Here He does not specify what it is that He commanded to be joined. However, He indicated that among it are the ties of kinship (al-arham), in His saying: ﴿So would you, if you were to take charge, cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ [Muhammad: 22].

And He indicated in another place that among it is belief in all the Messengers, so it is not permissible to sever some of them from others in that regard by believing in some of them and not in the others. This is in His saying: ﴿And they say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and they intend to adopt a way in between. Those are the disbelievers, truly.﴾ [An-Nisa': 150-151].

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿هو الَّذِي خَلَقَ لَكم ما في الأرْضِ جَمِيعًا ثُمَّ اسْتَوى إلى السَّماءِ﴾

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth; then He turned to the heaven﴾. Its apparent meaning is that everything on the earth was created in actuality before the heaven. But He explained in another place that what is meant by His creating it before the heaven is its determination (taqdir), and the Arabs call determination "creation" (khalq), as in the verse of Zuhayr:

؎Indeed you cut (tafri) what you have made, while some of the people make but do not cut

And that is in His saying: ﴿And He determined therein its sustenance﴾ [Fussilat: 10]. Then He said: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Baqarah: 29].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author (al-Mu'allif) said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He is the One who created for you all that is on the earth; then He turned to the heaven﴾, to the end of the verse.

This verse indicates that the creation of the earth was before the creation of the heaven, by the evidence of the particle "thumma" (then), which is for sequence and separation. Likewise the verse of "Ha Mim, the Prostration" (Surat as-Sajdah) also indicates that the earth was created before the heaven, because He said in it: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days?﴾ [Fussilat: 9], up to His saying: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven, and it was smoke﴾, to the end of the verse [Fussilat: 11]. Yet the verse of "an-Nazi'at" indicates that the spreading of the earth (dahw al-ard) was after the creation of the heaven, because He said in it: ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He constructed it﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 27]. (p-206) Then He said: ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 30].

Know first that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about reconciling the verse of "as-Sajdah" with the verse of "an-Nazi'at", and he answered that Allah created the earth first, before the heaven, not spread out (madhuwwah). Then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens in two days, then He spread out the earth after that and placed in it the mountains, the rivers and other things. So the origin of the creation of the earth is before the creation of the heaven, while its spreading out with its mountains, its trees and the like is after the creation of the heaven. What supports this is that He said: ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ and did not say "He created it", then He explained His spreading of it with His saying: ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 31]. This reconciliation by which Ibn 'Abbas reconciled these two verses is clear, free of difficulty, and understood from the apparent meaning of the Great Qur'an. However, a difficulty arises from this verse of al-Baqarah, and its clarification is that Ibn 'Abbas reconciled by saying that the creation of the earth was before the creation of the heaven, and its spreading out with what is in it was after the creation of the heaven.

In this verse there is an explicit statement that all that is in the earth was created before the creation of the heaven, because He said in it: ﴿He is the One who created for you all that is on the earth; then He turned to the heaven﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Anbiya': 29]. I spent a long time thinking about the solution to this difficulty, until Allah guided me to it one day, and I understood it from the Great Qur'an. Its clarification is that this difficulty is removed in two respects, each of which is indicated by a verse of the Qur'an:

The first: What is meant by the creation of all that is in the earth before the creation of the heaven is the linguistic creation, which is determination (taqdir), not the creation in actuality, which is bringing into existence from non-existence. The Arabs call determination "creation", and from this is the saying of Zuhayr:

؎Indeed you cut what you have made, while some of the people make but do not cut

The evidence that what is meant by this creation is determination is that He explicitly stated this in Surat Fussilat, where He said: ﴿And He determined therein its sustenance﴾ [Fussilat: 10], then He said: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven, and it was smoke﴾, to the end of the verse [Fussilat: 11].

The second: When He created the earth unspread, and it is the origin of everything in it, everything in it was as if it had been created in actuality because its origin existed in actuality. The evidence from the Qur'an that the existence of the origin makes it possible to apply the term "creation" to the branch, even if it does not yet exist in actuality, is:

(p-207) His saying: ﴿And We certainly created you, then We fashioned you, then We said to the angels﴾ [al-A'raf: 11].

His saying: ﴿We created you, then We fashioned you﴾ means: by Our creating and fashioning of your father Adam, who is your origin.

Some scholars reconciled the meaning of His saying: ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 30] as "along with that" (ma'a dhalik), so the word "ba'da" (after) here means "ma'a" (with). Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Violent, and after that, of illegitimate birth﴾ [al-Qalam: 13].

Accordingly, there is no difficulty in the verse. This view is supported by the anomalous reading (al-qira'ah ash-shadhdhah), and Mujahid recited with it: "And the earth along with that He spread out." Others reconciled it with weak views, because they are based on the premise that the creation of the heaven was before the earth, which contradicts what is verified. Among them is the view that "thumma" means "wa" (and), and among them that it is for sequence in mention (at-tartib adh-dhikri), as in His saying: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Balad: 17].

**

His saying: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾, to the end of the verse.

Here Allah the Exalted used the singular word "as-sama'" (the heaven), and He returned to it a pronoun in the plural form in His saying "fa-sawwahunna" (and He made them). There are two explanations for combining a plural pronoun with its singular referent:

The first: What is meant by "as-sama'" is its genus, which applies to the seven heavens. In this case the "al" is the "al" of genus (al-jinsiyyah).

The second: There is no disagreement among the people of the Arabic language that a singular noun may be used to mean the plural, whether it is definite, indefinite, or in construct. This is frequent in the Great Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs. Among its examples in the Qur'an, where the word is definite, is His saying: ﴿and you believe in the Book, all of it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119], meaning "in the Books, all of them", by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Each believed in Allah, His angels, His books﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285].

• And His saying: ﴿And say: I believe in what Allah has sent down of Book﴾ [ash-Shura: 15].
• His saying: ﴿The host will be routed and will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45], meaning "the backs" (al-adbar), as is clear.
• His saying: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the high chamber﴾ [al-Furqan: 75], meaning "the chambers", by the evidence of His saying: ﴿For them are chambers above them, built chambers﴾ [az-Zumar: 20].
• His saying: ﴿And they will be secure in the chambers﴾ [Saba': 37].
• His saying: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angel, rank upon rank﴾ [al-Fajr: 22], meaning "the angels", by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of cloud, with the angels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210].
• His saying: ﴿Or the children who have not yet attained knowledge of hidden aspects of women﴾, to the end of the verse [an-Nur: 31], meaning "the children who have not attained".
• His saying: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾ (p-208) to the end of the verse [al-Munafiqun: 4], meaning "the enemies".

Among its examples where the word is indefinite is His saying: ﴿Indeed the righteous will be in gardens and rivers﴾ [al-Qamar: 54], meaning "and rivers", by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Therein are rivers of water unchanged﴾, to the end of the verse [Muhammad: 15].
• And His saying: ﴿And make us a leader for the righteous﴾ [al-Furqan: 74], meaning "leaders".
• His saying: ﴿Scoffing at it by night, talking nonsense﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 67], meaning "those who scoff".
• His saying: ﴿Then We bring you forth as a child﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], meaning "as children".
• His saying: ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 136], meaning "between them".
• His saying: ﴿And excellent are those as companions﴾ [an-Nisa': 69], meaning "as companions".
• His saying: ﴿And if you are in a state of major impurity, purify yourselves﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], meaning "in a state of major impurity" in dual or plural form.
• His saying: ﴿And the angels after that are supporters﴾ [at-Tahrim: 4], meaning "supporters", as the context in all of these indicates the plural. Sibawayh (Sibawayh, the grammarian) cited this with His saying: ﴿But if they give you willingly of it, a portion﴾ [an-Nisa': 4], meaning "portions" (anfusan).

Among its examples where the word is in construct is His saying: ﴿Indeed these are my guests﴾ [al-Hijr: 68], meaning "my guests", and His saying: ﴿Let those who oppose his command beware﴾ [an-Nur: 63], meaning "his commands".

Sibawayh cited for the use of the singular with the meaning of the plural the words of the poet, who is 'Alqamah ibn 'Abadah at-Tamimi:

؎Therein are the carcasses of the exhausted, as for their bones they are white, and as for their skins they are hard

meaning "and as for their skins, they are hard" in the plural.

He also cited for it the words of another:

؎Eat in part of your bellies, that you may be spared, for your time is a lean time

meaning "in some of your bellies".

Among his evidences is the saying of 'Aqil ibn 'Ullafah al-Muzanni:

؎The Banu Fazarah were the worst paternal cousins, and I was to them like the worst of the Banu al-Akhinah

meaning "the worst of paternal cousins".

And the saying of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas as-Sulami:

؎So we said: Submit, for we are your brothers, and the breasts are free of rancor

(p-209) meaning "for we are your brothers", and the saying of another:

؎O my blamers, do not desire to blame me, for the blamers have no command over me

meaning "they have no commanders over me".

This use applies regularly to the modifying of a noun by a verbal noun (masdar), as in the saying of Zuhayr:

؎When a people quarrel, their chiefs say: They are between us, they are content and they are just

And because of observing this, the words "as-sam'" (hearing), "at-tarf" (glance) and "ad-dayf" (guest) are not used in the plural in the Qur'an, because their origin is verbal nouns, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7].
• His saying: ﴿Their glance does not return to them, and their hearts are void﴾ [Ibrahim: 43].
• His saying: ﴿They look with a furtive glance﴾ [ash-Shura: 45].
• His saying: ﴿Indeed these are my guests﴾ [al-Hijr: 68].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a khalifah (successor)"﴾ ... the verse. Concerning His saying "khalifah," scholars have offered two interpretations:

The first: that what is meant by the khalifah is our father Adam, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace, because he is the khalifah of Allah on His earth, in carrying out His commands. It was also said: because he became a successor (khalaf) to the jinn who used to inhabit the earth before him; according to this, khalifah is on the pattern fa'ilah in the sense of fa'il. It was also said: because when he dies, someone after him succeeds him; according to this, it is from fa'ilah in the sense of maf'ul. That the khalifah is Adam is the apparent meaning that comes immediately to mind from the context of the verse.

The second: that His saying "khalifah" is singular but intended as plural, i.e., khala'if (successors). This is the view chosen by Ibn Kathir. A singular noun that is a noun of genus (ism jins) is frequently used in Arabic speech with a plural meaning intended, as in:

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be among gardens and rivers﴾ [al-Qamar: 54], meaning "and rivers," as evidenced by His saying: ﴿therein are rivers of water unaltered﴾ [Muhammad: 15], the verse.
• And His saying: ﴿and make us an imam (leader) for the righteous﴾ [al-Furqan: 74].
• And His saying: ﴿And if they give you willingly of it, a thing of it, [as] a gift﴾ [an-Nisa': 4].

A parallel to this in Arabic speech is the saying of 'Aqil ibn 'Ullafah al-Muri:

Verse (al-Wafir):
"The Banu Fazarah were the worst of paternal cousins, and you were to them like the worst of our brothers."

And the saying of al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami (al-Wafir):
"We said: 'Submit, for we are your brothers,' and the breasts have been cleansed of rancor."

Sibawayh recited for him the saying of 'Alqamah ibn 'Abadah al-Tamimi (al-Tawil):
"In it are the carcasses of the exhausted; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their skins, they are hard."

And the saying of another (al-Wafir):
"Eat in part of your bellies, that you may abstain, for your time is a time of hunger."

Since this noble verse admits of the two mentioned interpretations, know that other verses indicate the second interpretation, namely that what is meant by khalifah is the successors from Adam and his offspring, not Adam (p-21) himself alone, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?"﴾ the verse [al-Baqarah: 30].

It is known that Adam, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace, is not one who causes corruption therein, nor one who sheds blood.

And like His saying: ﴿It is He who has made you successors upon the earth﴾ the verse [Fatir: 39],
and His saying: ﴿And it is He who has made you successors of the earth﴾ the verse [al-An'am: 165],
and His saying: ﴿and makes you successors﴾ the verse [an-Naml: 62].
And similar verses.

This can be answered by saying that what is meant by khalifah is Adam, and that Allah informed the angels that there would come from his offspring those who would do that corruption and shedding of blood; so they said what they said. And that what is meant by Adam's khilafah is the legislated khilafah, while the khilafah of his offspring is more general than that, namely that a generation passes from among them and another generation succeeds it.

* *

Admonition
Al-Qurtubi said in his commentary on this noble verse: This verse is a foundation for appointing an imam and khalifah who is listened to and obeyed, so that the word is united through him and the rulings of the khalifah are implemented. There is no disagreement among the Ummah, nor among the scholars, regarding the obligation of this, except what is reported from al-Asamm, when he was deaf to the Shari'ah. Until he said: Our evidence is the saying of Allah, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a khalifah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Dawud, indeed We have made you a khalifah upon the earth﴾ [Sad: 26]. And He said: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe among you and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth﴾ [an-Nur: 55], meaning: He will make from among them khulafa' (successors), along with other verses.

And the Companions unanimously agreed upon giving precedence to al-Siddiq after a difference that occurred between the Muhajirun and the Ansar at the Saqifah of Banu Sa'idah regarding the appointment, until the Ansar said: "From us an amir and from you an amir." Abu Bakr and 'Umar and the Muhajirun repelled them from that, and said to them: "The Arabs will not submit except to this tribe of Quraysh," and they related to them the report on that, so they returned and obeyed Quraysh. If the imamate were not obligatory, neither in Quraysh nor in others, this debate and dialogue over it would not have been valid; and someone would have said: "It is not obligatory, neither in Quraysh nor in others. There is no benefit to your dispute over a matter that is not obligatory." Furthermore, when al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, was approaching death, he designated 'Umar for the imamate, and no one said to him: "This is a matter not obligatory upon us or upon you." This indicates its obligation, and that it is a pillar of the religion by which the Muslims are sustained. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds. End of quotation from al-Qurtubi.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: It is clear and known from the necessity of the religion that Muslims are obligated to appoint an imam through whom the word is united, and through whom the rulings of Allah are implemented on His earth. No one dissented in this except one who is not regarded, such as Abu Bakr al-Asamm the Mu'tazili, who was mentioned in al-Qurtubi's words, and like Dirar and Hisham al-Futi and their likes.

Most scholars hold that the obligation of the major imamate is by way of the Shari'ah, as the aforementioned verse and its like indicate, and the consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Also, Allah, may He be exalted, restrains by the authority what He does not restrain by the Qur'an, as He said: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance that people may maintain justice. And We sent down iron, wherein is great military might and benefits for the people﴾, because His saying: ﴿and We sent down iron, wherein is great military might﴾ contains an allusion to the use of the sword when refusal occurs after the establishment of the proof.

The Imamiyyah said: the imamate is obligatory by reason, not by the Shari'ah.

And from al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Jahiz, and al-Balkhi: it is obligatory by both reason and Shari'ah together. Know that what the Imamiyyah fabricate of falsehoods against Abu Bakr and 'Umar and their likes among the Companions, and what they fabricate concerning the Twelve Imams, and the hidden awaited infallible Imam, and similar superstitions and their baseless lies, all of it is false and has no basis.

If you wish to verify this, then refer to the book "Minhaj al-Sunnah al-Nabawiyyah fi Naqd Kalam al-Shi'ah al-Qadariyyah" by the great scholar Shaykh Taqi al-Din Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah, for he has presented in it what cannot be surpassed of decisive proofs and shining evidences refuting all those fabricated superstitions. When you have verified the obligation of appointing the supreme imam upon the Muslims, know that the imamate is established for him by one of several matters:

The first: that the Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly designates that so-and-so is the imam, in which case the imamate is established for him by that.

Some scholars said: the imamate of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, is of this category, because the Prophet's (ﷺ) putting him forward to lead the prayer, which is the most important matter, contains an indication of putting him forward for the major imamate, and this is evident.

The second: the agreement of the people of loosening and binding (ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd) upon his allegiance.

Some scholars said: the imamate of Abu Bakr is of this category, due to the consensus of the people of loosening and binding among the Muhajirun and the Ansar upon it after the disagreement, and no account is taken of the non-consent of some of them, as occurred from Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, may Allah be pleased with him, in his not accepting the allegiance to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.

The third: that the preceding khalifah designates him as successor, as occurred from Abu Bakr to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

Of this category is 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, making the khilafah a shura among six of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he died while being pleased with them.

The fourth: that he overpowers the people by his sword and seizes the khilafah by force, until the matter is firmly established for him and the people submit to him, because revolting against him at that time would involve splitting the unity of the Muslims and shedding their blood.

Some scholars said: Of this category is the standing of 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan against 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, and his killing him in Makkah at the hand of al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, so the matter became firmly established for him, as Ibn Qudamah said in "al-Mughni."

And among the scholars is one who says: the imamate is established for him by the allegiance of one person, and they considered 'Umar's giving allegiance to Abu Bakr at the Saqifah of Banu Sa'idah to be of this kind, and al-Qurtubi inclined to it. Imam al-Haramayn related consensus upon it. It was also said: by the allegiance of four, and it was said other than that.

This is the summary of the scholars' words regarding what the major imamate is established by. The implication of the words of Shaykh Taqi al-Din Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah in "al-Minhaj" is that it is established only by the allegiance of one whose strength is firm, by whom he is able to implement the rulings of the imamate, because one who has no capacity for that, like ordinary people, is not an imam.

* *

Know that the supreme imam must fulfill conditions: The first: that he be of Quraysh. Quraysh are the descendants of Fihr ibn Malik, and it was said: the descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah. So the Fihri is undisputedly Qurashi. As for one who is among the descendants of Malik ibn al-Nadr or the descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah, there is disagreement over whether he is Qurashi or not. And whoever is from the descendants of Kinanah other than al-Nadr is undisputedly not Qurashi.

(p-24) Al-Qurtubi said in his commentary on this noble verse, in mentioning the conditions of the imam: The first: that he be from the pure lineage of Quraysh, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The imams are from Quraysh," and there has been disagreement regarding this.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The disagreement that al-Qurtubi mentioned regarding the stipulation that the supreme imam be Qurashi is weak. The sound hadiths indicate the precedence of Quraysh in the imamate over others, and the majority of Muslim scholars have agreed upon it.

More than one scholar related consensus upon it. The claim of consensus requires interpretation of what Imam Ahmad reported from 'Umar, with a chain whose narrators are trustworthy, that he said: "If my term reaches me while Abu 'Ubaydah is alive, I would appoint him as successor." He mentioned the hadith, and in it: "If my term reaches me and Abu 'Ubaydah has died, I would appoint Mu'adh ibn Jabal."

It is known that Mu'adh was not Qurashi, and its interpretation is by the claim that consensus was formed after 'Umar, or that he changed his opinion to agree with the majority. Thus, the stipulation that he be Qurashi is the truth. However, the legal texts indicate that this obligatory precedence of theirs in the imamate is conditioned upon their establishing the religion and obeying Allah and His Messenger. If they oppose the command of Allah, then others who obey Allah, may He be exalted, and implement His commands, are more deserving than them.

Among the evidences indicating this is what al-Bukhari reported in his "Sahih" from Mu'awiyah, where he said: Chapter: The Commanders are from Quraysh. Abu al-Yaman narrated to us, Shu'ayb informed us, from al-Zuhri, who said: "Muhammad ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im used to narrate that it reached Mu'awiyah, while he was with him in a delegation of Quraysh, that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr was narrating that there would be a king from Qahtan. So he became angry, stood up, praised Allah with what He is worthy of, then said: To proceed: It has reached me that men among you narrate hadiths that are not in the Book of Allah, nor transmitted from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and those are your ignorant ones. Beware of wishful thinking which misleads its people, for I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'This matter will remain in Quraysh; no one opposes them except that Allah casts him on his face, as long as they establish the religion.'" End of quotation from the Sahih of al-Bukhari, in its wording.

The point of evidence in it is his saying (ﷺ): "as long as they establish the religion," because the particle "ma" in it is a temporal verbal (masdariyyah zarfiyyah) particle, restricting his saying: "This matter is in Quraysh." The meaning, stated plainly: this matter is in Quraysh for the duration of their establishing the religion, and its implication: if they do not establish it, it will not remain among them. This is the verification, beyond doubt, of the meaning of the hadith.

* *

[p. 25]

Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari* (*Fath al-Bari*, the commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari), in discussing the hadith of Mu'awiyah, the following: "A report similar to what occurred in the hadith of Mu'awiyah has also come from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. Muhammad ibn Ishaq mentioned it in his large book, relating the story of the Saqifah of Bani Sa'idah and the pledge of allegiance to Abu Bakr. In it, Abu Bakr said: 'Indeed, this affair belongs to Quraysh, so long as they obeyed Allah and remained steadfast in His command.'

The hadiths I have referred to come in three types. The first: a warning of being cursed if they do not uphold what has been commanded, as in the hadiths I mentioned in the chapter before this one, where he said: 'The rulers are from Quraysh. They have three rights: when they judge, they judge justly...' (the hadith continues), and in it: 'Whoever among them does not do that, upon him is the curse of Allah.' There is nothing in this that requires the affair to be removed from them.

The second: a warning that they will be subjected to someone who greatly harms them. In the *Musnad* of Ahmad and in the *Musnad* of Abu Ya'la, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'You are the people of this affair so long as you do not innovate. When you change, Allah will send upon you someone who will beat you as a stick is beaten.' Its narrators are trustworthy, except that it is narrated by Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah ibn Mas'ud from his paternal uncle Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and he did not meet him. This is the transmission of Salih ibn Kaysan from Ubayd Allah. Habib ibn Abi Thabit disagreed with him: he narrated it from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah, from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari, and its wording is: 'This affair will not cease to be among you while you are its governors'..., (the hadith continues).

There is a question about Ubayd Allah's hearing from Abu Mas'ud, which depends on the disagreement over the year of Abu Mas'ud's death. It has a supporting report in the *mursal* (a report in which the Successor omits the companion) of Ata' ibn Yasar, which al-Shafi'i and al-Bayhaqi recorded through his chain with a sound isnad to Ata'. Its wording is that he (ﷺ) said to Quraysh: 'You have the greater right to this affair so long as you are upon the truth, unless you turn away from it, and then you will be bent (lit. struck) as this palm-stalk is bent.' There is no explicit statement in this that the affair is removed from them, though it does hint at it.

The third: permission to rise against them and fight them, and an announcement that the affair is removed from them, as al-Tayalisi and al-Tabarani recorded from the hadith of Thawban, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Be upright toward Quraysh so long as they are upright toward you. If they are not upright, then place your swords on your shoulders and eradicate their green (i.e., their wealth and strength). If you do not do that, then be farmers, wretched ones.' Its narrators are trustworthy, except that there is a break in it, because Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd did not hear from Thawban. It has a supporting report in al-Tabarani from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir with a similar meaning." (End of the quotation.)

[p. 26]

Ahmad recorded, from the hadith of Dhu Mikhbar (with a kasrah on the mim, a sukun on the mu'jamah letter, and a fathah on the muwahhadah letter after them, followed by a ra'), who was the nephew of al-Najashi, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This affair was among Himyar, then Allah took it from them and placed it among Quraysh, and it will return to them." Its isnad is good, and it is a strong supporting report for the hadith of the Qahtani, for Himyar traces its lineage to Qahtan. By this it is strengthened that the implication (mafhum) of the hadith of Mu'awiyah, "so long as they establish the religion," is that if they do not establish the religion, the affair is removed from them. End of the quotation.

Know that the statement of Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As, which Mu'awiyah rejected in the aforementioned hadith, that "there will be a king from Qahtan," if Abd Allah ibn Amr, may Allah be pleased with both of them, meant by it the Qahtani whose kingship was established by a sound report, then there is no basis for rejecting it, since it is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will not come until a man from Qahtan emerges, driving people with his staff." Al-Bukhari recorded it in the *Book of Tribulations*, in the chapter "Changing of the Times until they worship idols," and in the *Book of Virtues*, in the chapter "Mentioning Qahtan." Muslim recorded it in the *Book of Tribulations and Signs of the Hour*, in the chapter "The Hour will not come until a man passes by the grave of a man and wishes that he were in the place of the dead man because of the trial."

This Qahtani's name is not known to most scholars. Some scholars said his name is Jahjah, and some said his name is Shu'ayb ibn Salih. Ibn Hajar, in discussing this hadith of the Qahtani, said the following: "It was mentioned in the *Book of Hajj* that the House will be performed for pilgrimage after the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj. The reconciliation between that and the hadith 'The Hour will not come until the House is no longer visited for pilgrimage, and Dhu al-Suwaykatayn from Abyssinia will destroy the Ka'bah' has also been mentioned. From this it follows that when the Abyssinians destroy the House, the Qahtani will emerge against them and destroy them; that the believers before that will make pilgrimage in the time of Isa after the emergence and destruction of Ya'juj and Ma'juj; and that the wind which takes the souls of the believers will begin with those who remain after Isa, and the people of Yemen will be the last after it." 

It is possible that this is among what the statement "Faith is Yamani" is interpreted by: that is, faith will be the last to be lost from the whole earth, and it will return to Yemen after its disappearance from all the earth. Muslim recorded the hadith of the Qahtani right after the hadith of the destruction of the Ka'bah by Dhu al-Suwaykatayn, so perhaps he alluded to this. End of his words verbatim, and Allah knows best, and to attribute knowledge to Him is safest.

Second: among the conditions of the supreme Imam is that he be male, and there is no disagreement about this among scholars. [p. 27] This is indicated by what is established in the *Sahih of al-Bukhari* and others from the hadith of Abu Bakrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that when the Prophet (ﷺ) learned that the Persians had made the daughter of Kisra their ruler, he said: "A people will never prosper who have entrusted their affairs to a woman."

Third: among the conditions of the supreme Imam is that he be free. He cannot be a slave, and there is no disagreement about this among scholars.

If it is objected that there is in the Sahih what indicates the permissibility of a slave's leadership, for al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Listen and obey, even if an Abyssinian slave with a head like a raisin is appointed over you." 

And in Muslim, from the hadith of Umm al-Husayn: "Listen and obey, even if a slave is appointed over you who leads you by the Book of Allah."

Also in Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him: "My beloved friend (ﷺ) enjoined me to obey and listen, even if he is an Abyssinian slave with mutilated limbs."

The answer comes in several aspects. The first: an example may be given with something that does not actually occur in existence.
