The mention of an Abyssinian slave is for the sake of emphasizing the command to obey, even though it is not conceivable in the Shari'ah that he would hold such a position. Ibn Hajar mentioned this answer from al-Khattabi. This aspect resembles the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers.﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 81], according to one of the interpretations.

The second aspect: that by the employment of the Abyssinian slave is meant that he be appointed as a governor by the supreme Imam over some regions, and this is the most apparent of the aspects. He is therefore not the supreme Imam.

The third aspect: that the term "slave" was applied to him in consideration of his previous condition of being a slave, even though at the time of his appointment he was free. Its parallel is the application of the term "orphan" to an adult in consideration of his previous state, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [An-Nisa: 2], and so on. All of this applies to what occurs by way of choice. As for if a slave seizes power in actuality by force, then obeying him is obligatory, to extinguish strife and to preserve blood, so long as he does not command disobedience, as the indication of this was mentioned earlier.

The meaning of "raisin" in this hadith is a single raisin, the known edible raisin made from grapes when they dry. The purpose of the comparison is belittling and describing his appearance as ugly, because if listening and obeying are obligatory for one in such a condition, that indicates obligation in every state except in disobedience, as [p. 28] will come. The words of the Prophet (ﷺ), "as if his head were a raisin," resemble the words of a poet satirizing a black-skinned person:

"Dirty garments, as if the skin of his head had been planted, and its two sides grew fenugreek (fulfulan)."

Fourth: among its conditions is that he be an adult. Therefore it is not permissible for a child to be imam, by consensus (ijma'), because he is unable to bear the burdens of the caliphate.

Fifth: that he be sane. Therefore it is not permissible for an insane person or an imbecile (ma'tuh) to be imam, and there is no dispute about this.

Sixth: that he be just (adl). Therefore it is not permissible for a wrongdoer (fasiq) to be imam. Some scholars cited as evidence the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people." [Abraham] said, "And of my descendants?" He said, "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers."﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 124]. Included in the condition of justice is the condition of Islam, because one who is not Muslim cannot be just.

Seventh: that he be among those who are qualified to be a judge among the judges of the Muslims, a mujtahid who can dispense with seeking the rulings of others regarding events.

Eighth: that he be sound in his limbs, not disabled, nor blind, and so forth. The following two last conditions, namely knowledge and physical soundness, are supported by the words of Allah, the Exalted, concerning Saul (Talut): ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and increased him abundantly in knowledge and physical stature.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 247].

Ninth: that he be experienced and possess sound judgment regarding matters of war, the management of armies, guarding the frontiers, protecting the realm of the Muslims, deterring the community, exacting retribution from the wrongdoer, and taking back from the oppressor for the oppressed. As Laqit al-Iyadi said (Basit meter):

"And entrust your affair to Allah, may your well-being be safe, to one of wide reach with the arm, who is informed in matters of war."

Tenth: that he be one who is not moved by softness (ruqqah) in establishing the hudud (the fixed penalties), nor fearful of striking necks or cutting limbs. The consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, on the fact that the Imam must be such indicates this. Al-Qurtubi said this.

* * *

Issues:

The first: If the supreme Imam becomes a wrongdoer, or calls to an innovation, does this become a reason for his removal and for rising against him, or not? Some scholars said: If he becomes a wrongdoer or a caller to innovation, it is permissible to rise against him to depose him. The verified position, about which there is no doubt, is that it is not permissible to rise against him to depose him, unless he commits open disbelief (kufr bawah), concerning which there is a proof from Allah.

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded in their two Sahihs, from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to listen and obey in ease and hardship, in our willingness and reluctance, and in hardship and ease, and to not dispute the affair with its people. He said: 'Except that you see open disbelief with you, concerning which you have a proof from Allah.'"

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The best of your imams are those whom you love and who love you, and for whom you pray and who pray for you. The worst of your imams are those whom you hate and who hate you, and whom you curse and who curse you." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, should we not oppose them at that time?" He said: "No, so long as they establish the prayer among you. No, so long as they establish the prayer among you. But whoever is governed by a ruler, and he sees him committing something of the disobedience to Allah, then let him hate what he does of the disobedience to Allah, and let him not withdraw his hand from obedience."

Also in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There will be rulers; you will recognize some and deny some. Whoever recognizes is free of blame, whoever denies is safe, but whoever is pleased and follows (is the one who is at fault)." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, should we not fight them?" He said: "No, so long as they pray."

The two Shaykhs recorded in their two Sahihs, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sees something he dislikes in his ruler, let him be patient, for no one separates from the community by a hand's span and then dies, except that he dies a death of the Jahiliyyah (Age of Ignorance)."

Muslim recorded in his Sahih, from the hadith of Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever removes his hand from obedience will meet Allah on the Day of Resurrection with no proof for him, and whoever dies without a pledge of allegiance on his neck dies a death of the Jahiliyyah." The hadiths on this are numerous.

[p. 30] These texts indicate the prohibition of rising against a ruler, even if he commits what is impermissible, unless he commits manifest disbelief (*kufr bawah*) that has been established by clear legal proof from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ. That is, it is evident and apparent, with no ambiguity in it.

Al-Ma'mun, al-Mu'tasim and al-Wathiq called people to the innovation (*bid'ah*) of saying that the Qur'an is created, and they punished the scholars on account of it with killing, beating, imprisonment and various kinds of humiliation. No one held that it was obligatory to rebel against them because of this. The matter continued for some fifteen years, until al-Mutawakkil assumed the caliphate, abolished the inquisition (*mihnah*), and ordered the Sunnah to be made manifest.

Know that all Muslims have agreed that there is no obedience to an imam or to anyone else in disobedience to Allah the Exalted. The sound and explicit ahadith that contain no ambiguity and no objection have come with this, such as the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Listening and obedience are incumbent upon the Muslim person in what he loves and in what he dislikes, so long as he is not commanded to commit an act of disobedience. If he is commanded to commit an act of disobedience, then there is no listening and no obedience." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim, and by Abu Dawud.

And from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the detachment whose commander ordered them to enter the fire: "If they had entered it, they would never have come out of it. Obedience is only in what is right." In the Noble Book is the verse: ﴿and they will not disobey you in what is right﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 12].

The second issue: Is it permissible to appoint two caliphs, each of whom is independent of the other? On this there are three opinions.

The first: the opinion of the Karramiyyah, that it is permissible absolutely, arguing that 'Ali and Mu'awiyah were both imams whose obedience was obligatory upon those with them, and that this leads to each of them being more capable in what is in his hands and more precise in what is under his responsibility. And that since it was permissible to send two prophets in one era without that voiding prophethood, the imamate is more deserving of it.

The second: the opinion of the majority of the scholars of the Muslims, that it is not permissible to have more than one supreme imam. Rather, it is obligatory that he be one, and that no region of the regions be governed except by his appointed governors. They argue by what Muslim related in his *Sahih* from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If allegiance is given to two caliphs, kill the other of them."

And also in Muslim, from the hadith of 'Arfajah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Whoever comes to you while your affair is united under one man, wanting to split your staff or divide your community, then kill him." In another narration: "Then strike him with the sword, whoever he may be."

Also in Muslim, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, may Allah be pleased with them both: "And whoever pledges allegiance to an imam, giving him the handshake of his hand and the fruit of his heart, let him obey him if he can. If another comes disputing with him, then strike the neck of the other." Then he said: My two ears heard it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and my heart retained it.

They refuted the argument of the Karramiyyah, that Mu'awiyah during his dispute with 'Ali did not claim the imamate for himself but claimed the governorship of Syria by appointment from the imams before him. What indicates this is the consensus of the community in their era that the imam is only one of them, not each of them. And that the argument from each being more capable in what is in his hands and more precise in what is under his responsibility, and from the permissibility of sending two prophets at one time, is refuted by his saying ﷺ: "Then kill the other of them." Also, appointing two caliphs leads to discord and the emergence of strife.

The third opinion: a distinction is made. The appointment of two imams is prohibited in one city and in nearby lands, and it is permitted in distant regions such as al-Andalus and Khurasan. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of this noble verse, the following text: "But if the regions are far apart and separated, such as al-Andalus and Khurasan, that is permissible, as its explanation will come, Allah willing." End of quotation, verbatim.

What is referred to in his words is the appointment of two caliphs. Among those who held the permissibility of this is al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq, as Imam al-Haramayn transmitted it from him, and Ibn Kathir transmitted it from him, and al-Qurtubi in his tafsir of this noble verse.

Ibn Kathir said: I say: this resembles the situation of the caliphs: the 'Abbasids in Iraq, the Fatimids in Egypt, and the Umayyads in the Maghrib.

The third issue: may the imam dismiss himself?

Some scholars said: he may. Al-Qurtubi said: The evidence that he may dismiss himself is the statement of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "Dismiss me, dismiss me," and the statement of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them: "We will not dismiss you, nor will we ask you to step down. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ put you forward for our religion, so who would delay you? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was pleased with you for our religion, so should we not be pleased with you?"

He said: Had it not been permissible for him, the Companions would have rejected that from him and said to him: "It is not for you to say this."

Other scholars said: he does not have the right to dismiss himself, because he has taken on the rights of the Muslims, so he has no right to abandon them.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, said: If his dismissal of himself is for a reason that requires it, such as quelling a strife that would have ignited had he not dismissed himself, or because he knows in himself an inability to bear the burdens of the caliphate, then there is no dispute over the permissibility of his dismissing himself. Hence all Muslims have agreed to praise the grandson of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, for dismissing himself and handing over the affair to Mu'awiyah, after the people of Iraq had pledged allegiance to him, in order to preserve the blood of the Muslims. His grandfather, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, praised him for this before it occurred, by saying: "Indeed this son of mine is a master, and perhaps Allah will reconcile through him between two groups of the Muslims." Related by al-Bukhari and others, from the hadith of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.

The fourth issue: is it obligatory to call witnesses to the contract of the imamate?

Some scholars said: it is not obligatory, because requiring witnesses needs evidence from transmitted texts, and there is no evidence for it from them. Other scholars said: it is obligatory to call witnesses to it, lest a claimant allege that the imamate was contracted for him in secret, which would lead to discord and strife.

Those who said that calling witnesses to the contract of the imamate is obligatory said: two witnesses suffice, contrary to al-Jubba'i, who required four witnesses, along with the one who contracts and the one for whom it is contracted. They derived this from 'Umar leaving the matter as a consultation (*shura*) among six, so the affair settled upon one contractor, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, and one contracted for, 'Uthman, and the other four remained as witnesses. The weakness of this derivation is not hidden, as al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir pointed out. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then He presented them to the angels﴾, meaning the named things (al-musammayat) and not the names, as may be imagined from the apparent wording of the verse.

And he indicated that they are the named things by His saying: ﴿Inform Me of the names of these﴾, and so on, as is clear.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what you used to conceal﴾. Here He did not specify what it was that they used to conceal. Some scholars have said: it is what Iblis (Satan) was harboring of arrogance (kibr). According to this view, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Except Iblis. He refused and was arrogant﴾ clarifies it.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 2, verse 34:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾. He does not state here whether He said this to them before the creation of Adam or after his creation. He has, however, made it explicit in Surah al-Hijr and Surah Sad that He said this to them before the creation of Adam. In al-Hijr He said: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay, from black mud altered [and molded]. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My [created] spirit, then fall down to him in prostration"﴾ [verses 28, 29]. In Surah Sad He said: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My [created] spirit, then fall down to him in prostration"﴾ [verses 71, 72].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except Iblis; he refused and was arrogant﴾. He does not state here the cause of his arrogance according to his own claim, but He has explained it in other places, such as His saying: ﴿[Iblis] said, "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay"﴾ [Al-A'raf: 12], and His saying: ﴿[Iblis] said, "I would never prostrate to a human whom You created from clay, from black mud altered [and molded]"﴾ [Al-Hijr: 33].

**Note (tanbih):**

Iblis's reasoning, by which he compared himself to his element, which is fire, and compared Adam to his element, which is clay, and concluded from this that he was better than Adam, is of the same kind. It is not fitting that one be commanded to prostrate to someone who is better than him, in the presence of the explicit text, which is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾. In the terminology of the jurists of legal theory (usuliyyun), this is called fasid al-i'tibar (invalid analogy, i.e., an analogy that is void because it contradicts an established text). To this refers the saying of the author of Mara'i al-Su'ud, in verse:

"Opposition to a text, or to consensus, is what every discerning person calls fasid al-i'tibar."

Therefore, every one who rejects the texts of revelation in favor of analogies has Iblis as his predecessor in this. The analogy of this Iblis, may Allah curse him, is false for three reasons:

The first: it is fasid al-i'tibar, because it contradicts the explicit text, as has been mentioned shortly before.

The second: we do not grant that fire is better than clay. Rather, clay is better than fire, because the nature of fire is lightness, recklessness, corruption and dispersal, while the nature of clay is steadiness and reform. It takes in the seed and gives you back an ear of grain, and takes in the date pit and gives you back a palm tree.

If you wish to know the worth of clay, look at the lush gardens, with their delicious fruits, beautiful flowers and pleasant fragrances, and you will know that clay is better than fire.

The third: even if we grant, for the sake of argument, that fire is better than clay, it does not follow from this that Iblis is better than Adam, because the nobility of the origin does not require the nobility of the branch. Rather, the origin may be noble while the branch is lowly, as the poet said:

"When you boast of fathers who have nobility, we say: 'You have spoken truly, but evil are the sons they begot.'"

And another said:

"The lineage of Hashim avails nothing if the soul is from Bahila."

(p-34)

The author said in (Dafʿ Ihām al-Iḍṭirāb ʿan Āyāt al-Kitāb):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾, and so on.

It may be imagined that this contradicts His saying: ﴿...and eat therefrom freely wherever you will﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35].

The answer is that His saying "uskun" (dwell) is a command to take up residence (al-uskunā), not a command to stillness (al-sukūn), which is the opposite of motion. So the command to take the Garden as a dwelling does not preclude moving about within it and eating from it wherever the two of them wished.

Allah's statement: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾. He did not specify here what these words were, but He specified them in Surah al-A'raf, in His statement: ﴿They said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers."﴾ [the verse 23].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾. He did not specify here what this favour was that He bestowed upon them, but He specified it in other verses,

• such as His saying: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds and sent down upon you the manna and the quail﴾ [al-Baqarah: 57],

• and His saying: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment﴾, to the end of the verse,

• and His saying: ﴿And We wished to confer favour upon those who were oppressed in the land and make them leaders and make them inheritors, and to establish them in the land and show Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers from them that which they feared﴾ [al-Qasas: 5, 6].

And other than these verses.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fulfil My covenant; I will fulfil your covenant﴾. He did not specify here what His covenant is or what their covenant is, but He specified that in other places, such as His saying: ﴿And Allah said, "Indeed, I am with you. If you establish prayer and give zakah and believe in My messengers and support them and loan Allah a goodly loan, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 12]. So their covenant is what is mentioned in His saying: ﴿If you establish prayer and give zakah and believe in My messengers and support them and loan Allah a goodly loan﴾, and His covenant is what is mentioned in His saying: ﴿I will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾.

(p-35) He also alluded to their covenant in His saying: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture, [saying], "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 187], and other than these verses.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 41:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it, and do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾, and so on.

In this verse, the address comes in the plural form in His saying: ﴿And do not be﴾ and "do not exchange" (la tashtaruu).

He used the singular word "kafir" (disbeliever) and did not say "awwala kafirin" (first disbelievers). The reconciliation of the singular and plural within one phrase is that the meaning of ﴿do not be the first disbeliever﴾ is, in effect, "the first group that disbelieves." Thus the wording is singular while the meaning is plural, and it is permissible to observe either of the two. The poet combined both usages in his saying:

"When they eat, they are the basest of eaters, and when they go hungry, they are the worst of the hungry."

It has also been said that this is an instance of using the singular to denote the plural, like the saying of Ibn 'Ullafa:

"The Banu Fazara were the worst of paternal cousins..."

as has been mentioned shortly before.

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾. The truth with which they mixed falsehood is their belief in some of what is in the Torah, and the falsehood with which they mixed the truth is their disbelief in some of what is in the Torah and their denial of it, such as the attributes of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and other things which they concealed and denied. This is clarified by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do you believe in some of the Book and disbelieve in some?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85], and so on. The consideration is with the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasions of revelation, as has been previously mentioned."

Almighty's saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾. Seeking help through patience in matters of this world and the Hereafter is not problematic. As for the outcome of seeking help through prayer, the Most High has indicated it in verses of His Book. He mentioned that among the results of seeking help through it is the forbidding of what is unseemly, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ankabut: 45], and that it brings provision, in His saying: ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you, and the best outcome is for righteousness﴾. For this reason, when a matter distressed him, the Prophet (ﷺ) would hasten to prayer.

The explanation of this is that when the servant stands before his Lord, communing with Him and reciting His Book, everything in this world becomes insignificant to him, out of desire for what is with Allah and awe of Him. So he distances himself from everything that does not please Allah, and Allah provides for him and guides him.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿alladhina yazunnuna annahum mulaqu rabbihim﴾ (2:46), and the meaning of *ẓann* here, is *yaqin* (certainty), as shown by His saying ﴿and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4], and His saying ﴿and those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab*:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who think that they will meet their Lord﴾. (p-210) This verse, on its apparent meaning, indicates that *ẓann* suffices in matters of the Return. Other verses have come indicating the opposite, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾ [Yunus: 36], and His saying: ﴿They only follow conjecture﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78]. The way to reconcile them is that *ẓann* here means *yaqin* (certainty). The Arabs use *ẓann* to mean both certainty and doubt, and the use of *ẓann* to mean certainty is frequent in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs. Among its examples in the Qur'an is this verse, and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who think that they will meet Allah said, "How many a small company has overcome a large company by Allah's permission"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249], and His saying: ﴿And the guilty will see the Fire and will think that they are about to fall into it﴾ [al-Kahf: 53], meaning they were certain. And His saying: ﴿Indeed, I thought that I would meet my account﴾ [al-Haqqah: 20], meaning I was certain.

A parallel to this in the speech of the Arabs is the saying of Umayrah ibn Tariq:

"That you deceive my people, and I remain among you, and I make of myself a hidden thing, stoned, out of *ẓann*."

Meaning: I make of myself a hidden thing of certainty.

And the saying of Durayd ibn al-Simmah:

"So I said to them, 'Be certain (*ẓunnū*) of two thousand armored men, their chiefs among the Persian woven mail.'"

So his saying *ẓunnū* means *ayqinū* (be certain).

The author said in *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab* (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book):

His statement, exalted is He, to the Children of Israel: ﴿And that I preferred you over the worlds﴾.

It does not contradict His statement, exalted is He, concerning the preference of this nation: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110], and the rest of the verse, because the meaning of "the worlds" is the worlds of their own time. This is shown by the verses and hadiths that explicitly state that this nation is better than them, such as the hadith of Mu'awiya ibn Haydah al-Qushayri, recorded in the *Masanid* (collections of hadith arranged by the names of the Companions who narrated them) and the *Sunan* (collections of hadith arranged by legal topics). He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You will complete seventy nations; you are the best of them and the most honored of them before Allah."

Do you not see that Allah made the *muqtasid* (the moderate) among them the highest in rank, when He said: ﴿Among them is a moderate nation, but many of them—evil is what they do﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66]? And He made in this nation a rank higher than the rank of the moderate, which is the rank of the *sabiq bil-khayrat* (those foremost in good deeds), when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾, and the rest of the verse [35].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 48:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And no intercession will be accepted from it﴾ — the verse. The apparent meaning of this verse is that intercession is not accepted at all on the Day of Resurrection. However, He clarified in other places that the intercession that is negated is intercession for the disbelievers, and intercession for others without the permission of the Lord of the heavens and the earth.

As for intercession for the believers by His permission, it is established by the Book, the Sunnah (prophetic tradition) and the consensus (ijma', the scholarly agreement of the Muslim community). He stated the absence of intercession for the disbelievers in His saying: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28]. He also said: ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ [az-Zumar: 7], and He, may He be exalted, said about them, affirming this: ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 100] (p-36) and He said: ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 48], and so on through other verses.

And He said regarding intercession without His permission: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. He said: ﴿And how many an angel in the heavens whose intercession will not avail at all except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾ [an-Najm: 26]. He said: ﴿On that Day, intercession will not benefit except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted and whose word He approves﴾ [Ta-Ha: 109], and so on through other verses.

Claiming that there are intercessors with Allah for the disbelievers, or without His permission, is one of the types of disbelief in Him, may He be glorified and exalted, as He explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿And they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah." Say, "Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?" Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate﴾ [Yunus: 18].

Caution (tanbih)

What we have established, that intercession for the disbelievers is absolutely impermissible by the Law, is excepted by his (ﷺ) intercession for his uncle Abu Talib, in moving him from one place in the Fire to another place within it, as was established from him (ﷺ) in the Sahih. This case that we have mentioned is an instance of specifying the Book by the Sunnah.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 49:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿They inflicted on you dreadful torment﴾ — He explained it by His words after it: ﴿slaughtering your sons and sparing your women﴾, the verse.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab [Removing the Illusion of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book]):

(p-211) His words, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women﴾, the verse.

The apparent meaning of this noble verse indicates that the sparing of the women was part of the torment which Pharaoh inflicted upon them. Another verse has come indicating that females are a gift (hibah) from the gifts of God to whomever He bestows them upon, namely His words, exalted is He: ﴿He bestows female [children] upon whom He wills and bestows male [children] upon whom He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 49]. So the survival of some of the children in this state is better than the death of them all, as al-Hudhayl said:

"I praised my God after 'Urwa, when Khirash was saved,
and some evil is easier than some other evil."

The answer to this is that although females are a gift from God to whomever He bestows them upon, their remaining under the hand of the enemy, who does with them whatever he wills of indecency and disgrace and employs them in arduous labour, is a kind of torment, and their death is a relief from this torment. The Arabs used to wish for the death of females out of fear of such things.

One of the Arab poets said concerning a daughter of his named Mawaddah:

"Mawaddah longs for the life of an old man who is pleased by her,
for her death before night would be [better], if only she knew.

He fears for her the neglect of people after him,
and there is no son-in-law hoped for whom I would love more than the grave."

Another said:

"Your life is dear to me, and I wish her death out of compassion,
and death is the most honourable guest for the free."

And one of their rajaz-poets said:

"Indeed I, even if a dowry were brought to me,
a slave, two thousand, and ten she-camels,
the grave is the dearest of my in-laws to me."

Some of the men of letters said: In the Qur'an there is an indication that a person is distressed by the humiliation of his weak offspring after his death, in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And let those fear [God] who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would fear for them﴾ [al-Nisa: 9].

"The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when We parted the sea for you and saved you﴾ — here He did not explain the manner in which the sea was parted for them, but He explained that in other places, such as His saying: ﴿So We inspired Moses: Strike the sea with your staff. And it parted, and each part was like a great mountain﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 63], and His saying: ﴿And We had inspired to Moses, saying: Travel by night with My servants and strike for them a dry path through the sea, not fearing being overtaken or afraid﴾ — the verse [Ta-Ha: 77].

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾ — here He did not explain the manner of their drowning, but He explained it in other places, such as His saying: ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾ ﴿And when the two groups sighted each other, the companions of Moses said: Indeed, we are overtaken!﴾ ﴿He said: No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me﴾ ﴿So We inspired Moses: Strike the sea with your staff. And it parted, and each part was like a great mountain﴾ ﴿And We brought the others near﴾ ﴿And We saved Moses and those with him, all of them﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 60–66], and His saying: ﴿So Pharaoh followed them with his soldiers, and there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78].

And His saying: ﴿And leave the sea parted; indeed, they are an army to be drowned﴾ [ad-Dukhan: 24], and His saying: ﴿rahwan﴾ (p-37), meaning: still, in the state of its being parted, until they enter into it — and other than that from the verses.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 51:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We appointed for Musa forty nights﴾. He did not specify here whether He appointed them to him as a single continuous period or as separate periods? But He made clear in Surat al-A'raf that they were separate periods, and that He first appointed him thirty, then completed them with ten. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We appointed for Musa thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾ [al-A'raf: 124].

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 2, verse 53:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion, so that you might be guided﴾.

The apparent meaning is that the Furqan (the Criterion) is the same Book that was given to Moses. The verse joins it to itself by coordination, because the difference in attributes is treated as if it were a difference in essences. That Book, which is the Tawrat (Torah), is described by two qualities. The first is that it is a written text that Allah wrote for His Prophet Moses, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace.

The second is that it is a Furqan, that is, it distinguishes between truth and falsehood. So the Furqan is coordinated with the Book, even though it is the same thing, in view of the difference between the two attributes, as in the words of the poet (Mutaqarib metre):

*To the mighty king and the son of the noble chief, and the lion of the battalion in the thick of the crowd.*

Indeed, the Arabs sometimes coordinate a thing with itself when only the wording differs, and they are content with the difference in wording alone. As in the words of the poet (Basit metre):

*Indeed I am exalted in the breast of the warrior, despite what was in me of tajdir (shortness) and qisar (brevity).*

Qisar is exactly the same as tajdir. And as in the words of another (Wafir metre):

*I cut the hide for its wrists, and she found her words to be lies and falsehood.*

Al-main (falsehood) is exactly the same as al-kadhib (lying). And as in the words of another (Tawil metre):

*Ah, how lovely is Hind, and the land in which Hind dwells, and Hind, between whom and us stand distance and remoteness.*

Al-bu'd (remoteness) is exactly the same as al-na'y (distance). And as in the words of 'Antarah in his Mu'allaqah:

*Greetings to you from a campsite whose traces have grown old, which has weathered and become desolate after Umm al-Haytham.*

Al-iqfar (desolation) is exactly the same as al-iqwa' (abandonment).

The evidence from the Qur'an that the Furqan is what was given to Moses is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses and Aaron the Criterion﴾ (al-Anbiya: 48), and the rest of the verse.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 54:

(p-38) His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf﴾. He did not specify here what this calf was that was worshipped besides Allah. However, He clarified that in other places, such as His statement: ﴿And the people of Moses took, after him, from their ornaments a calf, a body that had a lowing﴾ [al-A'raf: 148], and His statement: ﴿But we were made to carry burdens of the ornaments of the people, so we threw them, and thus did as-Samiri cast.﴾ ﴿And he brought forth for them a calf, a body that had a lowing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 87, 88]. He did not mention the second object of "taking" (ittikhadh) anywhere in the Qur'an, and its implied meaning is: "by your taking the calf as a god," as He indicated in the surah of "Ta-Ha" with His statement: ﴿And thus did as-Samiri cast. And he brought forth for them a calf, a body that had a lowing. So they said, "This is your god and the god of Moses"﴾ [al-A'la: 88]. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We raised above you the mount﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. He clarified it with His statement: ﴿And [recall] when We shook the mountain over them as if it were a canopy﴾ [al-A'raf: 171].

The author said in (Dafʿ Īhām al-Iḍṭirāb ʿan Āyāt al-Kitāb):

(p-212) His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quail. Eat of the good things with which We have provided you.﴾

This noble verse indicates that Allah honoured the Children of Israel with two kinds of food, namely the manna (al-manna, a sweet exudation) and the quail (al-salwa). In another verse there is what indicates that they had only one kind of food, and it is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]. There are several ways of reconciling the two:

The first: the manna, which is tarankabin (a sweet substance, Alhagi/tamarisk manna) according to the view of the majority, is of the category of drink, and the single food is the quail. The quail, according to the view of the majority, is the sumani (a bird of the quail type) or a bird resembling it.

The second way: what is placed on one table is called by the Arabs one food, even if its kinds differ. From this is their saying: "We ate the food of so-and-so," even if it consisted of various kinds. What makes this way more correct than the first is that interpreting the manna specifically as tarankabin is refuted by the agreed-upon hadith: "The truffle is of the manna..." ... the hadith.

The third: they called it one food because it does not change or vary each day; it is one kind of food, and this is evident.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. He does not clarify here what this thing that We gave them is. But He clarifies in another place that it is the Book that distinguishes between truth and falsehood (al-Kitab al-Fariq), and that is in His saying: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion (al-Furqan), that you might be guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 53].

Allah's saying: ﴿And you certainly know those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath﴾. He summarized their story here and explained it in Surah al-A'raf in His saying: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea﴾ [7:163].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 68:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what she is."﴾ He did not make clear their intent by their saying "what is she" except that the answer to their question indicated that their meaning by their saying "what is she" in the first place was: what is her age? This is evidenced by His saying: ﴿He said, "Indeed, He says she is a cow neither old nor virgin, median between that."﴾ And that their meaning by their saying "what is she" in the other place was: is she working or not? Is there a defect in her or not? Is there a mark in her contrary to her color or not? This is evidenced by His saying: ﴿He said, "Indeed, He says she is a cow neither trained to plow the earth nor to irrigate the field, sound and without blemish."﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 71].

The Exalted said: ﴿And [recall] when you killed a soul and disputed over it.﴾ He did not state explicitly whether this soul was male or female. He did, however, indicate that it was male, by His saying: ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it."﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:73]

Allah's saying: ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life, and shows you His signs﴾ — the verse [continues]. In this verse he indicates that the bringing to life of the slain man of the Children of Israel is a proof of the resurrection of people after death, because whoever brings a single soul back to life after its death is able to bring back to life all souls. He stated this explicitly in His saying: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul﴾ [Luqman: 28].

Almost-verbatim translation:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they became like stones⟩ — the verse. Here He did not explain the cause of the hardening of their hearts, but He indicated it in other places, such as His saying: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant We cursed them and made their hearts hard⟩ [al-Ma'idah: 13], and His saying: ﴿So the term grew long upon them, and their hearts hardened⟩ — the verse [al-Hadid: 16].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 78:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them are unlettered people who know not the Book, except wishful fancies (amani)﴾. The scholars differed over the meaning of "wishful fancies" (amani) here, according to two views:

The first: that the meaning of "wishful fancy" (umniyah) is recitation; that is, they know nothing of the Book except the recitation of words without comprehending their meanings. However, this view does not fit with His saying ﴿and among them are unlettered people﴾, because the unlettered (ummi) does not read.

The second: that the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), and the meaning is: they do not know the Book, but they wish for false wishes (amani batilah). The saying of Allah, exalted is He, supports this view: ﴿And they say, "None will enter Paradise unless he be a Jew or a Christian." Those are their wishful fancies (amaniyyuhum)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], and His saying: ﴿It is not by your wishful fancies, nor the wishful fancies of the People of the Book﴾ [al-Nisa': 123].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 85:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you are those who kill your own selves﴾ — the verse — means: you kill your brothers. That this is the intended meaning is shown by how often it occurs in this manner in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And do not defame one another﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], i.e., let none of you defame his brother.

• And His saying: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of one another?﴾ [al-Nur: 12], i.e., of their brothers.

• And His saying: ﴿So kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54].

i.e., by the innocent among those who did not worship the calf killing those among them who had worshipped it, and other such verses.

This meaning is clarified by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The likeness of the believers in their mercy, their love and their compassion for one another is like the likeness of a single body: when one of its limbs is afflicted, the rest of the body responds to it with sleeplessness and fever."

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you then believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾

It becomes clear from what precedes it that the part they believed in is the ransoming of their captives from among them, and the part they disbelieved in is their expulsion from their homes, their killing, and aiding the enemy against them, even though they disbelieved in other parts of the Book and believed in other parts of it.

(p-40) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs⦆. He did not specify here what these clear proofs were, but He specified them in other places, such as His saying: ﴿And [make him] a messenger to the Children of Israel: "Indeed, I have come to you with a sign from your Lord. Indeed, I will create for you from clay like the form of a bird, then I will breathe into it and it will be a bird by permission of Allah. And I will cure the blind and the leper, and I will give life to the dead, by permission of Allah. And I will inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses."⦈ [Al-Imran: 49], and other signs besides these.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We supported him with the Holy Spirit⦈. It is Jibril according to the more correct view, and this is indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down⦈ [Ash-Shu'ara: 193], and His saying: ﴿So We sent to her Our Spirit⦈, the verse [Maryam: 17].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is it that every time a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you became arrogant? So a group you denied and a group you kill⦈.

This verse indicates that they killed some of the messengers. Its parallel is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you say. So why did you kill them?"⦈, the verse [Al-Imran: 183].

And His saying: ﴿Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a group they denied and a group they kill⦈ [Al-Ma'idah: 70].

And there has come in other verses what indicates that the messengers are victorious and supported, such as His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I will surely overcome, I and My messengers"⦈ [Al-Mujadilah: 21], and such as His saying: ﴿And My word has already preceded for Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they would be the supported. And indeed, Our army – they would be the victorious⦈ [As-Saffat: 171–173], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So their Lord inspired to them: "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers. And We will surely settle you in the land after them"⦈ [Ibrahim: 13–14]. And He, may He be exalted, made clear that this victory is also in the worldly life, as in this last verse, and as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believed in the worldly life⦈, the verse [Ghafir: 51].

What appears in the answer to this is that the messengers are of two kinds: a kind commanded to fight in the way of Allah, and a kind commanded to patience and to restraining from people. Those who were commanded to fight, Allah promised them victory and dominance in the mentioned verses, and those who were commanded to restraint and patience are those who were killed, so that Allah might increase their elevated ranks by their being killed while wronged. This combination is understood from the verses, because victory and dominance in them carry the implication of jihad and fighting. And the saying of the Most High is not an objection to this combination: ﴿And how many a prophet fought, with him many devoted scholars⦈, the verse [Al-Imran: 146].

As for the reading "qatala" in the active form of the verb from faala, the matter is clear. As for the reading "qutila" in the passive form, the subject of the verb is His saying "Ribbiyyun" [many devoted scholars], not the pronoun of "nabiyy" [prophet], and the possibility of an alternative interpretation undermines the argument. As for the view that the dominance and victory of the messengers is through argument and proof, then there is no difficulty in the verse. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 92:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs⁠—﴾

He did not specify here what these clear proofs (al-bayyinat) were, but He specified them in other places,

such as His saying: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood, and the locusts, and the lice, and the frogs, and the blood as distinct signs⁠—﴾ [al-A'raf: 133],

and His saying: ﴿So he threw his staff, and suddenly it was a serpent, clearly visible. And he drew out his hand, and suddenly it was white⁠—﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 32–33], and the verse [continues],

and His saying: ﴿Then We inspired to Moses, "Strike the sea with your staff," and it parted⁠—﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63], and the verse [continues].

And [He specified them in] other verses besides these.

The Qur'an verse: "Take what We have given you with strength and listen" (verse 93), and so on...

Some scholars said: it means listening in the sense of responding (al-ijaba). From this comes their saying "sam'an wa ta'atan" (we hear and obey), meaning "ijaba wa ta'atan" (response and obedience). From this also comes "sami'a Allahu liman hamidah" (God hears those who praise Him) in the prayer, meaning that He answers the supplication of whoever praises Him. The following verse supports this meaning: ﴿The only saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger so that He may judge between them, is that they say: "We hear and we obey."﴾ [al-Nur: 51]. This is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur). It was also said that the meaning of "wasma'u" (and listen) is with your ears, and do not refuse the act of hearing itself.

This view is supported by the fact that some disbelievers would sometimes refuse even to listen at all, for fear of hearing the words of the prophets, as in the words of God concerning Nuh and his people: ﴿And every time I called them so that You might forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted, and grew arrogant with great arrogance.﴾ [Nuh: 7].

And His words concerning the people of our Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you may overcome."﴾ [Fussilat: 26], and His words: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, you can recognize denial on the faces of those who disbelieve; they nearly assault those who recite Our verses to them.﴾ [al-Hajj: 72] (p-41) and His words: ﴿They said: "We hear and we disobey."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 93]. This is because the hearing that does not contradict disobedience is hearing with the ears, not hearing in the sense of responding.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 96:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Each one of them would love to be granted a life of a thousand years, but his being granted a long life would not remove him from the punishment﴾ (2:96).

The meaning of the verse: one of those mentioned wishes to live a thousand years, and the length of his life does not move him away from the punishment, meaning it does not keep him far from the punishment. The verbal noun formed from "an" (that) and its clause in His saying, ﴿an yu'ammara﴾ (that he be granted a long life), is the subject (fa'il) of the active participle which is "muzahzihihi" (one who moves him away), according to the most correct of the grammatical analyses (i'rab). Regarding "law" (if/would that) in His saying, ﴿law yu'ammaru﴾ (if he were granted a long life), there are two views:

The first, which is the view of the majority, is that it is a verbal particle (harf masdari, a particle that turns the following clause into a verbal noun), and it and its clause are in the position of a direct object (maf'ul bihi) of "yawaddu" (would love), and the meaning is: ﴿Each one of them would love﴾, that is, wishes for the granting of a thousand years. "Law" may indeed be a masdari particle, as in the saying of Qatilah bint al-Harith:

"What harm would it have done you if she had shown favor? Often a young man bestows favor while he is enraged and resentful."

That is, what harm would it have done you from her.

Some scholars said: here "law" is the conditional particle, and its answer (jawab) is omitted, and its estimated form is: "If he were granted a life of a thousand years, that would be the most beloved thing to him." The omission of the answer of "law" when the context indicates it is found in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. From the Qur'an is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, if you knew with the certainty of knowledge﴾ (102:5), meaning: if you knew with the certainty of knowledge, you would not have been distracted by ﴿rivalry in worldly increase﴾ (102:1), and His saying: ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains were moved﴾ (13:31), meaning: this Qur'an would have been it, or they would have disbelieved in the Most Merciful. From Arabic speech is the saying of the poet:

"I swear, if any thing had come to us from his messenger other than you, but we found no way to repel it for you."

That is: if any thing had come to us from his messenger other than you, we would have repelled it.

Once you know the meaning of the verse, know that Allah has clarified this meaning by making clear that a person, even if he is given enjoyment of years, and then that enjoyment ends and the punishment comes upon him, that the enjoyment which has passed does not benefit him and does not avail him anything after its end and the punishment's descent upon him. This is in His saying: ﴿Have you considered: if We let them enjoy for years, then there comes to them what they were promised, what they were given enjoyment of will not avail them﴾ (26:205-207). This is the greatest verse in removing the incurable disease, which is long hope. May Allah protect us and the believers from its evil.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril – for he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah﴾. The apparent meaning of this verse is that Jibril cast the Qur'an into the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ) without hearing a recitation. A similar example is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down ﴾ ﴿upon your heart﴾, and the rest of the verse [al-Shu'ara': 193, 194]. However, He made clear in other passages that the meaning of that is that the angel recites it to him until he hears it from him, and then its meanings reach his heart after hearing it, and that is the meaning of its being sent down upon his heart. This is as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾ ﴿Then upon Us is its clarification﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16, 19], and His saying: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you, and say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ [Taha: 114].

The Words of the Exalted: ﴿Are they not the defiantly disobedient? Is it not that whenever they make a covenant, a party among them casts it aside? Rather...﴾

In this verse He mentions that whenever the Jews made a covenant, a party among them cast it aside. In another place He states explicitly that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the one with whom they made the covenant, and that they broke their covenant every time. This is in His words: ﴿Surely the worst of creatures in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve, and they will not believe. Those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time, and they do not fear Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 55-56]. And He states explicitly in another verse that they are a people of treachery, except a few of them, in His words: ﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them, except a few of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 101:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when there came to them a Messenger from Allah, confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Scripture threw the Book of Allah behind their backs﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:101], the verse. In this noble verse He mentions that many of the Jews threw the Book of Allah behind their backs and did not believe in it. And He makes clear in another place that those who did not believe in the Book were the majority, and that is in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Had the People of the Scripture believed, it would have been better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:110].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 108:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾ He has not specified here what it was that Moses was questioned about before. However, He specified it in another place, in His saying: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven. But they had asked Moses for greater than that, when they said, "Show us Allah openly," ...﴾ [al-Nisa: 153] to the end of the verse.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿الحَقُّ فاعْفُوا واصْفَحُوا حَتّى يَأْتِيَ اللَّهُ﴾ هَذِهِ الآيَةُ في أهْلِ الكِتابِ كَما (p-43) هُوَ واضِحٌ مِنَ السِّياقِ، والأمْرُ في قَوْلِهِ (بِأمْرِهِ).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Forgive and overlook until Allah brings His command.﴾ This verse concerns the People of the Scripture, as is clear from the context. The word "amr" (command) in His saying "بِأمْرِهِ" (by His command)

Some scholars said: it is the singular of "al-awamir" (commands). Others said: it is the singular of "al-umur" (matters). According to the first view, it is the command that is the opposite of the prohibition, since the command referred to is the one stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day, and who do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and who do not adopt the religion of truth from among those who were given the Scripture, until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29]. According to the view that it is the singular of "al-umur" (matters), it is what Allah stated in the verses that indicate what befell the Jews of killing and dispersal, such as His saying: ﴿So Allah came to them from where they did not expect, and cast terror into their hearts; they destroy their houses by their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take warning, O you with vision.﴾ And: ﴿And had not Allah decreed for them exile, He would have punished them in this world.﴾ [al-Hashr: 2, 3], and so on through other verses. The verse is not abrogated (mansukhah, i.e., by naskh, abrogation) according to the verified view.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 114:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein and strives for their ruin?﴾ – to the end of the verse.

Some scholars said: It was revealed concerning the polytheists' hindering the Prophet (ﷺ) from the Sacred House during the expedition of al-Hudaybiyah in the sixth year (AH).

According to this view, the ruin (kharab) is figurative, meaning the ruin of the mosques by preventing worship in them. This view is clarified and supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque﴾ – to the end of the verse [al-Fath: 25].

Other scholars said: The ruin mentioned is literal (hissi) ruin. The verse was revealed concerning the one who destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis, namely Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar) or someone else. This view is clarified and supported by His saying, may He, the Majestic and Exalted, be praised: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter came, they would sadden your faces and enter the mosque as they had entered it the first time and destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction﴾ [al-Isra': 7].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein﴾ – to the end of the verse.

The interrogative in this verse is one of denial, and its meaning is negation. So the meaning is: no one is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah. But other verses have come that give the understanding of the opposite of this, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ – to the end of the verse [al-An'am: 144].

And His saying: ﴿Then who is more unjust than one who lies against Allah?﴾ [39], and His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the verses of his Lord?﴾ ... to the end of the verse [al-Kahf: 57], and other verses besides these.

There are several ways to reconcile these verses:

One of them is to restrict each occurrence to the meaning of its context: that is, no one among those who prevent is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah, and no one among those who fabricate is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah. When each is restricted by its context, the problem disappears.

Another is that the restriction is relative to precedence: that is, since no one had preceded them in the like of it, they were judged to be more unjust than those who came after them following their path. This ultimately returns in meaning to what came before it, because the intended precedence is in preventing or fabricating, for example.

Another, which Abu Hayyan claimed to be the correct one, is that the negation of superiority does not necessitate the negation of equality. Thus none of those described by this is greater than the other, because they are equal in being most unjust. The meaning becomes: no one is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah, nor than one who fabricates a lie against Allah, nor than one who denies the signs of Allah. There is no problem with these being equal in injustice, and it does not indicate that one of them is more unjust than another, just as when you say: "No one is more knowledgeable than so-and-so and so-and-so," for example. The author of al-Itqan mentioned these two ways.

As for what some later scholars mentioned, that the interrogative in His saying ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ is intended for emphasis and denunciation without intending to affirm injustice in the one mentioned in reality or to negate it from others, as al-Itqan's author related from him, its weakness is evident, because it contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 115:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾ ... the verse.

In this verse He mentioned the east (mashriq) and the west (maghrib) in the singular, and in the surah "al-Rahman" He dualized them in His saying: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman: 17], and in the surah "Sa'ala Sa'il" He gathered them in His saying: ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 40], and in the surah "al-Saffat" He gathered the easts in His saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and Lord of the easts﴾ [al-Saffat: 5].

The answer is that His saying here, "To Allah belong the east and the west," the intended meaning is the genus (jins) of east and west, so it applies to every east among the easts of the sun, which are three hundred and sixty, and every west among its wests, which are likewise, as has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

Ibn Jarir said in his commentary on this verse, the following text:

"The meaning of that is: ﴿To Allah belong the east﴾ from which the sun rises each day, and ﴿the west﴾ in which it sets each day. Its interpretation, if that is its meaning, is: And Allah possesses what lies between the two regions of the east and the two regions of the west, when the rising of the sun each day is from a place in it to which it does not return for its rising until the next position, and likewise its setting." End of quotation in his own words.

As for His saying, ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾, it means the east of winter and the east of summer and their two wests, as the majority hold. It was said: the east of the sun and the moon and their two wests. As for His saying, ﴿by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾: (p-215) that is, the easts of the sun and its wests as previously mentioned. It was said: the easts and wests of the sun, the moon and the stars. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 116:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ This alleged son, upon the one who claims it, is the curses of Allah. It has come explained in other verses, such as His saying: ﴿And the Jews say, "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." That is their statement from their mouths; they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them. May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded?﴾ [At-Tawbah: 30], and His saying: ﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters﴾ [An-Nahl: 57], the verse.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Allah has taken a son." Exalted is He above that. Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾

In this verse He used "mā" (what), the relative pronoun that indicates non-rational beings, and then in His saying "qānitūn" (devoutly obedient) He used the masculine plural form specific to rational beings.

The reason for the plural form is that what is in the heavens and the earth of creation includes both rational and non-rational beings. So the relative pronoun favours the non-rational, while the plural form favours the rational. The point in this is that He said: "Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth," and all creatures, in relation to Allah's dominion over them, are equal, rational and otherwise. The rational being, in his weakness and incapacity in relation to Allah's dominion, is like the non-rational. When qunut (devout obedience) was mentioned, and it is more apparent in rational beings than in others, He used a form that indicates rational beings, giving them precedence (taghlīban lahum).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 118:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We have made the verses clear for a people who are certain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 118].

This verse, by its apparent meaning, indicates that the clarification is specific to those who are certain.

Other verses have come indicating that the clarification is general to all people, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear His verses to the people that they may become righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], and His saying: ﴿This is a clarification for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 138]. The way to reconcile them is that the clarification is general to all creation, but since benefiting from it is specific to the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), it is restricted in this verse to them, because what has no benefit in it is like nonexistence. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45], and His saying: ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder﴾ [Ya-Sin: 11], even though he is a warner to the black and the red. He restricted the warning to those who fear and those who follow the Reminder only because they are the ones who benefit from it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 124:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers."﴾ It is understood from this verse that Allah knew that among the descendants (dhurriyyah) of Ibrahim there would be wrongdoers. And He, the Exalted, has stated explicitly in other places that among them are both a wrongdoer and one who is not a wrongdoer, such as His saying: ﴿And among their descendants are the good-doer and the one who wrongs himself openly﴾ [al-Saffat: 113], and His saying: ﴿And He made it a word that remains in his posterity﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 28], and the verse continues.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 127:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Ishmael [with him]﴾. In this verse He mentions the raising by Abraham and Ishmael of the foundations of the House. In surah "al-Hajj" He explained that He showed him its place, by His saying: ﴿And when We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾ [al-Hajj: 26], i.e., We designated for him its site and made him aware of it. It was said: He guided him to it by a cloud whose shade was the size of its area. It was also said: He guided him to it by a wind called al-Khujuj, which swept away the sand from it until its ancient foundation appeared, and Abraham and Ishmael built upon it, peace be upon them and upon our Prophet.

﴿Our Lord, make us submitting to You, and from our descendants a nation submitting to You. Show us our rites, and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves.﴾

Here He does not specify who this nation is, whom Allah answered in response to the supplication of His Prophet Ibrahim and Isma'il. Nor does He specify here who this messenger is whom they asked Allah to send among them. However, in Surat al-Jumu'ah He makes clear that this nation is the Arabs, and the messenger is the master of the messengers, Muhammad (ﷺ). This is in His saying: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered (al-ummiyyin, i.e., the unlettered Arabs) a messenger from among them, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, although they were before in clear error. And [He has sent him to] others of them who have not yet joined them.﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 2, 3]. This is because the unlettered are the Arabs by ijma' (scholarly consensus), and the messenger mentioned is, by ijma', our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). No messenger has been raised from the descendants of Ibrahim and Isma'il except our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) alone.

It is established in the Sahih (the authentic collections) that he is the messenger for whom Ibrahim supplicated. This does not contradict the universality of his message (ﷺ) to the black and the red (i.e., all of mankind).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 130:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Ibrahim?﴾ (the verse). Here he did not specify what the religion (millah) of Ibrahim is, but he specified it in His saying: ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a correct religion, the religion (millah) of Ibrahim, a Hanif, and he was not of those who associate others with Allah."﴾ [al-An'am: 161]. Thus in this verse He explicitly stated that it is the religion of Islam with which Allah sent His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). Likewise in His saying: ﴿Then We revealed to you, "Follow the religion (millah) of Ibrahim, a Hanif, and he was not of those who associate others with Allah."﴾ (the verse) [al-Nahl: 123].

This is the commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 132:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you the religion﴾

He indicates that this religion is Islam here, by His saying: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾. He made this explicit in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam﴾ (p-45) [Aal 'Imran: 19], and His saying: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and he will be in the Hereafter among the losers﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 85].

The Lord's words: ﴿And what was sent down to Abraham﴾. He did not specify here what was sent down to Abraham. However, He specified in Surah "al-A'la" that it was scrolls (suhuf), and that among what is in those scrolls is: ﴿But you prefer the worldly life﴾ ﴿while the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [al-A'la: 16-17]. That is in His words: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scrolls﴾ ﴿the scrolls of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la: 18-19].

And that is in His words: ﴿And what was given to Moses and Jesus﴾. He did not specify here what Moses and Jesus were given, but He specified it in other places. He mentioned that what was given to Moses is the Torah, which is referred to as "scrolls" in His words: ﴿the scrolls of Abraham and Moses﴾. This is like His words: ﴿Then We gave Moses the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 154], and it is the Torah by consensus (ijma'). He also mentioned that what was given to Jesus is the Gospel (Injil), as in His words: ﴿And We sent after them Jesus, son of Mary, confirming what was before him of the Torah, and We gave him the Gospel﴾ [al-Hadid: 27].

The Lord's words: ﴿The Prophets, from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them﴾. Allah commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims in this verse to believe in what all the Prophets were given, and not to distinguish between any of them, when He said: ﴿Say: We believe in Allah and in what has been sent down to us﴾ up to His words: ﴿and what was given to the Prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them﴾. He did not mention here whether they did this or not, nor did He mention their reward if they did it. However, He explained all of that in another place. He explicitly stated that they obeyed the command in His words: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and the believers. Each one believes in Allah, His angels, His books, and His messengers. We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285]. He mentioned their reward for that in His words: ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and do not distinguish between any of them — those, He will give them their rewards. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa': 152].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 142:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west; He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. Here He did not specify the straight path, but He specified it in His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have earned [Your] anger or of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 143:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Thus We have made you a community of the middle way﴾ (wasat), the verse [continues]; that is, choice ones, upright and just. What indicates that al-Wasat means the choice and the just is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿You are the best community ever raised up for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. This is well known in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the verse of Zuhayr:

"They are the middle, whose judgment men are pleased with, when one of the calamitous nights descends upon the great."

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾ does not specify here whether he is a witness over them in this world or in the Hereafter. But He has specified in another place that he is a witness over them in the Hereafter, in His statement: ﴿How then, when We bring from every community a witness, and We bring you as a witness against these?﴾ and ﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them, and they will not conceal from Allah a word﴾ [An-Nisa': 41, 42].

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We might know﴾, the verse [continues]. The apparent meaning of this verse may lead the ignorant to imagine that He, exalted is He, gains through testing a knowledge He did not previously have, far exalted is He above that, highly exalted. Rather, He, exalted is He, knows everything that will occur before it occurs. He has clarified that He does not gain through testing any knowledge He did not already have, in His statement, majestic and exalted: ﴿And that Allah may test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts; and Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. His statement, ﴿and Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, after His statement "that He may test", is a decisive proof that He does not gain through testing anything He did not know, far exalted is He above that, highly exalted; for the One who knows what is within the breasts is free of need for testing. In this verse there is a great clarification for all the verses in which Allah mentions His testing of His creation. The meaning of ﴿except that We might know﴾ is: knowledge upon which reward and punishment are based; so it does not contradict His having known it before that. The benefit of the testing is the manifestation of the matter to people. As for the Knower of the secret and the whisper, He knows everything that will occur, as is not hidden.

As for His statement: ﴿who follows the Messenger﴾, it indicates that the Messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ), by His statement addressing him: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face﴾, the verse [continues]; because this address to him is by consensus.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith be lost﴾, that is, your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis according to the most correct view, and this is inferred from His statement before it: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face﴾, especially according to the view that considers the indication of juxtaposition (dalalat al-iqtiran), and the disagreement concerning it is well known in the principles of jurisprudence (usul).

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾, the verse [continues].
