His statement, exalted is He, in this verse: "except that We might know" gives the impression that He was not aware of who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels, even though He, exalted is He, knows everything before it occurs; He knows what the creatures will do, as many verses indicate, such as His statement: ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth and when you were fetuses in the wombs of your mothers; so do not attribute purity to yourselves﴾ [53], and His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And they have deeds other than that which they are doing﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 63]. The answer to this is that the meaning of His statement, exalted is He: "except that We might know" is: knowledge upon which reward and punishment are based, so it does not contradict His being aware of it before it occurs. Allah, exalted is He, has indicated that He does not gain through testing new knowledge, because He knows what will be, as He said: ﴿And that Allah may test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts; and Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. His statement: ﴿and Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ after His statement "that He may test" is evidence that testing does not give Him knowledge He did not already have, far exalted is He above that; rather, He, exalted is He, knows everything His creation will do and knows everything before it occurs, as there is no disagreement among the Muslims about it: ﴿Not an atom's weight escapes Him﴾, the verse [Saba': 3].

Shinqiti's commentary on the verse: "We shall surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with" (Qur'an 2:144).

His saying, "﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾" and the rest of the verse, explains it [2:144].

The author said in (*Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab*, "Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book"):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead." Rather, they are living, but you do not perceive﴾ and so on.

This verse, on its apparent meaning, indicates that the martyrs are living and not dead. In another verse, He said about one who is greater than all the martyrs (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [39].

The answer to this is that the martyrs do undergo the worldly death, so their wealth is inherited and their wives are married off, by the consensus (*ijma'*, scholarly agreement) of the Muslims. And this death is the one of which Allah informed His Prophet that he would die (ﷺ).

It is established in the *Sahih* that his companion, al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), said when he (ﷺ) passed away: "My father and mother be sacrificed for you! By Allah, Allah will not make you taste two deaths. As for the death that Allah had decreed for you, you have indeed tasted it." And he said: "Whoever used to worship Muhammad, then Muhammad has died." He cited the Qur'an as evidence for this, and all the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) returned to it.

As for the life that Allah affirmed for the martyrs in the Qur'an, and his (ﷺ) life, which is established in the hadith that he returns the greeting to whoever greets him, both of these are a life of the barzakh (the intermediate state) that is not comprehensible to the people of this world.

Regarding the martyrs, He, exalted is He, explicitly stated this by His saying: ﴿but you do not perceive﴾ [al-Baqarah: 154]. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it as meaning that their spirits are placed in the crops of green birds that graze in Paradise and take refuge in lamps suspended beneath the Throne; they enjoy themselves thereby.

As for what is established from him (ﷺ), that no one sends greetings upon him except that Allah returns his spirit to him until he returns the greeting, and that Allah has appointed angels who convey to him the greetings of his community, that life too is not truly comprehended by the people of this world, because it belongs to him (ﷺ). Moreover, his noble spirit is in the highest of the ʿIlliyyin (the highest level of the record of the righteous), with the Exalted Companion (*al-Rafiq al-A'la*), above the spirits of the martyrs. So the connection of this pure spirit, which is in the highest ʿIlliyyin, with this noble body that the earth does not consume, is something whose reality Allah knows and creation does not know.

Just as He said regarding the same kind of thing: ﴿but you do not perceive﴾. Had it been a life like the life known to the people of this world, al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) would not have said that he (ﷺ) had died, nor would his burial have been permissible, nor would a successor other than him have been appointed. Uthman would not have been killed, his Companions would not have differed, and what happened to ʿAʾishah would not have happened. They would have asked him about the rulings on which they differed after him, such as *al-ʿAwl* (the increase in the shares of inheritance heirs), the inheritance of the grandfather and the brothers, and similar matters.

Since the Qur'an has declared that the martyrs are living in His saying: ﴿Rather, they are living﴾, and has declared that this life's reality is not known to the people of this world in His saying: ﴿but you do not perceive﴾, and since the Prophet (ﷺ) confirmed his life in the grave, such that he hears the greeting and returns it, while his Companions who buried him (ﷺ) do not perceive that life with their senses, we know that it is a life that the people of this world also do not comprehend. And what brings this closer to the mind is the life of the sleeper: he differs from the living in all of his actions, yet he perceives visions and comprehends meanings. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in *Kitab al-Ruh* (The Book of the Soul), in its exact wording: "It is known by necessity that his (ﷺ) body in the earth remains fresh and moist. The Companions asked him: 'How will our prayers be presented to you when you have decayed?' He said: 'Indeed, Allah has forbidden the earth to consume the bodies of the Prophets.' Had his body not been in his tomb, he would not have answered with this answer.

It is also authentically reported from him that Allah has appointed angels to his grave who convey to him the greetings from his community.

It is authentically reported from him that he went out between Abu Bakr and ʿUmar and said: 'Thus shall we be resurrected.' This is alongside the certainty that his noble spirit is in the Exalted Companion, in the highest ʿIlliyyin, with the spirits of the Prophets.

It is authentically reported from him that he saw Musa praying in his grave on the night of the Isra' (the night journey), and he saw him in the sixth or seventh heaven. So the spirit was there, and it has a connection with the body in the grave, and an oversight of it, and an attachment to it, such that it prays in its grave and returns the greeting of whoever greets him, while it is in the Exalted Companion. There is no contradiction between the two matters, for the affair of spirits is not the affair of bodies." The quotation from Ibn al-Qayyim's words ends here, the point of relevance. It indicates that the life mentioned is not known in its reality to the people of this world. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, they are living, but you do not perceive﴾. And knowledge is with Allah.

"His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those—Allah curses them, and the cursers curse them﴾. He did not specify here who the cursers are, but He alluded to that in His saying: ﴿Upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of mankind, all together﴾ [al-Baqarah: 161]."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 164:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ and the verse [continues]. Here He did not explain the aspect in which they are a sign (āyah), but He explained that in other places,

• such as His saying: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it and adorned it, and it has no rifts?﴾ ﴿And the earth – We spread it out and cast into it firm mountains and caused to grow in it of every beautiful kind [of plant]﴾ ﴿As an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back [to Allah]﴾ [Qaf: 6, 7, 8],

• and His saying: ﴿He who created seven heavens in layers. You see no inconsistency in the creation of the Most Merciful. So return your sight; do you see any flaw?﴾ ﴿Then return your sight twice; your sight will return to you humbled while it is fatigued﴾ ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps and made them as missiles against the devils, and We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 3, 4, 5],

• and His saying concerning the earth: ﴿It is He who made the earth submissive to you, so walk among its slopes and eat of His provision, and to Him is the resurrection﴾ [al-Mulk: 15].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the alternation of the night and the day﴾ Here He did not explain the aspect in which their alternation is a sign, but He explained that in other places, such as His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than Allah could bring you light? Will you not then listen?﴾ ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than Allah could bring you a night in which you rest? Will you not then see?﴾ ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty, and that you may be grateful﴾ [al-Qasas: 71, 72, 73], and other verses besides these.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the clouds subjected between the heaven and the earth﴾ Here He did not explain the manner of their subjection, but He explained that in other places, such as His saying: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy, until when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land and send down water therefrom and bring forth from it of all the fruits. Thus do We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], and His saying: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds, then joins them together, then makes them into a heap, so you see the rain coming forth from within them﴾ [al-Nur: 43].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 165:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if only those who did wrong could see when they will see the punishment﴾ — the verse. The intended meaning of "those who did wrong" is the disbelievers (kuffar). This is made clear by His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿And they will never leave the Fire﴾ [167]. What supports this is His saying, exalted is He, quoting Luqman as he admonished his son: ﴿O my son, do not associate others with Allah. Indeed, association [with Him] is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 31].

(p-48) His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254], and His saying: ﴿And do not invoke other than Allah that which neither benefits you nor harms you, for if you did, you would then be of the wrongdoers﴾ [Yunus: 106].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 166:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ and so on. Here He points to the mutual disputing of the people of the Fire. He has clarified in other places more than what is mentioned here, such as His saying: ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, sending back the word to one another. Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant: "Had it not been for you, we would have been believers."﴾ ﴿Those who were arrogant will say to those who were oppressed: "Did we turn you away from guidance after it had come to you? Rather, you were criminals."﴾ ﴿And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant: "Rather, it was the scheming of night and day, when you were ordering us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him."﴾ [Saba': 31, 32, 33], and other verses besides these.

Almighty God's words: ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾. He did not mention here the harm that results from following his steps, but He pointed to that in Surat "al-Nur" with His words: ﴿And whoever follows the steps of Satan - indeed, he enjoins immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-Nur: 21], and so on, to the end of the verse.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَأنْ تَقُولُوا عَلى اللَّهِ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (And that you say about God what you do not know). He did not specify here what it is that they say about God without knowledge. However, He explained it in other places. He mentioned that what they say without knowledge is that God forbade the *bahira* (a she-camel whose ear was slit and was released for idols, so it was not ridden or milked) and the *sa'iba* (a camel released freely, similarly dedicated) and the like, that He has offspring, and that He has partners, exalted is He far above that with great exaltation. He declared that He did not forbid these things in His saying: ﴿God did not institute any bahira, sa'iba, wasila or ham; but those who disbelieve fabricate lies against God﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 103].

• And His saying: ﴿They forbade what God had provided them, fabricating against God﴾, to the end of the verse [al-An'am: 140].

• And His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered what God has sent down to you of provision, and you made some of it unlawful and some lawful?﴾, to the end of the verse [Yunus: 59].

• And His saying: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues falsely describe, "This is lawful and this is unlawful"﴾ [al-Nahl: 116], and other verses. He also declared Himself free of the alleged partners:

• by His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him, exalted above what they associate with Him﴾ [Yunus: 18], and similar verses. And He declared Himself free of the alleged offspring:

• by His saying: ﴿They say, "God has taken a son." Glory be to Him﴾ [al-Baqara: 116], and similar verses.

Thus it becomes clear from these verses the detailing of (*ma*), which was stated in general terms in the relative noun (*ism al-mawsul*) that is (*ma*) in His saying: ﴿And that you say about God what you do not know﴾.

The author said in (*Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab*):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything, nor were they guided?﴾

This noble verse indicates, by its apparent meaning, that the disbelievers have no intellects at all, because His saying "*shay'an*" (anything) is an indefinite noun (*nakirah*) in a negative context (*siyaq al-nafy*), so it denotes generality. Other verses have come indicating that the disbelievers do have intellects with which they understand in this world, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Satan made their deeds appear fair to them and barred them from the way, though they were discerning﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 38].

The answer is that they understand the affairs of this world but not the affairs of the Hereafter, as He, Exalted, explained by His saying: ﴿[It is] a promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in His promise, but most of the people do not know﴾ ﴿They know an apparent [aspect] of the worldly life, while they are, concerning the Hereafter, heedless﴾ [al-Rum: 6-7].

**(p. 49)** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood...﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:173], and the rest of the verse. The apparent meaning of this verse is that all kinds of carrion and blood are forbidden. However, He clarified in another place that the carrion of the sea is excluded from that prohibition, in His saying: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:96], since the sea has no food other than its game, except its carrion. As for what some scholars have mentioned, that by its food is meant its salted, dried flesh, for example, and by its game is meant its fresh catch, this goes against the apparent meaning, because dried flesh of its game is still game that has been made into dried meat. The majority of scholars hold that by its food is meant its carrion. Among them are Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Zayd ibn Thabit, Abdullah ibn Umar, and Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with them all, as well as Ikrimah, Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan al-Basri, and others, as Ibn Kathir transmitted from them. In another place He also indicated that blood that is not poured forth is not forbidden, in His saying: ﴿Unless it be carrion or poured-forth blood﴾ [al-An'am 6:145]. From this it is understood that blood that is not poured forth, such as the reddish residue that rises on the pot from cutting meat, is not forbidden. For if it were like poured-forth blood, the restriction by His saying ﴿poured forth﴾ would have no purpose.

* *

**Benefit**

It has come from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah has made lawful for him and for his community two kinds of carrion and two kinds of blood. As for the two kinds of carrion: fish and locusts. As for the two kinds of blood: the liver and the spleen." The discussion of this hadith will come in al-An'am, if Allah the Exalted wills.

And from him (ﷺ) concerning the sea: "Its water is pure and its carrion is lawful." It was narrated by Malik, the authors of the Sunan collections, Imam Ahmad, al-Bayhaqi and al-Daraqutni in their Sunan, al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak, Ibn al-Jarud in al-Muntaqa, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and it was authenticated by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, and al-Bukhari.

The apparent generality of this hadith and the generality of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and its food﴾, indicate the permissibility of the carrion of the sea without restriction. It is also established from him (ﷺ), in a hadith agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), that he ate from the anbar, which is a fish that the sea cast up dead, and its story is well known.

The summary of the jurisprudential detail of this question is that the carrion of the sea is of two types. One type cannot live except in water, and if it is taken out of it, it dies, like fish. The other type lives on land, like frogs and the like.

As for that which cannot live except in water, like fish, its carrion is lawful according to all scholars, (p. 50) except that Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, disagreed regarding what dies in the sea and floats on the surface of the water. He said concerning it that it is disliked to eat. Unlike what a person has killed, or what the sea receded from and it died, for that is permissible to eat according to him.

As for what lives on land of the sea's animals, such as frogs, the turtle, the crab, and the water-tortoise, the scholars have disagreed about it. Malik ibn Anas held that the carrion of the sea among all of these is permissible to eat, whether it died by itself, was found floating, or was caught by hunting, or was taken out alive, or was thrown into fire, or was buried in mud.

Ibn Nafi' and Ibn Dinar said: the carrion of the sea among what lives on land is impure.

Ibn Arafah reported a third view, distinguishing between dying in water, in which case it is pure, and dying on land, in which case it is impure, and he attributed it to Isa, from Ibn al-Qasim. According to Malik, sea frogs are permissible to eat even if they die.

In the al-Mudawwanah: "There is no harm in eating frogs even if they die, because they are game of the water." End of quote.

As for the carrion of land frogs, it is forbidden without any disagreement among the scholars. The most apparent of the views is the prohibition of frogs absolutely, even if they were slaughtered according to the ritual, because of the evidence for that, as will come, if Allah the Exalted wills.

As for the water-dog and its swine (i.e., the water-hog), the well-known position of the Maliki school regarding them is that they are disliked. Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Maliki said in his Mukhtasar, coordinating them with what is disliked: "and the water-dog and its swine."

Al-Baji said: As for the sea-dog and its swine, Ibn Shabban narrated that it is disliked, and Ibn Habib said the same.

Ibn al-Qasim said in the al-Mudawwanah: Malik would not answer us about the water-swine with anything, and he would say: "You call it a swine!"

Ibn al-Qasim also said: "I avoid it. If a man were to eat it, I would not consider it forbidden." This is the summary of Malik's school on the issue, and his argument for permitting the carrion of sea animals, whether they live on land or not, is:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:96], and it has no food other than its game except its carrion, as stated by the majority of scholars, and this is the truth. It is supported by his (ﷺ) saying about the sea: (p. 51) "Its water is pure and its carrion is lawful." We have already established the authenticity of this hadith, and in it there is an explicit statement from the Prophet (ﷺ) that the carrion of the sea is lawful, and this is decisive on the point of contention. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that a singular noun when annexed to a definite noun is among the forms of generality, like His saying: ﴿Let those who oppose his command beware﴾ [al-Nur 24:63], and His saying: ﴿And if you count Allah's favor, you cannot enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim 14:34].

And to this he alluded in Maraqi al-Su'ud (a didactic poem on the principles of law), in his saying, coordinating it with the forms of generality: [Rajaz meter]

"And what has the definite article (al-) or is found,
or by annexation to a definite noun, when specificity is established, it negates."

And by this we know that his saying (ﷺ) "its carrion" by its apparent meaning includes every carrion from what is in the sea.

The position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, on this question is that what cannot live except in the sea, its carrion is lawful without disagreement, whether it is floating on the water or not.

* *

As for what lives on land of the sea's animals, the soundest of the views on it, which is the one stated explicitly by al-Shafi'i in al-Umm and Mukhtasar al-Muzani, and the differing views of the Iraqi scholars, is that its carrion in its entirety is lawful, because of the evidence we presented just above. The opposing views are two:

The first: prohibition of the carrion of the sea animal that lives on land, absolutely.

The second: a distinction between what has a counterpart on land that is eaten, such as the cow and the sheep, so the carrion of the sea animal of that kind is permitted, and what has no eaten counterpart on land, such as the swine and the dog, so the carrion of the sea animal of that kind is forbidden. It is not hidden that the argument of the first is more apparent because of the generality of his saying (ﷺ): "Its carrion is lawful," and His saying, exalted is He: (and its food), as previously mentioned.

As for the position of Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, it is that everything that cannot live except in water, its carrion is lawful, and the floating of it and other than it is the same. As for what lives on land of the sea's animals, its carrion is forbidden according to him. So it must be slaughtered by the ritual method (dhakah), except what has no blood in it, like the crab, for it is permitted according to him without ritual slaughter. He argued for the non-permissibility of the carrion of what lives on land by saying that it is an animal that lives on land and has a flowing soul (nafs sa'ilah), so it is not permitted without ritual slaughter, like birds. And he took the evidence we mentioned to refer specifically to what cannot live except in the sea. End of quote.

The water-dog, according to him, is lawful if it is slaughtered by the ritual method. And it is not hidden that specifying general evidence requires (p. 52) a textual proof. Therefore the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i is more evidentially sound, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

As for the position of Imam Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, it is that every animal that lives on land, its sea counterpart is not eaten at all, because it is considered repugnant. As for what cannot live except in the sea, which is fish in all its varieties, its carrion is lawful according to him, except if it died of natural causes in the sea and floated on the surface of the water, in which case eating it is disliked according to him. So what a person killed, or what the sea receded from and it died, is lawful according to him, unlike what floats on the surface of the water. His argument regarding what lives on land of it is that it is repugnant, and Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and He makes unlawful for them the wretched things﴾ [al-A'raf 7:157]. His argument for the disliking of floating fish is what Abu Dawud narrated in his Sunan: Ahmad ibn Abdah narrated to us, Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi narrated to us, Isma'il ibn Umayyah narrated to us, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What the sea casts up or what recedes from it, eat it; and what dies in it and floats, do not eat it." End of quote.

Abu Dawud said: Sufyan al-Thawri, Ayyub, and Hammad narrated this hadith from Abu al-Zubayr, but they stopped it at Jabir (i.e., it is a statement of Jabir, not a hadith from the Prophet). It has also been traced back through a weak chain, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ). End of quote.

The majority answered the first argument by saying that the wording of the texts is general regarding the carrion of the sea, and that specifying a general text necessarily requires a proof from the Book or the Sunnah indicating the specification, as has already been mentioned.

And the bare claim that it is repugnant does not override the generality of the explicit evidences concerning the generality of the carrion of the sea. As for the second argument, they answered by weakening the hadith of Jabir mentioned above.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab, his exact words: As for the answer to the hadith of Jabir which the earlier scholars used as evidence, it is a weak hadith by the agreement of the hadith masters (huffaz), and it may not be used as evidence even if nothing opposed it. How much more so when it is opposed by what we have mentioned of the evidences from the Book and the Sunnah, and the widespread statements of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all?

This hadith is from the narration of Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi, from Isma'il ibn Umayyah, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir.

Al-Bayhaqi said: Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi frequently made errors and had poor memorization. He said: Others have narrated it from Isma'il ibn Umayyah as a statement of Jabir (not a hadith from the Prophet). He said: al-Tirmidhi said: I asked al-Bukhari about this hadith, and he said: "It is not preserved (mahfuz), and the report from Jabir is other than this." He said: I do not know of any report of Ibn Umayyah from Abu al-Zubayr.

Al-Bayhaqi said: It was also narrated by Yahya ibn Abi Unaysah, from Abu al-Zubayr, as a marfu' (attributed to the Prophet), but Yahya ibn Abi Unaysah is abandoned (matruk) and not used as evidence. He said: It was also narrated by Abd al-Aziz ibn Ubayd Allah, from Wahb ibn Kaysan, from Jabir, as a marfu', but Abd al-Aziz is weak and not used as evidence. He said: It was also narrated by Baqiyyah ibn al-Walid, from al-Awza'i, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, as a marfu', and one does not use as evidence what Baqiyyah alone narrates, so how about what contradicts [the majority]? He said: The consensus of the Companions contrary to the statement of Jabir, together with what we have narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said about the sea: "Its water is pure and its carrion is lawful," (is decisive). End of quote.

Al-Bayhaqi also said in al-Sunan al-Kubra, in the chapter "Whoever disliked eating the floating," his exact words: Abu Bakr ibn al-Harith al-Faqih informed us, Ali ibn Umar al-Hafiz informed us, Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Fayruz narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Hassani narrated to us, Ibn Numayr narrated to us, Ubayd Allah ibn Umar narrated to us, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to say: "What the sea strikes (casts up), or what recedes from it, or what is hunted in it, eat it; and what dies in it, then floats, do not eat it." And with a similar meaning it was narrated by Abu Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Ibn Juraij, Zuhayr ibn Mu'awiyah, Hammad ibn Salamah, and others, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, as a mawquf (a statement of Jabir). And Abd al-Razzaq, Abd Allah ibn al-Walid al-Adani, Abu Asim, Mu'ammal ibn Isma'il, and others narrated from Sufyan al-Thawri as a mawquf. But Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri opposed them, narrating it from al-Thawri as a marfu', and he erred in it. Abu al-Hasan ibn Abdan informed us, Sulayman ibn Ahmad al-Lakhmi informed us, Ali ibn Ishaq al-Isfahani narrated to us, Nasr ibn Ali narrated to us, Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "If the fish floats on the water, do not eat it; and if the sea recedes from it, eat it; and what is on its shore, eat it." Sulayman said: No one raised this hadith from Sufyan except Abu Ahmad. Then al-Bayhaqi mentioned after these words the hadith of Abu Dawud that we presented earlier, and the statement of al-Nawawi that we quoted.

Its annotator, may Allah pardon him, said: So the conclusion is that the hadith of Jabir concerning the prohibition of eating floating fish (*al-samak al-tafi*) has been judged weak by many scholars, who do not accept it as evidence. Al-Nawawi reported the agreement of the *huffaz* (hadith memorizers, sing. *hafiz*) on its weakness, as we quoted from him earlier, and they ruled that its being a statement of Jabir alone (*mawquf*, i.e., ending with a Companion rather than the Prophet) is more firmly established. Accordingly, it is a statement of a Companion, opposed by the statements of a group of Companions, among them Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, (p. 54) and opposed by the verse and the hadith mentioned earlier.

It may appear to the one who examines this that the discipline of hadith and the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*) do not require rejecting the hadith of Jabir mentioned above, because its *marfu'* form (traced back to the Prophet, ﷺ) has come through multiple chains, some of which are sound. As for the *marfu'* report of Abu Dawud that we quoted earlier, they have declared it weak because its chain includes Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi, who had poor memory.

Yet another has narrated it as *marfu'*, even though Yahya ibn Sulaym mentioned is among the narrators of al-Bukhari and Muslim in their *Sahihs*. The *marfu'* report of Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri from al-Thawri, recorded by al-Bayhaqi and al-Daraqutni, has been declared weak on the grounds that he erred in it. They said: Waki' and others opposed him in it, and they narrated it from al-Thawri as *mawquf*.

It is well known that Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri mentioned, who is Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr ibn Amr ibn Dirham al-Asadi, is *thiqah* (trustworthy) and *thabt* (firm), even though Ibn Hajar said in *al-Taqrib* that he sometimes errs in the narrations of al-Thawri. These two *marfu'* reports are strengthened by the *marfu'* narration of Baqiyyah ibn al-Walid, recorded by al-Bayhaqi and others. Baqiyyah mentioned is among the narrators of Muslim in his *Sahih*, although many scholars have criticized him. This is further supported by the narration of Abd al-Aziz ibn Ubayd Allah, from Wahb ibn Kaysan, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, *marfu'*.

Also the narration of Yahya ibn Abi Unaysah, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, *marfu'*. Even though Abd al-Aziz ibn Ubayd Allah and Yahya ibn Abi Unaysah mentioned are weak, their narrations are strengthened by the narration of a trustworthy narrator. This is also supported by the narration of Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, *marfu'*, recorded by al-Tirmidhi and others. Therefore, it appears that one should not rule that the hadith of Jabir mentioned is not established, given the *marfu'* chains through which it has been transmitted, some of which are sound, such as the narration of Abu Ahmad mentioned above. The *marfu'* form is an additional report, and an additional report from a reliable narrator is accepted.

In *Maraqi al-Su'ud* he said: [Rajaz]
"The *marfu'* and the *muttasil* (continuous chain), and an addition to the wording, are accepted by the imam of memorization."
Etc. . . . Yes, one may say: It is opposed by something stronger than it, because the general meaning of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food﴾, and the words of the Prophet ﷺ concerning the sea: "Its water is pure, and its carrion is lawful," are stronger than this hadith of Jabir. This is supported by its being reinforced by analogy (*qiyas*), because there is no difference in analogy between floating fish and others. It may be answered that a general and a specific ruling do not conflict, and the hadith of Jabir concerning floating fish specifically is a specifier of the general evidence for permissibility.

So the evidence for the disliking (*karahah*) of eating floating fish is not free from some strength, and Allah the Exalted knows best. The meaning of floating fish is that which dies in the sea and then floats on the surface of the water. Everything that rises above the surface of the water and does not sink in it, the Arabs call *tafi* (floating). From this is the saying of Abd Allah ibn Rawahah, may Allah be pleased with him: [Wafir]
"And that the Throne is floating upon the water,
And above the Throne is the Lord of the worlds."

It is related in the anecdotes of the madmen that a madman passed by a group of Banu Rasib and a group of Banu Tufawah who were disputing over a boy. The madman said to them: Throw the boy into the sea. If he sinks in it, he is of Banu Rasib, and if he floats on his face, he is of Banu Tufawah.

Al-Bukhari said in his *Sahih*: Chapter on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 96]. Umar said: Its game is what is hunted, and its food is what it casts out.

Abu Bakr said: The floating fish is lawful. Ibn Abbas said: Its food is its carrion, except what is foul of it. The *jarri* (a scaly fish), the Jews do not eat it, but we eat it. Shurayh, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ, said: Everything in the sea is slaughtered. Ata' said: As for birds, I think one should slaughter them.

Ibn Juraij said: I said to Ata': The game of rivers and of water-pools left by floods, is it game of the sea? He said: Yes. Then he recited: ﴿This is sweet and palatable, pleasant to drink, and this is salty and bitter; and from both you eat fresh flesh﴾ [Fatir: 12]. Al-Hasan rode on a saddle made of the skins of water-dogs. Al-Sha'bi said: If my family ate frogs, I would feed them. Al-Hasan saw no harm in the tortoise.

Ibn Abbas said: Eat of the game of the sea, whether you are Christian, Jew, or Magian. Abu al-Darda' said concerning *al-muri* (a fermented fish sauce): The fish-*nin* and the sun have slaughtered the wine. End of quotation from al-Bukhari in his wording. It is well known that al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, does not cite with a firm wording (*ta'liq bi-sighat al-jazm*) except what he considers sound and established.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari*, in discussing these suspended narrations (*mu'allaqat*) mentioned by al-Bukhari, the following text: His saying "Umar said" — he is Ibn al-Khattab — "its game" is what is hunted, and "its food" is what it casts out. The author connected it in *al-Tarikh*, and Abd ibn Humayd, through the route of (p. 56) Umar ibn Abi Salamah, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: When I came to Bahrain, its people asked me about what the sea casts up. I ordered them to eat it. When I came to Umar, I mentioned the story, and he said: Umar said: Allah the Exalted said in His Book: ﴿Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food﴾; so its game is what is hunted, and its food is what it casts out.

His saying: Abu Bakr said — he is al-Siddiq: the floating fish is lawful. Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tahawi, and al-Daraqutni connected it through the narration of Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Bashir, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: I bear witness on Abu Bakr that he said: The floating fish is lawful. Al-Tahawi added: for whoever wishes to eat it. Al-Daraqutni recorded it, and likewise Abd ibn Humayd and al-Tabari from it. In some versions: I bear witness on Abu Bakr that he ate the floating fish on the water. Al-Daraqutni has another route from Ibn Abbas, from Abu Bakr: Allah has slaughtered for you what is in the sea, so eat all of it, for it is *dhaki* (slaughtered, lawful).

His saying: Ibn Abbas said: Its food is its carrion, except what you find foul of it. Al-Tabari connected it through the route of Abu Bakr ibn Hafs, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, concerning the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food﴾; he said: Its food is its carrion. Abd al-Razzaq recorded from another route, from Ibn Abbas, and mentioned the game of the sea: Do not eat from it what is floating; in its chain is al-Ajlah, who is weak, and the hadith of Ibn Abbas mentioned before it weakens this report.

His saying: The *jarri*, the Jews do not eat it, but we eat it. Abd al-Razzaq connected it, from al-Thawri, from Abd al-Karim al-Jazari, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, that he was asked about the *jarri*, and he said: There is no harm in it; it is only something the Jews disliked. Ibn Abi Shaybah recorded it from Waki', from al-Thawri, with it, and in his narration he said: I asked Ibn Abbas about the *jarri*, and he said: There is no harm in it; the Jews only forbid it, but we eat it. This chain is according to the conditions of the sound (*al-sahih*). He also recorded similar from Ali and a group. The *jarri* with the letter *jim* vowelled with a *fatha*; Ibn al-Tin said: In one copy with a *kasra*, and this is the vowelling of *al-Sihah*. The heavy *ra* is with a *kasra*. He said: It is also called *al-jarrit*, which is what has no scales.

Ibn Habib of the Malikis said: I only dislike it because it is said that it is of the transformed (*mamsukh*) creatures. Al-Azhari said: *Al-jarrit* is a type of fish that resembles snakes. It was said: a fish without scales; it is also called *al-marmahi*, and *al-sallur* is like it. Al-Khattabi said: It is a kind of fish that resembles snakes. Others said: a type that is wide in the middle and thin at the ends.

His saying: Shurayh, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ, said: Everything in the sea is slaughtered. Ata' said: As for birds, I think you should slaughter them. The author connected it in *al-Tarikh* and Ibn Mandah in (p. 57) *al-Ma'rifah*, through the narration of Ibn Juraij, from Amr ibn Dinar and Abu al-Zubayr, that they both heard Shurayh, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ, saying: Everything in the sea is slaughtered. He said: I mentioned that to Ata', and he said: As for birds, I think you should slaughter them. Al-Daraqutni and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Sahabah* recorded it as *marfu'* from the hadith of Shurayh, but the *mawquf* form is more sound.

Ibn Abi Asim recorded it in *al-At'imah*, through the route of Amr ibn Dinar: I heard an old man swearing by Allah that there is no creature in the sea except that Allah has slaughtered it for the children of Adam. Al-Daraqutni recorded from the hadith of Abd Allah ibn Sarjis, raised to the Prophet: "Allah has slaughtered everything in the sea for the children of Adam." Its chain has weakness. Al-Tabarani recorded from the hadith of Ibn Umar, raised similarly, and its chain is also weak. Abd al-Razzaq recorded with two good chains from Umar, and then from Ali: The fish is *dhaki* (lawful) entirely.

His saying: Ibn Juraij said: I said to Ata': The game of rivers and of water-pools left by floods, is it game of the sea? He said: Yes. Then he recited: ﴿This is sweet and palatable, pleasant to drink, and this is salty and bitter; and from both you eat fresh flesh﴾. Abd al-Razzaq connected it in *al-Tafsir* from Ibn Juraij with the same wording. Al-Fakihi recorded it in his book *Makkah* through the narration of Abd al-Majid ibn Abi Rawwad, from Ibn Juraij, more complete than this, and in it: I asked him about the fish of the pool of al-Qushayri, which is a great well in the Haram, are they hunted? He said: Yes. I asked him about the *ibn al-ma'* (water-eel) and the like: is it game of the sea or game of the land? He said: Wherever it is more common, it is game.

*Qilat* (water-pools) is with a *kasra* on the *qaf*, lightening of the *lam*, and ending with a *ta'* with two dots; in the narration of al-Asili it appears with a *ta'* with three dots, but the correct one is the first: the plural of *qalt* with a *fatha* on its first letter, like *bahr* and *bihar*, and it is the hollow in the rock where water collects. His saying: Al-Hasan rode on a saddle made of the skins of water-dogs. Al-Sha'bi said: If my family ate frogs, I would feed them. Al-Hasan saw no harm in the tortoise. As for the first statement of al-Hasan, it was said he is the son of Ali, and it was said he is al-Basri. What supports the first is that it appears in a narration: Al-Hasan, peace be upon him, rode, and his saying: on a saddle of skins, meaning made from the skins of water-dogs. As for the saying of al-Sha'bi: *al-dafadi'* (frogs) is the plural of *dif'dai'* (frog), with a *kasra* on its first letter and a *fatha* on the *dal*, and also with a *kasra* on it, and the vowelling with a *damma* on the first letter with a *fatha* on the *dal* is also reported, and *al-difadi* without the letter *ayn* is a dialect of it. Ibn al-Tin said: al-Sha'bi did not clarify whether it is slaughtered or not. The school of Malik is that it is eaten without slaughter, and among them some distinguished between what lives in water and what does not. From the Hanafis there is a narration, and from al-Shafi'i a narration: slaughter is necessary.

* *

(p. 58) Its annotator, may Allah pardon him, said: The carrion of land frogs should not be disputed as to its impurity, because of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and it is not of the creatures of the sea, because it is terrestrial. As Abd al-Haqq clearly stated, its carrion is impure according to the school of Malik. Al-Hattab, al-Mawwaq, and others quoted it from him in the commentary on the words of Khalil: "And the aquatic creature, even if it lived long on land." Ibn Hajar said, connecting it to the previous discussion: As for the statement of al-Hasan on the tortoise, Ibn Abi Shaybah connected it through the route of Ibn Tawus, from his father, that he did not see harm in eating the tortoise; and through the route of Mubarak ibn Fadalah, from al-Hasan, who said: There is no harm in eating it. The tortoise (*al-sulahfa*) is with a *damma* on the unpointed *sin*, a *fatha* on the *lam*, a silent unpointed *ha'*, then a *alif*, then a *ha'*; the final *ha'* may be replaced by a *hamza*, as reported by Ibn Sidah, and this is the narration of Abdus.

It is also reported in *al-Muhkam*: with a silent *lam* and a *fatha* on the *ha'*.

It is also reported: *sulahfiyah*, like the first, but with a *kasra* on the *fa'*, followed by a *ya'* with a *fatha*.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 173 (part 3 of 6):

His statement: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Eat of the game of the sea, (whether it was caught by a) Christian, a Jew, or a Magian."

Al-Kirmani said: "So it is in the old copies, and in some of them 'whatever he caught' (ma sadahu) appears before the word 'Christian'." I say: This suspended report (ta'liq) was connected by al-Bayhaqi through the route of Simak ibn Harb, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Eat whatever the sea casts up and whatever is caught from it; it was caught by a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian."

Ibn al-Tin said: "Its implication is that the game of the sea is not eaten if it was caught by anyone other than these, and this is the view of a group."

Ibn Abi Shaybah related, with a sound chain, from 'Ata' and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and with another chain from 'Ali, the disapproval of a Magian's catching fish. End of quotation from Fath al-Bari, in its wording.

As for the saying of Abu al-Darda': "In al-Muri, the nunan slaughtered the wine, and the sun (did too)." In its wording, "dhabaha" is a past-tense verb, "al-khamr" is its object, "al-nunan" is the subject of "dhabaha," and "al-shams," in the nominative, is coordinated with the subject, which is "al-nunan." "Nun" is a plural of "nun," meaning the fish. "Al-muri," with a dammah on the mim and a sukun on the ra' after it followed by a ya', is the correct reading, contrary to the authors of al-Sihah and al-Nihayah, who vocalized it with a dammah on the mim and a kasrah on the doubled ra', attributing it to "al-marr," the well-known taste. The al-muri mentioned is a food that was made in Syria: wine is taken, salt and fish are put into it, and it is placed in the sun, where it changes from the taste of wine and becomes vinegar. The change that the fish, the salt and the sun bring to it from the taste of wine is the removal of its intoxicating quality. This is what Abu al-Darda' meant by "slaughtering" the fish and "the sun" for it; he used "slaughter" metaphorically for removing the intoxicating strength by which intoxication occurs. This report of Abu al-Darda' was connected by Ibrahim al-Harbi in his Gharib al-Hadith, through the route of Abu al-Zahiriyyah, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Abu al-Darda', and he related it in the same wording.

Abu al-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him) held the permissibility of making wine into vinegar deliberately, while many scholars hold that deliberately making it vinegar is prohibited. If it turned to vinegar on its own, without any cause on the part of a person, then it is lawful by consensus. Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: "Abu al-Darda' and a group would eat this al-muri made with wine." Al-Bukhari included it under the purity of game of the sea, meaning that fish is pure and lawful, and that its purity and lawfulness extend to other things, like salt, so that what is forbidden and impure becomes pure and lawful by adding them to it. This is the view of those who permit making wine into vinegar, and it is the saying of Abu al-Darda' and a group.

The one who wrote this, may Allah pardon him, says: The apparent ruling is the prohibition of eating frogs absolutely, because the prohibition of killing them is established from the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Dawud said in his Sunan: Muhammad ibn Kathir narrated to us, Sufyan informed us, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from Sa'id ibn Khalid, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Uthman: "A physician asked the Prophet ﷺ about a frog he put in a medicine, and the Prophet ﷺ forbade killing it."

al-Nasa'i said in his Sunan: Qutaybah informed us, saying: Ibn Abi Fudayk narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from Sa'id ibn Khalid, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Uthman: "A physician mentioned a frog in a medicine in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade killing it."

al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: As for the hadith forbidding killing the frog, Abu Dawud related it with a good chain, and al-Nasa'i with a sound chain, through 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Uthman ibn 'Ubayd Allah al-Taymi, the Companion, who is the nephew of Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah, who said: "A physician asked the Prophet ﷺ about a frog he put in a medicine, and he forbade killing it." The further explanation of the prohibition of eating frog will come, Allah willing, in surah al-An'am, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me﴾ [al-An'am: 145].

The absolute prohibition of frog that we mentioned was held by Imam Ahmad and a group, and it is the sound position in the school of al-Shafi'i. al-'Abdari transmitted from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'Umar, 'Uthman, and Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them) that all dead creatures of the sea are lawful except the frog. So said al-Nawawi.

It is reported from Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) what indicates that the crocodile is not eaten. al-Awza'i said: "There is no harm in it for whoever desires it."

Ibn Hamid said: The crocodile is not eaten, nor the kawsaj, because they eat people. It is reported from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and others that he said: "They used to dislike the predators of the sea as they dislike the predators of the land," because of "the Prophet ﷺ's prohibition of every animal with fangs among the predators."

Abu 'Ali al-Najjad said: What is forbidden in its counterpart on land is forbidden in the sea, such as the water dog, its pig, and its human. This is the view of al-Layth, except regarding the dog, for he permits the land dog and the sea dog. So said Ibn Qudamah in al-Mughni. Some scholars prohibited eating the sea turtle. And Allah knows best.

* *

A NOTE
The root of "dam" (blood) is "damiya," which has a ya' as its final radical. It is among the nouns from which the Arabs deleted the final radical without compensating for it, and they made its inflection on the middle letter. Its final radical returns in the diminutive, so one says "dumay," with the diminutive ya' merged into the ya' of the root. It also returns in the broken plural, so the hamzah in "al-dima'" is substituted for the ya' that is the final radical. It sometimes also remains in the dual, and from it is the saying of Suhaym al-Riyahi:

"Had we been upon a stone, when slaughtered, the two bloods would have flowed with the certain news."

Likewise its final radical remains in the past and the present tenses and in the descriptive form derived from it. One says in the past "damiyat yaduhu" (his hand bled), like "radiya," and from it is his saying:

"Are you not but a finger that has bled, and what you have met in the way of Allah?"

One says in the present: "yadma," with the ya' changed to alif, as in "yarda," "yas'a," "yakhsha." From it is the poet's saying:

"We are not, on our heels, with our wounds bleeding, but upon our feet the blood drips."

One says in the descriptive form: "asbaha juhuruhu damiyan" (his wound became bleeding), and from it is the rajaz-poet's saying:

"We return its first to its last; we return it bleeding in both its parts."

The verified view is that its final radical is originally a ya', and it was said the original is a waw; it was changed to ya' in the past only because it came at the end after a kasrah, as in "qawiya," "radiya," "shajiya," whose original final radical is a waw, since they derive from "al-ridwan," "al-quwwah," and "al-shajw."

Some said: The original form of it is "dama" with a fatha on the mim, and it was said: with a sukun on it. And Allah knows best.

His exalted saying: ﴿So whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then there is no sin﴾. Here He did not specify the cause of the compulsion, nor did He specify the meaning of "desiring" (baghin) and "transgressing" (adin). However, He indicated in another place that the cause of the compulsion mentioned is hunger (makhmasah), which is the hunger, in His saying: ﴿Whoever is compelled by hunger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and He indicated that the meaning of "desiring" and "transgressing" is the one who inclines toward sin, in His saying: ﴿Whoever is compelled by hunger, not inclining toward sin﴾. "Mutajanif" means inclining, and from it is al-A'sha's saying:

"My she-camel deviates from the stone of Yamamah, and does not head toward your dwelling."

From the verse it is understood that both the desiring and the transgressing are inclining toward sin, and this is the furthest that can be understood from it.

Some scholars said: The sin toward which the one who desires inclines is rebellion against the Imam of the Muslims; the term "baghy" is often applied to opposing the Imam. The sin toward which the transgressor inclines is terrorizing the road and cutting it off from the Muslims, and every journey in disobedience to Allah is included in this. End of quotation.

Some scholars said: The sin of the one who desires and the transgressor is their eating what is forbidden while another is available, and on this view it is like an emphasis on His saying: ﴿So whoever is compelled﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173]. On the first view, it is not permissible for the highway robber and the one who rebels against the Imam to eat carrion even if they fear death, so long as they do not repent; on the second view, it is permissible for them, if they fear death, to eat carrion even if they do not repent.

Al-Qurtubi related from Qatadah, al-Hasan, al-Rabi' , Ibn Zayd, and 'Ikrimah that the meaning of "neither desiring" is: in eating it beyond his need, "nor transgressing," by finding an alternative to these prohibited things and eating them anyway.

He also related from al-Suddi that the meaning of "neither desiring" is: in eating them for appetite and pleasure, "nor transgressing" (by) pursuing eating to the point of satiety.

Al-Qurtubi also said, and Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and others said: The meaning of "neither desiring" is against the Muslims, "nor transgressing" against them. Thus included among the desiring and transgressing are highway robbers, the one who rebels against the ruler, the traveler who severs kinship ties, raiding the Muslims, and what resembles these. This is correct, for the original meaning of baghy in the language is seeking corruption; one says: "baghat al-mar'ah tabghi bighaan" when a woman committed fornication.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. Baghy is sometimes used for seeking something other than corruption, and the Arabs say: "The man went out in search (bighaa') of his camels," meaning seeking them. From it is the poet's saying:

"Let not the seeking (bighaa') of good, with its knotted reins, prevent you; indeed the ill-omened are like the auspicious, and the auspicious are like the ill-omened."

Al-Qurtubi related from Mujahid that the meaning of compulsion in this verse is coercion to eat what is forbidden, like a man whom the enemy seizes and forces to eat pork or other things that disobey Allah the Exalted. He also mentioned that according to the majority of scholars the meaning is hunger (makhmasah), as we mentioned.

We have already stated that the verse ﴿So whoever is compelled by hunger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] explains this, and the ruling on being coerced to eat what has been mentioned is derived from His saying: ﴿Except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest with faith﴾ [al-Nahl: 106], by way of a fortiori reasoning, and from the hadith: "Allah has overlooked for me from my ummah mistake, forgetfulness, and what they have been coerced into."

* *

Issues related to compulsion to eat carrion

First issue: The scholars agreed that the one compelled may eat from carrion what sustains his life and keeps his soul, and they also agreed that it is forbidden for him to eat beyond satiety. They differed over satiety itself: whether he may eat his fill of carrion, or whether he may not go beyond what sustains life and keeps him safe from death.

Malik (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) held that he may eat his fill of carrion and take provision from it. He said in his Muwatta': "The best that has been heard concerning a man compelled to carrion is that he eats from it until he is satisfied and takes provision from it; if he finds other food, he discards it."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: The proof of Malik is that the compelled one is not among those for whom carrion is forbidden; so when it is lawful for him, he eats from it what he wishes until he finds other food, and then it becomes forbidden to him. Ibn al-Majishun and Ibn Habib of the Malikis held that he may eat from it only the amount that sustains life and keeps him alive. Their proof is that carrion is permitted only in necessity, and when sustaining life is achieved, the necessity ends for what exceeds that.

Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Maliki followed their view in his Mukhtasar, where he said: "For necessity is what sustains, other than a human."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: The locus of this disagreement among the Malikis is when hunger is rare; but when it is constant, there is no disagreement about the permissibility of eating one's fill from it.

The school of al-Shafi'i is according to the two views attributed to the Malikis, and their proof for the two views is like the Malikis' proof for them, which we have explained. The two views are well known among the Shafi'is.

al-Muzani chose that he should not exceed sustaining life, and al-Qaffal and many others preferred it.

al-Nawawi said: It is the sound view. Abu 'Ali al-Tabari in al-Ifsah, and al-Ruyani and others, preferred the permissibility of eating one's fill, as al-Nawawi also said.

The Shafi'i school has a third opinion on this question, which is that if one is far from inhabited areas, eating to satiety is permitted, and otherwise it is not. Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) and al-Ghazali mentioned a more detailed distinction on this question, which is that if one is in the desert and fears that, by refraining from eating to satiety, he will not cross it and will perish, then it is definitive that he should eat to satiety. If he is in a town and expects to find pure (tahir) food before the necessity returns, then it is definitive that he should limit himself to warding off the ruin of his strength (sadd al-ramaq, the minimum to keep himself alive). If it does not appear that pure food will be available, and it is possible that he will need to return to eating carrion time after time if he does not find pure food, then this is the place of disagreement.

Al-Nawawi said: This distinction that Imam al-Haramayn and al-Ghazali mentioned is a good distinction, and it is the preferred view. There are also two narrations from Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, on this question.

(p-64) Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: There are two narrations regarding eating to satiety. The more apparent of them is that it is not permitted. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, one of the two narrations from Malik, and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i.

Al-Hasan said: He eats only the amount that keeps him standing, because the verse indicates the prohibition of carrion and excepts what one is compelled to. When the necessity is removed, it is not lawful for him to eat, as in the initial state. Also, after warding off his ruin he is no longer compelled, so it is not lawful for him to eat, by the verse. This is confirmed by: after warding off his ruin he is in the same state as before he was compelled, and in that state eating was not permitted to him, so it is likewise here.

The second narration: It is permitted for him to eat to satiety. Abu Bakr chose this, based on what Jabir ibn Samura narrated: that a man settled in al-Harrah, and a she-camel of his died. His wife said to him: "Skin it, so that we may dry its fat and its meat and eat it." He said: "Until I ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He asked him, and he said: "Do you have any wealth that suffices you?" He said: "No." He said: "Then eat it." And he did not distinguish. Narrated by Abu Dawud.

Also, the hadith of al-Fujay' al-'Amiri in the same collection supports this: that the Prophet ﷺ permitted him to eat carrion, even though he would drink milk in the morning and evening (yaghtabiq wa-yastabih). This indicates that the self may take its need of sustenance from it. Also, whatever it is permissible to ward off one's ruin with, it is permissible to eat to satiety with, like the lawful food. It is possible to distinguish between a case where the necessity is continuous and a case where it is expected to end. If it is continuous, like the state of the Bedouin who asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, then eating to satiety is permitted, because if he limits himself to warding off ruin, the necessity returns to him soon, and he cannot keep away from carrion for fear of future necessity, and this leads to the weakening of his body, and perhaps to his destruction. Unlike the case where the necessity is not continuous, for he hopes to be free of it by what is lawful. And Allah knows best. End of what I took from al-Mughni in its wording.

Imam al-Haramayn said: The meaning of satiety is not that one fills himself until he cannot swallow, but that when the violence of hunger is broken such that the name of "hungry" no longer applies to him, he stops. (Quoted by al-Nawawi.)

* *

Question two: The limit of the necessity that permits eating carrion is the fear of destruction, either by knowledge or by assumption.

Al-Zurqani said in his commentary on Malik's words in al-Muwatta' concerning one who is compelled to eat carrion. End of quote.

The limit of necessity is that one fears for his own self destruction, by knowledge or by assumption. It is not required that he reach a state in which he is on the brink of death, for eating at that point is of no benefit.

(p-65) Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: The second point concerns the definition of necessity. Our companions said: There is no disagreement that strong hunger alone does not suffice for consuming carrion and the like. They said: There is also no disagreement that one is not required to refrain until he is on the brink of destruction, for eating at that point is useless, and if he reached that state, it would not be lawful for him to eat it, because it would not benefit him. They agreed that eating is permissible if he fears for his own self, if he does not eat, from hunger or weakness in walking or riding, and he is cut off from his company and gets lost, and similar cases.

If he fears the occurrence of an illness that is dangerous in its kind, then it is like fear of death. If he fears that the illness will be prolonged, then it is likewise according to the more correct of the two opinions. It has been said that these are two opinions. If his patience is exhausted and hunger overcomes him, is carrion or the like lawful for him, or is it not lawful until he reaches the least of the strength to keep alive? There are two opinions, mentioned by al-Baghawi and others. The more correct is that it is lawful.

Imam al-Haramayn and others said: It is not required in what he fears that he be certain it will occur if he does not eat; rather, a preponderant assumption suffices. End of his wording.

Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: When this is established, the necessity that permits (the eating) is that by which he fears perishing if he leaves off eating. Ahmad said: If he fears for his own self, whether from hunger, or he fears that if he leaves off eating he will be unable to walk and will be cut off from his company and perish, or will be unable to ride and perish, this is not restricted to a fixed time.

The limit of necessity according to the Hanafis is: that he fears destruction for his own self, or for one of his limbs, whether with certainty or with assumption. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

* *

Question three: Is eating carrion and the like obligatory if one fears destruction, or is it permitted without obligation? The scholars differed on this. The more apparent of the two opinions is obligation, based on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾ [2:195], and His words: ﴿And do not kill yourselves; indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you﴾ [4:29].

From here a group of the scholars of legal theory (usul) said: The concession (rukhsah, a legal dispensation) may be obligatory, like eating carrion when one fears destruction if he does not eat from it. This is the correct view of the Maliki school, one of the two views of the Shafi'is, one of the two views among the Hanbalis as well, and it is the choice of Ibn Hamid. This is also the position of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on them all.

Masruq said: Whoever is compelled to eat carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine, and does not eat until he dies, enters the Fire, unless Allah pardons him.

Abu al-Hasan al-Tabari, known as al-Kiya, said: Eating carrion in necessity is not a concession, but a binding obligation (azimah). If he refrains from eating carrion, he is disobedient. Al-Qurtubi and others reported this.

Among those who chose that it is not obligatory, even if not eating leads to destruction, were Abu Ishaq of the Shafi'is, Abu Yusuf the companion of Abu Hanifa, and others. They argued that he has a valid aim in abstaining, which is avoiding impurity, and holding to the strict ruling.

Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni, regarding the reasoning for each of the two opinions, the following text: Is it obligatory for the one compelled to eat carrion? There are two views. One: it is obligatory, and this is the view of Masruq, and one of the two views of the companions of al-Shafi'i.

Al-Athram said: Abu 'Abd Allah (Ahmad) was asked about one who is compelled, finds carrion, and does not eat, and he mentioned the words of Masruq: whoever is compelled and does not eat or drink enters the Fire. This is the choice of Ibn Hamid. This is because of Allah's words: ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction﴾, and abstaining from eating while it is possible in this state is casting oneself into destruction with one's own hand. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not kill yourselves; indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you﴾. Also, he is able to preserve his life by what Allah has made lawful, so it is binding on him, as if he had lawful food with him.

The second view: It is not binding on him, because of what is reported from Abdullah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi, companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: that the tyrant of the Romans imprisoned him in a room, and placed with him wine mixed with water and roasted pork for three days. He did not eat or drink until his head drooped from hunger and thirst, and they feared his death, so they brought him out. He said: "Allah had made it lawful for me, because I am compelled, but I would not let you gloat over me regarding the religion of Islam." Also, the permission to eat is a concession, so it is not obligatory upon him, like the rest of the concessions. Also, he has an aim in avoiding impurity and holding to the strict ruling, and perhaps his soul will not be content with consuming carrion, and it differs from lawful food in its origin in these respects.

We have already stated that the more evidently supported of the two opinions is the obligation to take what sustains life, because a person is not permitted to destroy himself. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

* *

Question four: Does the one compelled prefer carrion or the property of another?

(p-67) The scholars differed on this. Malik held that he should prefer the property of another, provided he does not fear being made a thief and having his hand cut off. In his Muwatta' the following text: Malik was asked about a man who is compelled to eat carrion: does he eat from it, while he finds fruit belonging to a people, or crops, or sheep in that same place? Malik said: If he thinks that the owners of that fruit, crops, or sheep will accept his plea of necessity so that he is not counted a thief and his hand is cut, I think he should eat from whichever of these he finds, enough to ward off his hunger, and not carry any of it away. That is more beloved to me than that he eat carrion. If he fears that they will not accept it, and that he will be counted a thief for what he takes from that, then eating carrion is better for him in my view, and he has latitude in eating carrion in this way, while I fear that some transgressor among those not compelled to carrion may take it as a license to seize people's property, crops, and fruit without necessity. Malik said: This is the best I have heard. End of quote.

Ibn Habib said: If the owner is present, it is incumbent upon him to permit him to eat. If he refuses, it is permitted for the one who fears death to fight him, until he reaches eating what keeps his soul.

Al-Baji said: He means that he first calls on him to sell it for a price on credit. If he refuses, he asks him to feed him. If he refuses, he informs him that he will fight him for it.

Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Maliki said in his Mukhtasar, in which he stated what the legal opinion is, joining it to what the one compelled prefers over carrion: and food of another, if he does not fear amputation, and fights for it. This is the summary of the Maliki school on this question.

The Shafi'i position on it is what al-Nawawi stated in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab with his words: The eighth question: If the one compelled finds carrion and the food of another while the owner is absent, there are three views, and it has been said there are three opinions. The most correct is that eating carrion is obligatory. The second: eating the food is obligatory. The third: he chooses between them.

Imam al-Haramayn indicated that this disagreement is derived from the disagreement over the convergence of the right of Allah the Exalted and the right of the human being, even if the owner of the food is present. If he gives it without compensation, or at its equivalent price, or with an increase that people are usually willing to pay and he has its price, or he accepts it on credit, then acceptance is binding on him, and eating carrion is not permitted. If he will sell it only with a great increase, then the school's view, which the Iraqis, the Tabaris, and others were certain of, is that he is not obligated to buy it, but it is recommended. If he is not obligated to buy it, then it is like when he has not offered it at all. And if he has not offered it, the one compelled may not fight him for it if he fears for his own self from the fighting, or fears the destruction of the owner in the fighting; rather, he turns to carrion. If he does not fear, because the owner is weak and it is easy to repel him, then it is according to the disagreement mentioned regarding the absent owner. All of this is the branching out (tafri') upon the sound school.

Al-Baghawi said: He buys it at the high price and does not eat carrion. Then the earlier disagreement arises over whether he is obligated to pay the stated price or the equivalent price. He said: If he offers nothing at all, and we say the food of another is preferable to carrion, it is permissible for him to fight him and take it by force. And Allah knows best.

The essence of the position of Imam Ahmad on this question is that he prefers carrion over the food of another.

Al-Khiraqi said in his Mukhtasar: Whoever is compelled and finds carrion and bread whose owner he does not know, eats the carrion. End.

Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni, in his commentary on these words, the following text: This was said also by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Zayd ibn Aslam.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 173 (part 5 of 6):

Mālik said: If they (the owners) believe that he is in necessity (mudtarr, one in dire need), he may eat from the crops and fruit and drink the milk. If he fears that his hand will be cut off, or that his claim will not be accepted, he may eat carrion (maytah). The followers of al-Shāfi'ī have two opinions. The first is that he eats food. This is the view of 'Abd Allāh ibn Dīnār, because he is able to obtain lawful food, so it is not permissible for him to eat carrion, just as when its owner offers it to him.

Our (Mālikī) argument is that eating carrion is explicitly stated (in the text), while a human's property is subject to ijtihād (scholarly judgment). Turning to what is explicitly stated is preferable. Also, the rights of God Most High are based on leniency and ease, while the rights of human beings are based on stinginess and restriction. Also, a human's right must be compensated for, while God's right has no substitute.

* *

The fifth issue: If the one in necessity who needs carrion is in the state of iḥrām (ritual consecration for pilgrimage, muḥrim), and hunting (ṣayd, game) is possible for him, does he give precedence to carrion or to game?

The scholars differed on this. Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa (may God have mercy on them), and al-Shāfi'ī in the more correct of his two opinions held that he gives precedence to carrion.

From al-Shāfi'ī (may God Most High have mercy on him) there is an opinion giving precedence to game. This is based on the view that if the muḥrim slaughters a game animal, it does not become carrion.

The correct view is that the slaughter of a muḥrim for game is void and it is carrion. Carrion is lighter than game for the muḥrim, because it shares with game the designation of carrion, while game adds the prohibition of hunting and the prohibition of killing. A fuller explanation of this issue will come, God willing, in surah "al-Mā'idah."

Among those who held that game takes precedence over carrion for the muḥrim were Abū Yūsuf, al-Ḥasan, and al-Sha'bī. They argued that game is permissible for the muḥrim in cases of necessity, and when it is permissible and he is able to obtain it, the necessity is removed, so carrion is not lawful.

The majority argued that the lawfulness of eating carrion in necessity is explicitly stated, while the permissibility of game in necessity is subject to ijtihād, and the explicitly stated is preferable. So if the one in necessity finds only game while he is muḥrim, he may slaughter it and eat it, and he may eat his fill of it according to the verified view, because by necessity and the absence of anything else it has become a legally slaughtered animal (muzakkā dhakāh shar'iyyah), pure and lawful, and so it is not carrion. For this reason its legal slaughter is obligatory, and it is not permissible to kill it and eat from it without slaughter.

If the one in necessity finds carrion, the flesh of a swine, or the flesh of a dead human, then the apparent view is to give precedence to carrion over swine and human flesh.

Al-Bājī said: If the one in necessity finds carrion and a swine, then in my view it is more evident that he should eat the carrion, because the swine is carrion and is not permitted in any way. Likewise, he gives precedence to game over swine and over human flesh, according to the apparent view. Among the Mālikīs, it is not permissible to eat a human for necessity in any case. Killing a living human whose blood is protected (ma'ṣūm al-dam, one whose life is inviolable) in order to eat him in necessity is unlawful by consensus, whether he is a Muslim or a dhimmī (a non-Muslim living under Muslim protection).

If a dead person whose blood is protected is found, is it permissible to eat his flesh in necessity or not? The Mālikīs and the Ḥanbalīs prohibited it, while the Shāfi'īs and some of the Ḥanafīs permitted it.

The Ḥanbalīs argued for its prohibition based on the ḥadīth: "Breaking the bone of the dead is like breaking the bone of the living." Abū al-Khaṭṭāb among them chose the permissibility of eating it, and said: There is no proof in the ḥadīth here, because eating is from the flesh, not from the bone, and the intent of the ḥadīth is comparison in the basic prohibition, not in its degree, as is shown by their difference regarding liability for compensation and retaliation, and by the obligation to protect the living in ways that are not required for protecting the dead. He said this in al-Mughnī.

If the one in necessity finds a human who is not protected (ghayr ma'ṣūm), such as a ḥarbī (a non-Muslim at war with the Muslims) or an apostate (murtadd), then he may kill him and eat from him. This is the view of the Shāfi'īs, and al-Qāḍī of the Ḥanbalīs said the same. They argued that he has no inviolability, so he is like wild beasts. And God Most High knows best.

* *

The sixth issue: Is it permissible for the one in necessity to relieve his necessity by drinking wine? On this the scholars hold four opinions. The first: prohibition absolutely. The second: permission absolutely. The third: permission in the case of necessity to treat with it, but not for thirst. The fourth: the reverse of that.

The most correct of these views among the Shāfi'īs is prohibition absolutely.

The compiler (of this work), may God pardon him, says: The apparent view is that treating with wine is not permissible, because of what Muslim related in his Ṣaḥīḥ from the ḥadīth of Wā'il ibn Ḥujr (may God be pleased with him): "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked by Ṭāriq ibn Suwayd al-Ju'fī about wine, and he forbade him, or disliked that he make it. He said: 'I make it for medicine.' He said: 'It is not a medicine, but it is a disease.'" The apparent view is that it is permissible to use it for swallowing a lump that threatens death; this is the view of most scholars. The difference between swallowing a lump and drinking it for hunger or thirst is that removing the lump by it is known, while its removal of hunger or thirst is not certain.

Al-Bājī said: Is it permissible for one who may eat carrion to drink wine for his hunger or thirst? Mālik said: He does not drink it, and it will only increase his thirst.

Ibn al-Qāsim said: The one in necessity may drink blood but not wine, and may eat carrion but not approach the stray camels. Ibn Wahb also said this.

Ibn Ḥabīb said: Whoever chokes on food and fears for his life may wash it down with wine. Abū al-Faraj also said this.

As for treating with it, the well-known position of the school is that it is not lawful. If we say that treating with it is not permissible, while using it to swallow a lump is permissible, the difference is that treatment with it does not guarantee recovery from hunger or thirst. (End of quotation) from al-Mawwāq, in his commentary on Khalīl's words: "And wine for a lump." What we have quoted from Mālik, that wine only increases thirst, al-Nawawī quoted similar from al-Shāfi'ī. He said: Al-Rūyānī reported that al-Shāfi'ī (may God have mercy on him) explicitly prohibited drinking it for thirst, giving the reason that it causes hunger and thirst.

Al-Qāḍī Abū al-Ṭayyib said: I asked someone who knows this, and he said: The matter is as al-Shāfi'ī said: it quenches immediately, then it produces a great thirst.

Al-Qāḍī Ḥusayn said in his Ta'līq: The physicians said: Wine increases thirst, and drinkers are eager for cold water. By what we have mentioned, it does not benefit in averting thirst.

By the sound ḥadīth mentioned earlier on this issue, it is established that it does not benefit as a medicine, so its prohibition is established absolutely. And God Most High knows best. (End of quotation) from Sharḥ al-Muhadhdhab.

From this you know that what al-Ghazālī and Imam al-Ḥaramayn chose among the Shāfi'īs, and al-Abharī among the Mālikīs, of permitting it for thirst, is contrary to the correct view, and what Imam al-Ḥaramayn and al-Abharī mentioned, that it benefits with thirst, is also contrary to the correct view. And knowledge is with God Most High.

As for one who passes by an orchard belonging to another, containing fruit and crops, or by livestock having milk: if he is in necessity of the kind that permits carrion, then he may eat an amount that repels his hunger, by consensus, and it is not permissible for him to carry any of it away. If he is not in necessity, the scholars differed on whether he may eat from it.
