It was said: He may eat in his stomach without carrying anything from it. It was said: He may not do so. It was said: There is a distinction between an enclosed property, which is forbidden, and other property, which is permitted.

The argument of those who held prohibition absolutely is what is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the general wording: "Indeed your blood, your property, and your honor are forbidden, as the sanctity of this day of yours in this land of yours," and the general wording of God Most High: ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾ [al-Nisā': 29], and similar proofs.

The argument of those who held permission absolutely is what Abū Dāwūd transmitted from al-Ḥasan, from Samurah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When one of you comes upon livestock, if its owner is with it, he should ask his permission. If he gives permission, he may milk it and drink. If he is not there, he should call out three times. If someone answers, he should ask his permission. If he gives permission, (he may milk); otherwise he should milk and drink, but not carry away." End of quotation.

And what al-Tirmidhī transmitted from Yaḥyā ibn Sulaym, from 'Ubayd Allāh, from Nāfi', from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever enters an orchard, let him eat, but let him not take a khubnah (a fold of the garment used for carrying)." He said: This is a gharīb (a ḥadīth with a single transmission route) ḥadīth; we do not know it except from the ḥadīth of Yaḥyā ibn Sulaym. And what al-Tirmidhī also transmitted from the ḥadīth of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about hanging fruit, and he said: "Whoever takes from it, being in need, without making a khubnah, there is no fault upon him." He said regarding it: This is a ḥasan (good) ḥadīth.

And what is related from 'Umar (may God be pleased with him), that he said: "When one of you passes by an orchard, let him eat from it, but let him not make a thiyāb (a garment for carrying)."

Abū 'Ubayd said: Abū 'Amr said: It is what one carries a container in. If you carry it in front of you, it is a thiyāb, one says: "He has made a thiyāb." If you carry it on your back, it is ḥāl (a kind of carrying), one says from it: "I have transformed my cloak," when you put something in it and then carry it on your back. If you place it in your lap, it is khubnah. From it is the ḥadīth of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb raised to the Prophet: "And let him not make a khubnah." One says: In it, "I took (a fold), I take, a taking." Al-Qurṭubī said this.

And what is related from Abū Zaynab al-Taymī, who said: I traveled with Anas ibn Mālik, 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Samurah, and Abū Burdah, and they would pass by fruit and eat with their mouths. Ṣāḥib al-Mughnī related this.

The people of the first opinion applied these ḥadīths and reports to the state of necessity. What supports this is what Ibn Mājah transmitted with a ṣaḥīḥ chain, from 'Abbād ibn Shurahbīl al-Yashkurī al-Ghubarī (may God be pleased with him), who said: A famine struck us one year, so I came to Medina, I came to an orchard of its orchards, and I took an ear of grain, rubbed it, ate it, and put some in my cloak. The owner of the orchard came, beat me, and took my garment. I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: "You did not feed him when he was hungry or famished, nor did you teach him when he was ignorant." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to return his garment to him, and ordered for him a wasq (a measure) of food, or half a wasq. In this ḥadīth is evidence that the negation of cutting off the hand and of punishment is only because of the famine.

Al-Qurṭubī said in his Tafsīr, after quoting what we have mentioned from 'Umar (may God be pleased with him): Abū 'Ubayd said: What directs this ḥadīth is that he permitted it for the hungry one in necessity who has nothing with him to buy with, that he should carry only what is in his stomach, an amount for his sustenance. Then he said: I say: Because the agreed-upon principle is the prohibition of another's property except with his full consent. If there is a custom of doing this, as it was at the beginning of Islam, or as it is now in some lands, then that is permissible. This is to be understood as applying to times of famine and necessity, as has preceded. And God knows best. (End of quotation).

The argument of those who distinguished between enclosed property and other property is that enclosing it with a wall is evidence of its owner's stinginess with it and his unwillingness to be lenient about it. And the statement of Ibn 'Abbās: "If it has a wall around it, it is forbidden, so do not eat from it; and if it has no wall, there is no harm," related by the author of al-Mughnī and others. And what some scholars mentioned of a distinction between the property of a Muslim, which is permitted in necessity, and the property of a People of the Book (dhimmī), which is not permitted in any case, is not apparent.

And the ḥadīth of al-'Irbāḍ ibn Sāriyah in Abū Dāwūd, which prohibits entering the houses of the People of the Book and eating from their fruit except with permission, must be understood as applying to the absence of the compelling necessity that leads to eating carrion. And knowledge is with God Most High.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Īhām al-Iḍṭirāb 'an Āyāt al-Kitāb):

God Most High said: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion and blood﴾, and so on.

This verse, by its apparent meaning, indicates that all kinds of blood are forbidden. Similar is the statement of God Most High in surah "al-Naḥl": ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion and blood﴾, and so on [al-Naḥl: 115].

He has mentioned in another verse what indicates that blood is forbidden only when it is poured forth (masfūḥ), namely God Most High's statement in surah "al-An'ām": ﴿unless it be carrion or poured-forth blood﴾, and so on [al-An'ām: 145].

The answer is that this question is one of the issues of conflict between the general (muṭlaq) and the restricted (muqayyad). The principle followed by Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad is to apply the general to the restricted (ḥaml al-muṭlaq ʿalā al-muqayyad), especially when the ruling and the cause are the same, as here. For them it makes no difference whether the general comes after the restricted, as here, or before it. We have said here that the general comes after the restricted because the restriction is in the sūrah of al-An‘ām, and that sūrah was revealed before al-Naḥl, though both are Meccan except for certain well-known verses. The evidence that al-An‘ām came before al-Naḥl is the words of God, the Exalted, in al-Naḥl: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade what We have related to you﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:118]. What is meant by it is what was related to him in al-An‘ām in the words: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾ [al-An‘ām 6:146].

As for al-An‘ām having been revealed before al-Baqarah and al-Mā’idah, it is clear, because al-An‘ām is Meccan by consensus except for some verses in it, while al-Baqarah is Madinan by consensus, and al-Mā’idah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, and nothing in it was abrogated (naskh) because of its lateness.

On this basis, blood that is not poured forth (masfūḥ), such as the redness that appears in the cooking pot from the trace of cutting the meat, is not forbidden, because the general is applied to the restricted. Many scholars hold this view. What we have mentioned about al-Mā’idah not being abrogated is said by a group, and it is based on the view that the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them﴾ [al-Mā’idah 5:42] are not abrogated.

And His words: ﴿or two others from among other than you﴾ [al-Mā’idah 5:106] being unabrogated is correct; but on the view that these two are abrogated, it is not correct without qualification. And God knows best.

This is the commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 174:

The author said in (Dafʿ Īhām al-Iḍṭirāb ʿan Āyāt al-Kitāb, "Removing the Illusion of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book"):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are they who eat not into their bellies except the Fire, and Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, and so on, to the end of the verse.

This verse indicates, by its apparent meaning, that Allah does not speak to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and will not speak to them﴾, is a verb in a context of negation, and it has been established in the science of usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) that a verb in a context of negation is one of the forms of generality (ʿumum). This holds whether the verb is transitive or intransitive, according to the verified position, in contrast to al-Ghazali, who held that it is general in the transitive but not in the intransitive. The disagreement of Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, on this matter is a disagreement over a state, not over a reality, because he says that a verb in a context of negation is not in itself a form of generality, but it indicates generality by necessary implication (iltizam), that is, because it indicates the negation of the reality, and the negation of the reality necessarily entails the negation of all its individual instances.

So his saying, "I did not eat," for example, negates the reality of eating, and so it necessarily entails the negation of all its individual instances. The clarification of the generality of a verb in a context of negation is that the verb is resolved, according to the grammarians, into a verbal noun (masdar) and a tense, and, according to some rhetoricians, into a verbal noun, a tense and an attribution. The verbal noun is included in its meaning by consensus. Thus the negation, entering upon the verb, negates the verbal noun latent in the verb, and it thereby returns to the meaning of an indefinite noun in a context of negation.

It is remarkable that Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, agrees with the majority that a verb in a context of negation, if it is emphasized by a verbal noun, as in "I did not drink a drinking" for example, conveys generality, even though he does not agree that an indefinite noun in a context of negation conveys generality.

Verses have come that indicate that Allah does speak to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾ and ﴿He said, "Be driven away into it, and do not speak to Me."﴾ [al-Muminun: 107–108].

The answer to this is given in two matters:

The first, and it is the truth: the speech by which Allah negated that He would speak to them is the speech that contains good. As for rebuke, reproach and humiliation, Allah's speech to them with it is of the same kind as His punishment of them, and by the negation in His saying "and He will not speak to them" He did not intend it.

The second: that He does not speak to them at all, and that it is only the angels who speak to them, by His permission and command.

The commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And gives wealth, though he loves it﴾ and so on. He did not clarify here whether this verbal noun (maṣdar) is annexed to its agent, so that the pronoun refers back to "the one who gives the wealth" and the object is omitted, or whether it is annexed to its object, so that the pronoun refers back to the wealth. However, he mentioned elsewhere what indicates that the verbal noun is annexed to its agent, and that the meaning of ﴿on his love﴾ is the love of the one who gives the wealth for that wealth. This is his saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from that which you love﴾ [Al 'Imran: 92]. It is not hidden that there is a mutual implication in meaning between the two views.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and at the time of violence﴾. He did not clarify here what is meant by "violence" (ba's). However, he indicated elsewhere that ba's means fighting, in his saying: ﴿Already Allah knows those among you who hinder others, and those who say to their brothers, "Come to us," and they do not come to battle except a little﴾ [al-Ahzab: 18], as is apparent from the context of the speech.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 178:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Retribution is prescribed for you in the matter of those who are slain﴾.

This verse, by its apparent meaning, indicates that retribution (qisas) is a binding matter that cannot be avoided, based on His saying: ﴿prescribed for you﴾, because its meaning is that it was made obligatory and decreed upon you. Yet He, exalted is He, also mentioned that retribution is not fixed, since the guardian of the blood (waliy al-dam) has a choice, in His saying: ﴿But if he is pardoned by his brother in any way﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Baqarah: 178].

The answer is clear: the obligation and enforcement of retribution applies when the heirs of the blood, or some of them, do not pardon, as His saying indicates: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority, but let him not commit excess in killing﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Isra': 33].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 180:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches any of you, if he leaves wealth, that he make a bequest to parents and relatives in a reasonable manner; this is a duty upon the righteous.﴾ — the verse.

This verse appears to conflict with the verses of inheritance (ayat al-mawarith) when joined with the explanation of the Prophet ﷺ, because its intent is to nullify the bequest to those among them who are heirs, and that is his saying ﷺ: "Indeed Allah has given every rightful person his right, so there is no bequest to an heir."

The answer is evident: this verse of bequest is abrogated (mansukhah) by the verses of inheritance, and the mentioned hadith is an explanation of the abrogating text (al-nasikh). Some scholars held that it is muhkamah (established, not abrogated), and Ibn Hazm defended this view with the utmost vigor. On the view that it is muhkamah, it falls under the general that has been specified (al-'amm al-makhsus). Thus the parents and relatives who do not inherit have no bequest owed to them, by the evidence of the verses of inheritance and the hadith. As for the two parents who have no inheritance, such as two slaves, and relatives who do not inherit, a bequest would be obligatory for them on this view; but the position of the majority is contrary to this.

Al-'Abbadi, in al-Ayat al-Bayyinat, reported a consensus that it is abrogated, although a group of scholars said there is no abrogation.

The one who annotates it, may Allah pardon him, says: The verified position is that abrogation definitely occurs in it in part, because the bequest to parents who are heirs and to relatives who are heirs had its ruling lifted after it was established, by consensus. That is abrogation in part, not specification (takhsis), because specification is restricting a general term to some of its individual instances by evidence. But lifting a specific ruling after it has been established is abrogation, not specification, as is evident. It has been established in the science of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) that specifying part of the application of a general term after action has begun is abrogation. To this the author of Maraqi al-Su'ud alludes with his words:

"And if what is specified comes after the action has begun, it is abrogated; and a clear other-than-specifier (is a specifier)."

And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 2, verse 183:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ ﴿for a certain number of days﴾.

Some scholars ('ulama') said: they are three days of every month, and the day of 'Ashura'.

And some scholars said: they are Ramadan. According to this view, Allah, exalted is He, has explained them with His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan [is that in which the Qur'an was revealed]...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 184:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab [Removing the Illusion of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book]):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for those who are able to fast, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor person﴾.

This noble verse, by its apparent meaning, indicates that one who is capable of fasting Ramadan is given the choice between fasting and feeding (the poor). Another verse has come that indicates the obligation of fasting is fixed, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and so on.

The answer to this is in two matters:

The first, which is the truth, is that His saying ﴿And for those who are able to fast, there is a ransom﴾ has been abrogated (mansukh) by His saying ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and so on.

The second: the meaning of "yutiqunahu" (they are able to do it) is "la yutiqunahu" (they are not able to do it), with the negative particle "la" being understood (implied). On this reading the verse is muhkam (clear and not abrogated), and the obligation of feeding falls on one who is unable to fast, such as the very old and the chronically ill. This view is supported by the reading of some of the Companions, "yattawwaqunahu," with a fatha on the ya' and a shadda on the ta' and the waw, both fathah-marked, meaning "they strain themselves to do it while unable to." According to this view, the ransom is obligatory for the very old and the like, and this is the position chosen by al-Bukhari, who relied on the action of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 185:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾. Here he does not specify whether it was revealed during the night of that month or during its day. However, he has specified in another place that it was revealed on the Night of Decree (laylat al-Qadr) in Ramadan. This is in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it during a blessed night﴾ [al-Dukhan: 3]; because the blessed night is, in verification, the Night of Decree. Regarding the meaning of its revelation there are two views:

The first: that it was revealed in it as a whole to the lowest heaven (al-sama' al-dunya), as has been established from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

The second: that the meaning of its being revealed in it is the beginning of its revelation, as some scholars have said.

The Almighty says: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me that they may be guided.﴾

In this verse He states that He, exalted and glorified, is near and responds to the supplication of the one who supplicates. In another verse He makes this response conditional on His will, exalted and glorified, namely His saying: ﴿He will remove that for which you call upon Him, if He wills﴾ [al-An'am: 41].

Some scholars said: the conditioning on His will applies to the supplication of the disbelievers, as is apparent from the context of the verse, while the unconditional promise applies to the supplication of the believers. On this view, their supplication is not rejected: either they are given what they asked for, or something better is stored up for them, or evil is averted from them to an equivalent degree.

Some scholars said: the meaning of "supplication" here is worship, and the meaning of "response" is reward. On this view there is no difficulty.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. His saying ﴿of dawn﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187] explains it. The Arabs call the light of morning a "thread" (khayt), and the dark of night mixed with it a "thread." From this is the saying of Abu Dawud al-Iyadi [Mutaqarib meter]:

"When a dimness (sudfah, the dusky darkness before dawn) lit up for us, and a thread of the morning appeared and shone forth."

And the saying of another [Basit meter]:

"The white thread is the light of morning breaking forth, and the black thread is the concealed wing of the night."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 189:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah﴾

He does not state here explicitly what is meant by "one who fears Allah," but he clarifies it by His saying: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and the angels and the Book and the prophets, and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and for freeing slaves; and establishes prayer and gives zakah; and the ones who fulfill their promise when they promise; and the patient in poverty and hardship and during battle. Those are the ones who have been true, and it is those who are the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]. The statement in the verse is based on the omission of a modifier (mudaf); i.e., "But the one of righteousness is one who fears Allah." It has also been said: "But righteousness is the righteousness of one who fears Allah." A parallel to this verse in the speech of the Arabs is the saying of al-Khansa' [al-Basit]: (p-75)

"Do not become weary of time because of it, whenever she is mentioned; for it is nothing but advance and retreat."

i.e., one who possesses advance (iqbal). And the saying of the poet [al-Mutaqarib]:

"And how can you keep company with one whose companionship has become like that of Abu Marhab?"

i.e., like the companionship of Abu Marhab. And the saying of another [al-Tawil]:

"By your life, youths are not those whose beards have grown, but rather youths are every young man who is generous."

i.e., youths are not the youths of beard growth.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 190:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾. Regarding this, the scholars have three opinions:

The first: that what is intended by "those who fight you" is those whose nature is fighting, i.e., excluding others, such as women, children, the very old and frail, and the people of the monasteries (ṣawāmiʿ).

The second: that it is abrogated (mansūkha, "abrogated" in the sense of naskh) by the verses of the sword that indicate fighting them unconditionally.

The third: that what is intended by the verse is to stir up the Muslims and urge them to fight the disbelievers. It is as if He says to them: "These are the ones I have commanded you to fight; they are your adversaries and enemies who fight you." The most apparent of these is the first, but according to the third opinion the meaning is clarified by and supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress﴾, the verse [to its end].

(p-222) This verse, by its apparent meaning, indicates that they were not commanded to fight the disbelievers except when the disbelievers fought them. Yet other verses have come indicating the obligation of fighting the disbelievers unconditionally, whether or not they fight, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193].

And His saying: ﴿And when the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists wherever you find them, and capture them, besiege them, and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5].

And like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You will fight them, or they will submit﴾ [al-Fath: 16].

The answer to this is in several points:

The first, which is the best and closest of them: that what is intended by His saying ﴿those who fight you﴾ is to stir up the Muslims and urge them to fight the disbelievers. It is as if He says to them: "These whom I have commanded you to fight are your adversaries and enemies who fight you." The verse supporting this meaning is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36]. And the best way to interpret the Qur'an is by the Qur'an.

The second point: that it is abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾. From the standpoint of analysis, this is apparent and very good. Its clarification is that among the profound wisdoms of Allah in legislation is that when He wishes to legislate a great matter upon souls, He may legislate it gradually so that its difficulty is eased through gradualness. Thus, for example, when abstaining from wine was difficult for souls accustomed to it, He first mentioned some of its harms in His saying: ﴿Say: In them is great sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219].

Then after that He prohibited it at certain times and not others, as indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾, the verse [al-Baqarah: 43].

Then, when souls had become at ease with its prohibition in general, He prohibited it absolutely by His saying: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing to] idols, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90].

Likewise, fasting: when it was difficult for souls, He first prescribed it as optional between it and feeding (the poor), then He encouraged fasting along with the option by His saying: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. Then, when souls had become at ease with it, He made it obligatory absolutely by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So whoever sights the month among you, let him fast it﴾, the verse [al-Baqarah: 185].

(p-223) Likewise fighting, according to this opinion, is difficult for souls. He permitted it first without obligation by His saying: ﴿Permission has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged﴾, the verse [al-Hajj: 39].

Then He obligated on them fighting those who fight them, but not those who do not fight them, by His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾.

Then, when their souls became at ease with fighting, He obligated it upon them in a general obligation by His saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them, and capture them, and besiege them﴾, the verse.

The third point: and it is the choice of Ibn Jarir, and it appears to me that it is the correct view, that the verse is muhkam (decisive, not abrogated), and its meaning is: fight those who fight you, i.e., those whose nature is that they fight you.

As for the disbeliever whose nature is not fighting, such as women, offspring, the very old and frail, monks, and the people of the monasteries, and whoever offers you peace, then do not transgress by fighting them, because they do not fight you. This is indicated by the hadiths explicitly prohibiting the killing of a child, the people of the monasteries, a woman, and an aged old man when he is not sought for his opinion.

As for the one who holds an opinion (ṣāḥib al-ra'y), he is killed, like Durayd ibn al-Simmah. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him, interpreted this verse with this meaning, as did Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan al-Basri.

The author, in *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab* (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), said:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ — the verse.

This verse indicates the permissibility of seeking retribution, and Allah has permitted retribution in many verses, such as His saying: ﴿But whoever defends himself after having been wronged — those, there is no blame upon them. The blame is only upon those who wrong people﴾ [ash-Shura: 41], and His saying: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil in speech, except by one who has been wronged﴾ [an-Nisa': 148], and His saying: ﴿And whoever retaliates with the same as was done to him and then is wronged — Allah will surely support him﴾ [al-Hajj: 60], and His saying: ﴿And those who, when tyranny strikes them, they defend themselves﴾ [ash-Shura: 39], and His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [ash-Shura: 40].

(p-224) Other verses have come indicating pardon and abandoning retribution, such as His saying: ﴿So overlook with gracious forgiveness﴾ [al-Hijr: 85], and His saying: ﴿And those who restrain anger and pardon people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134], and His saying: ﴿Repel evil with that which is better﴾ [Fussilat: 34], and His saying: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives — indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [ash-Shura: 43], and His saying: ﴿Take what is pardoned, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], and His saying: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Furqan: 63].

The answer to this is in two matters:

The first: Allah explained the legislation of retribution, then guided to the superiority of pardon. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished. But if you are patient, it is better for the patient﴾ [an-Nahl: 126], and His saying: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil in speech, except by one who has been wronged﴾ [an-Nisa': 148], so He permitted retribution with His saying "except by one who has been wronged." Then He guided to pardon with His saying: ﴿Whether you disclose a good or conceal it or pardon an evil, indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent﴾ [an-Nisa': 149].

The second: Retribution has a place where it is fitting, and pardon has a place where it is likewise fitting. Its clarification: among wrongs is that in which patience over it involves violating the sanctity of Allah. Do you not see that if someone's slave-girl is seized from him, for example, and the usurper commits fornication with her, then his silence and pardon regarding this wrong is ugly, weakness and baseness by which the sanctities of Allah are violated? So retribution in such a case is obligatory, and the command in His saying "transgress against him" (the verse) is to be understood accordingly.

That is, just as when the disbelievers initiate fighting, their fighting is obligatory. In contrast, one who is wronged by some of his Muslim brothers with ugly speech or the like, his pardon is better and more excellent. Abu at-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi has said:

*When it is said "forbearance," there is a place for forbearance, but a young man's forbearance in other than its place is ignorance.*

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 196 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if you are prevented, then [send] what is easy of the offering﴾.

The scholars differed regarding the intended meaning of ihsar (being prevented/besieged) in this noble verse. A group said: it is the enemy's blocking of the one in ihram and his preventing him from circumambulating the House.

Another group said: it refers to the confinement of the one in ihram due to illness or the like.

A third group said: it refers to what encompasses all of these: enemy, illness, and the like.

However, His saying after this: ﴿But when you are secure﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196] indicates that the intended meaning of ihsar here is the blocking by an enemy of the one in ihram, because security (amn), when used without qualification in the language of the Arabs, is understood as security from fear, not recovery from illness or the like. This is supported by the fact that the thing from which security is sought is not mentioned, which shows that it refers back to the ihsar previously mentioned. Thus it is established that it is fear of the enemy.

As for what some scholars answered, that amn is also used of security from illness, as in the hadith, "Whoever sneezes and praises God is secured from the shaws, the lawsw and the 'ilawsw" (narrated by Ibn Majah in his Sunan), this is clearly untenable, because the security in it is restricted by being from illness. Were it unrestricted, it would be understood as security from fear. It may also be answered that he fears the occurrence of the mentioned ailments: shawṣ, which is toothache, lawṣ, which is earache, and 'ilawṣ, which is stomach ache, because before they occur to him he is described as fearful of their occurrence; so when he is secured from their occurrence, he is secure from fear.

But if they had actually befallen him, it would not be proper to say he was secured from them, because fear in the language of the Arabs is distress over a future matter, not one that has already occurred. This shows that the claim that amn may be applied to recovery from illness is contrary to the apparent meaning.

The summary of the investigation of this question is in two discussions. The first: the meaning of ihsar in the Arabic language. The second: determining its intended meaning in the noble verse, the opinions of the scholars and their evidences. We shall explain all of that, God willing.

Know that most of the scholars of Arabic say: ihsar is what results from illness or the like. They said: the Arabs say, "ahsarahu al-marad yuhsiruhu" (with a dammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the ṣād), ihsaran. As for what comes from an enemy, it is hasr. The Arabs say, "hasara al-'aduwwu yahsuruhu" (with a fatḥah on the yā' and a ḍammah on the ṣād), hasran, with fatḥah then sukūn. Among the uses of hasr in the Qur'an for what comes from an enemy is His saying: ﴿And seize them and besiege them﴾. Among the uses of ihsar for other than an enemy, as we have mentioned from the scholars of Arabic, is His saying: ﴿For the poor who are restricted in the way of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273], and the saying of Ibn Mayyadah: [Tawil]
"Nor is the desertion of Layla that she has become distant from you, nor that she has been prevented from you by preoccupation."

Some scholars of Arabic reversed this, saying: ihsar is from the enemy and hasr is from illness. This was said by Ibn Faris in al-Mujmal, quoted from him by al-Qurtubi, and al-Baghawi transmitted something similar from Tha'lab.

A group of scholars of Arabic said: ihsar is used for all of them, and likewise hasr. Among those who said that ihsar is used for all of them is al-Farra', and among those who said that both hasr and ihsar are used for all of them is Abu Nasr al-Qushayri.

* *

The author, may God pardon him, says: There is no doubt in the permissibility of applying ihsar to what comes from an enemy, as you will see its verification, God willing. This is the summary of the words of the people of Arabic regarding the meaning of ihsar. As for its intended meaning in the noble verse, the scholars differed on it in three opinions.

The first: that the intended meaning is the enemy's besieging alone, not illness or the like. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Anas, Ibn al-Zubayr, and it is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may God be pleased with them. Marwan and Ishaq also said it, and it is the well-known sound narration from Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and it is the school of Malik and al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on them.

According to this opinion, the intended meaning of ihsar is only what comes from an enemy. So whoever is prevented by illness or the like may not exit the state of ihram until he recovers from his illness, circumambulates the House and performs sa'y, and so he exits ihram by means of an 'umrah. The argument of this view is composed of two matters.

The first: the noble verse, which is His saying: ﴿But if you are prevented, then [send] what is easy of the offering﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], was revealed concerning the polytheists' blocking of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions while they were in ihram for 'umrah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, the sixth year, by the consensus of the scholars.

It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that the case that is the cause of revelation is definitively included, so it is not possible to exclude it by any specifier. Therefore, the inclusion of the enemy's besieging, which is the cause of its revelation, is definite, and it is impossible to exclude it from the verse in any way. It is narrated from Malik, may God have mercy on him, that the case that is the cause of revelation is probably included rather than definitely included, but this is contrary to the view of the majority. He alluded to this in Maraqi al-Su'ud with his words: [Rajaz]
"Affirm the inclusion of the cases that are the cause, and narrate from the Imam a probable view, you will be correct."

By this you know that the application of ihsar in the form of the quadriliteral to what comes from an enemy is undoubtedly correct in the Arabic language, as you see, and that the Noble Qur'an, which is at the highest levels of eloquence and inimitability, was revealed with it.

The second matter: what has been transmitted of reports that one prevented by illness or the like does not exit ihram except by circumambulation and sa'y. Among these is what al-Shafi'i narrated in his Musnad, and al-Bayhaqi from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "There is no ihsar except the ihsar of an enemy."

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: its chain is sound according to the conditions of al-Bukhari and Muslim, and Ibn Hajar also authenticated it. Among these is what al-Bukhari and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he used to say: "Is it not sufficient for you the sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)? If one of you is detained from the Hajj, he circumambulates the House and [performs sa'y between] al-Safa and al-Marwah, then he exits from everything until he performs Hajj in a coming year, and he offers a sacrifice or fasts if he does not find a sacrifice." Among these is what Malik narrated in al-Muwatta', and al-Bayhaqi, from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "The one prevented by illness may not exit until he circumambulates the House and runs between al-Safa and al-Marwah; then if he is compelled to wear some of the garments he must have or [to use] medicine, he does that and makes ransom."

Among these is what Malik narrated in al-Muwatta' and al-Bayhaqi also from Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, from a man of the people of Basra who was an ancient one, that he said: "I set out for Makkah, and when I was in some part of the way my thigh was broken. I sent to Makkah, where Abdullah ibn 'Abbas and Abdullah ibn 'Umar and the people were, and no one permitted me to exit ihram, so I stayed at that water for seven months until I exited by an 'umrah." The Basran man mentioned, whom Malik left unnamed, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said is Abu Qilabah 'Abdullah ibn Zayd al-Jarmi, the teacher and instructor of Ayyub, as narrated by Hammad ibn Zayd from Ayyub from Abu Qilabah. Ibn Jarir narrated it through several chains and named the man Yazid ibn 'Abdullah ibn al-Shikhkhir.

Among these is what Malik narrated in al-Muwatta' and al-Bayhaqi also from Sulayman ibn Yasar: "That Sa'id ibn Huzabah al-Makhzumi was thrown down in some part of the road to Makkah while he was in ihram, so he asked about the scholars at the water where he was, and found Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, and Marwan ibn al-Hakam. He mentioned to them what had befallen him, and all of them commanded him to treat himself with what he must have and to make ransom; and when he recovers, he performs 'umrah and exits from his ihram, then he must perform Hajj in a coming year, and sacrifice what is easy of the offering."

Malik said: "On this matter with us is the ruling concerning one who is prevented by other than an enemy." Umar ibn al-Khattab commanded Abu Ayyub al-Ansari and Habbar ibn al-Aswad, when they missed the Hajj and came on the day of sacrifice, to exit by an 'umrah and then return lawful, then perform Hajj in a coming year and offer sacrifices; whoever does not find [a sacrifice], then fasting three days during Hajj and seven when he returns to his family.

Among these is what Malik narrated in al-Muwatta' and al-Bayhaqi also from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, that she used to say: "The one in ihram is not released except by the House." And it is apparent that she means other than one prevented by an enemy, as al-Zurqani affirmed in his Sharh al-Muwatta'. This is the summary of the evidences of the view that the intended meaning of ihsar in the verse is what comes from the specific enemy, not what comes from illness or the like.

* *

(p-79) The second opinion regarding the intended meaning of ihsar: that it includes what comes from an enemy or the like, and what comes from illness or the like, from all impediments that prevent reaching the Haram. Those who said this view include Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatadah, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, 'Alqamah, al-Thawri, al-Hasan, Abu Thawr, Dawud, and it is the school of Abu Hanifah. The argument of this view regarding its inclusion of the enemy's besieging has already been presented in the argument of the previous view.

As for its inclusion of ihsar by illness, it is what Imam Ahmad, the authors of the four Sunan, Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'Ikrimah, from al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr al-Ansari, may God be pleased with him, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever is broken or lamed has exited, and upon him is another Hajj.'" I mentioned that to Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurayrah, and they said: "He spoke the truth."

In a narration of Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah: "Whoever is lamed, or broken, or ill," and he mentioned its meaning.

In a narration mentioned by Ahmad in the narration of al-Marwazi: "Whoever is detained by a break or illness." This hadith was left without comment by Abu Dawud and al-Mundhiri, and al-Tirmidhi graded it hasan.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab, after quoting this hadith of 'Ikrimah: "It was narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Bayhaqi and others with sound chains." By this you know the strength of the argument of the proponents of this view. The opponents rejected the use of this hadith of 'Ikrimah in two ways.

The first: what al-Bayhaqi mentioned in al-Sunan al-Kubra. He said: "Some people of knowledge, if it is authentic, interpreted it as meaning that he exits after missing [the Hajj] by what one exits by who misses the Hajj without illness. We have transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, established from him, that he said: 'There is no ihsar except the ihsar of an enemy.' And God knows best." End of his words verbatim.

The second way: that his exit mentioned in the hadith is restricted to the case where he stipulated in his ihram that he would exit wherever God detains him by an excuse. The verified view is the permissibility of stipulation in Hajj, by entering ihram and stipulating that his place of exit is wherever God detains him, and there is no weight to the words of one who prohibits stipulation, because it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, that she said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered upon Dubaʻah bint al-Zubayr and said to her: 'Perhaps you intend Hajj?' She said: 'By God, I find myself only ailing.' He said to her: 'Perform Hajj and stipulate, and say: O God, my exit is where You detain me.'" And she was under al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad.

(p-80) Muslim in his Sahih, Ahmad and the authors of the four Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "That Dubaʻah bint al-Zubayr said: 'O Messenger of God, I am a heavy woman, and I wish to perform Hajj; how do you command me? Shall I enter ihram?' He said: 'Enter ihram and stipulate that my exit is where You detain me.' He said: 'So she reached [the goal].'"

In a narration of al-Nasa'i: and he said: "Indeed for you with your Lord is what you stipulated."

* *

The third opinion: regarding the intended meaning of ihsar, that it is what comes from illness or the like specifically, not what comes from an enemy.

We have already mentioned that this is what is transmitted from most of the people of the language. The exit from the ihsar of an enemy, according to those who hold this view, is permitted only because it is an omission of the distinguishing factor and taking the ruling of the unmentioned from the mentioned. The ihsar of an enemy, in their view, is attached to the ihsar of illness by negating the distinguishing factor.

The rejection of this view is clear from what we have already set out: the noble verse was revealed concerning the siege of the enemy at al-Hudaybiyah, and the occasion of its revelation is definitive in its inclusion, as the majority of scholars hold, and this is the correct position.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: What appears to us to be preponderant on the basis of evidence among the views mentioned is the position of Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad in the more well-known of his two reports, that the intended meaning of *ihsar* (impediment, being prevented from completing the rites) in the verse is the impediment caused by the enemy, and that whoever is afflicted by illness or something similar may not exit the state of ihram except by performing *'umrah*. This is because this is the situation in which the verse was revealed, and it is indicated by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So when you are secure﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

This is especially so according to the view of those scholars who say that a concession (*rukhsah*) does not extend beyond its proper place, and this is the view of a group of the people of knowledge.

As for the hadith of 'Ikrimah, which he narrated from al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr, Ibn 'Abbas, and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them all, it cannot bear the weight of proof, because it must be understood as referring to the case where the person made this stipulation at the time of entering ihram. This is shown by the hadith of 'A'ishah in the two *Shaykhayn* (al-Bukhari and Muslim), which we mentioned earlier, and by the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in Muslim and the authors of the *Sunan* and others, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Duba'ah bint al-Zubayr ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib: 'Perform Hajj and stipulate.'" Had exiting the state of ihram been permissible without a stipulation, as is understood from the hadith of al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr, the stipulation would have served no purpose. The hadith of 'A'ishah and Ibn 'Abbas concerning stipulation is more authentic than the hadith of 'Ikrimah from al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr. Reconciling between the evidences is obligatory when it is possible, and he alluded to this in *Maraqi al-Su'ud* with his words:

*Reconciling is obligatory wherever it is possible; only when it is not, is abrogation clearly to be applied to the later.*

It is possible to reconcile the two hadiths by understanding the hadith of al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr as referring to the case where the stipulation was made at the time of ihram. Thus it agrees with the two hadiths established in the *Sahih*. If it is said that the hadiths can be reconciled in another way, namely by understanding the hadiths of stipulation as meaning that one may exit ihram without having to make another pilgrimage, and understanding the hadith of 'Ikrimah from al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr and others as meaning that one exits ihram but must then perform another pilgrimage, the evidence for this reconciliation is that the hadiths of stipulation do not mention any further pilgrimage.

As for the hadith of al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He has exited the state of ihram, but he owes another pilgrimage."

The reply is that if the obligation to make a replacement by another pilgrimage or another *'umrah* were required, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have commanded his companions to make up the *'umrah* that the polytheists had prevented them from completing. Al-Bukhari said in his *Sahih*, in the chapter titled "Whoever says there is no replacement for the one who is prevented," the following text: "Malik and others said: He slaughters his offering and shaves wherever he is, and there is no making up (*qada'*) upon him, because the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions at al-Hudaybiyah slaughtered, shaved, and exited from everything before performing the *tawaf* and before the offering reached the House. Then it was not reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded anyone to make up anything or to return for it, and al-Hudaybiyah lies outside the Sacred Precinct (*Haram*)." End of his words, verbatim.

Malik also said in the *Muwatta'* that it reached him that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions exited the state of ihram at al-Hudaybiyah; they slaughtered the offering, shaved their heads, and exited from everything before performing *tawaf* around the House and before the offering reached it. Then it was not known that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded any of his companions, or anyone who was with him, to make up anything or to return to anything. End of his words verbatim from the *Muwatta'*.

What we have mentioned is not opposed by what al-Waqidi narrated in *al-Maghazi* through the chain of al-Zuhri, and through the chain of Abu Ma'shar and others, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded his companions to perform *'umrah*, and none of them stayed behind except those who had been killed at Khaybar or had died, and a group who had not witnessed al-Hudaybiyah went out with him as pilgrims for *'umrah*, and their number was two thousand. This is because al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "What I understand from the reports of the people of the military expeditions (*maghazi*) resembles what I have mentioned, because we know from the widely transmitted accounts that there were well-known men with him at the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and then he performed the *'umrah* of making up (*'Umrat al-Qada'*), and some of them stayed behind in Madinah without any necessity regarding themselves or their wealth." End of quotation.

So this al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, affirmed with certainty that well-known men among them stayed behind without any necessity regarding themselves or their wealth. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that the one who affirms takes precedence over the one who negates.

Ibn Hajar said in *al-Fath*: "This can be reconciled with the previous report, if it is authentic, by saying that the command was in the manner of recommendation (*istihbab*), because al-Shafi'i is certain that a group stayed behind without an excuse."

Al-Shafi'i also said regarding the *'umrah* of making up: "It was called the *'Umrat al-Qada'* and *al-Qadiyyah* only because of the settlement (*al-Muqadah*) that took place between the Prophet (ﷺ) and Quraysh, not because they were obligated to make up that *'umrah*." End of quotation.

Al-Waqidi narrated something similar from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, as Ibn Hajar stated.

Al-Bukhari said in his *Sahih*, in the aforementioned chapter, the following text: "Rawh said, from Shibl, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: 'The replacement is only upon the one who breaks his Hajj by sexual enjoyment (*talladhdhudh*). As for the one who is prevented by an excuse or something else, he exits the state of ihram and does not return.'" End of the relevant point, verbatim.

Something similar was also reported from Ibn 'Abbas by another chain, which Ibn Jarir recorded through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from him, and in it: "If it was the obligatory Hajj (*Hajj al-Islam*), then he must make it up, and if it was not the obligatory one, then there is no making up upon him." End of his words.

When you know this, and know that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is among those from whom 'Ikrimah narrated the hadith reported from al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr, and that the one who narrates a hadith is among the people most knowledgeable of it, especially if he is Ibn 'Abbas, for whom the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed that he be taught the interpretation (*ta'wil*), and he explicitly states that the meaning of the Prophet's words in the hadith of al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr, "he owes another pilgrimage," refers to the case where the obligation is the obligatory Hajj, then you know that the first reconciliation which we mentioned is the one that is definitive, and it was chosen by al-Nawawi and other scholars of the Shafi'i school, and that the last reconciliation is not valid, because the pilgrimage mentioned must be understood as the obligatory Hajj. End of his words.

As for the view of those who say that there is no impediment except by the enemy alone, and that the one impeded by illness may not exit the state of ihram until he recovers, performs *tawaf* around the House and between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and then exits from everything, and performs Hajj in a following year, sacrificing or fasting if he does not find an offering, as established in the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, as already mentioned:

This view, from their standpoint, regards the sick person as not being impeded. He is like the one who enters ihram and then misses the standing at 'Arafah; he performs *tawaf* and *sa'y*, performs Hajj in a following year, and sacrifices or fasts if he does not find an offering. End of his words.

* * *

In this issue there is a fourth view: that there is no impediment after the Prophet (ﷺ) by any excuse whatsoever. This view is very weak, and scholars do not rely upon it, because the ruling on impediment is explicitly stated in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and no abrogation (*naskh*) of it has been reported. Therefore, claiming that it is removed without clear evidence is evidently baseless, as you can see. This is the summary of the discussion concerning the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But if you are impeded﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

As for His words: ﴿then [an offering] of what is easy to obtain of sacrificial animals﴾, the majority of scholars hold that what is intended is a sheep or more, and this is the position of the four imams. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, also said this, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas. Tawus, 'Ata', Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliyah, Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and others also said this, as Ibn Kathir and others reported from them.

A group of the people of knowledge said that what is intended by "what is easy to obtain of sacrificial animals" is only camels and cattle, not sheep. This view is reported from 'A'ishah, Ibn 'Umar, Salim, al-Qasim, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and others.

Ibn Kathir said: "The apparent basis for what these scholars held is the story of al-Hudaybiyah, for none of them is reported to have slaughtered a sheep in his exit from the state of ihram on that occasion; they only slaughtered camels and cattle."

Thus in the two *Sahihs* from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us to share in camels and cattle, each seven of us for one cow."

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: It is not hidden that the verified position in this matter is that what is intended by "what is easy to obtain of sacrificial animals" is whatever is readily available and is called a sacrificial animal (*hady*). This includes all livestock: camels, cattle, and sheep. If a sheep is readily available, it suffices, and a camel or a cow is more preferable for sufficiency.

It is also established in the two *Sahihs* from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) once sent a sheep as an offering."

* * *

**Branches related to this issue**

**First branch:** If the one who is impeded has an offering with him, he is obligated to slaughter it by consensus (*ijma'*). The majority of scholars hold that he slaughters it at the place where he was impeded, whether it is within the non-sacred area (*hill*) or the Sacred Precinct (*haram*). The Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions slaughtered at al-Hudaybiyah. Al-Shafi'i and others affirmed with certainty that the place where they slaughtered at al-Hudaybiyah was in the non-sacred area, not the Sacred Precinct, and he relied for this on clear evidence from the Qur'an, namely the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram, and [prevented] the offerings from reaching their place of sacrifice﴾ [al-Fath: 25]. This is an explicit text that the offering in question had not reached its place of sacrifice. Had it been within the Sacred Precinct, it would have reached its place.

Ya'qub ibn Sufyan narrated through the chain of Mujammi' ibn Ya'qub, from his father, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions were prevented, they slaughtered at al-Hudaybiyah, and Allah sent a wind which carried their hair and cast it into the Sacred Precinct." Ahmad al-Badawi al-Shinqiti included this in his poetic compilation on the military expeditions, concerning the battle of al-Hudaybiyah, with his words:

*They slaughtered and shaved, and a wind carried their hair toward the House, having been swept up.*

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in *al-Istidhkar*: "This indicates that they slaughtered in the non-sacred area." Ibn Hajar criticized this in *Fath al-Bari*: "It is possible that they sent their offerings with someone who would slaughter them in the Sacred Precinct." He said: "There is a hadith of Ibn Jundub ibn Jundub al-Aslami, who said: 'I said: O Messenger of Allah, send the offering with me so that I may slaughter it in the Sacred Precinct.'" It was recorded by al-Nasa'i through the chain of Isra'il, from Majza'ah ibn Zahir, from Najiyah, and al-Tahawi recorded it by another route from Isra'il, but he said "from Najiyah, from his father." However, it does not follow from the occurrence of this that it is obligatory. Rather, the apparent point of the story is that most of them slaughtered in their place while they were in the non-sacred area, and this indicates permissibility, and Allah knows best. End of Ibn Hajar's words.

Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, differed from the majority on this issue and said: "The impeded person may slaughter his offering only in the Sacred Precinct. He must send it to the Sacred Precinct, and when the offering reaches its place, he exits the state of ihram." He said: "The place where the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions slaughtered at al-Hudaybiyah was at the edge of the Sacred Precinct." He relied on His words after this verse: ﴿And do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. This argument is rejected by what we have already mentioned, that the Prophet (ﷺ) slaughtered in the non-sacred area, and that the Qur'an indicates this. Also, His words ﴿And do not shave your heads﴾ are connected to His words ﴿And complete the Hajj and 'Umrah for Allah﴾, not to His words ﴿then [an offering] of what is easy to obtain﴾. Or the meaning of "its place" is the place where it is permissible to slaughter it, and that is relative to the impeded person wherever he is impeded, even if it is in the non-sacred area.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The verified position in this issue is the detailed distinction held by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, namely that if he is able to send the offering to the Sacred Precinct, he sends it, and he does not exit the state of ihram until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice, since there is no basis for slaughtering the offering in the non-sacred area when the Sacred Precinct is accessible. If he is unable to send it to the Sacred Precinct, he slaughters it in the place where he was impeded, in the non-sacred area.

Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih, in the chapter "Whoever says there is no substitute for the one who is prevented (al-muhsar)," the following text: (p-85) Rawh narrated to us from Shibl, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The substitute is only due from the one who breaks his Hajj by indulging in pleasures. As for the one who is held back by an excuse or something else, he is released and does not return." And if he has an animal for sacrifice (hady) with him while he is prevented, he slaughters it if he is unable to send it; but if he is able to send it, he does not come out of ihram until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice. End of quotation. The purpose of it is in its wording, and it is not right to deviate from it, because its meaning is clear, as you see.

* *

Second branch: If the one who is prevented does not have an offering with him, is he required to buy an offering and not be released until he sacrifices it, or may he be released without an offering? The majority of scholars held that the offering is obligatory upon him, based on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you are prevented, then [send] what offering is feasible﴾. So it is not permissible for him to release himself without it if he is able to provide it. Ashhab, one of the companions of Malik, agreed with the majority, while Malik and Ibn al-Qasim differed from the majority on this question and said: there is no offering upon the one who is prevented if he did not drive it with him before the prevention.

The majority's proof is clear, namely the words of Allah: ﴿And if you are prevented, then [send] what offering is feasible﴾. His making "what offering is feasible" conditional upon being prevented is the making of the consequence conditional upon its condition. This indicates the obligation of the offering upon being prevented for the one who wishes to release himself by it, a clear indication as you see. If the one who is prevented is unable to provide the offering, is a substitute for it obligatory upon him or not?

Some scholars said: there is no substitute if he is unable to provide it. Among those who said there is no substitute for the offering of the one who is prevented is Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him; for the one who is prevented, in his view, if he does not find an offering, remains in ihram until he finds an offering or performs the circumambulation of the House.

Some of those who said there is no substitute for it said: if he does not find an offering, he is released without it, and if an offering becomes available to him afterwards, he sends it.

A group said: if he does not find the offering, he has a substitute. The people of this view differed about the substitute for the offering. Some of them said it is fasting ten days, by analogy with the one who is unable to provide what is feasible of offering in tamattu'. Imam Ahmad adopted this view, and it is one of the two reports from al-Shafi'i. The most authentic report among the Shafi'is regarding the substitute for the offering of the one who is prevented is that it is by feeding (the poor), as al-Shafi'i stated in the Kitab al-Awsat. So the sheep is valued, and its value is given in charity as food. If he is unable, he fasts one day for each mudd. It was also said that it is feeding like the feeding of the expiation for harm (fidyat al-adha), which is three sa' for six poor persons. It was also said: its substitute is fasting three days. (p-86) It was also said: its substitute is fasting by estimation: the sheep is valued, and the quantity of mudds equal to its value is determined, and he fasts one day for each mudd. None of these opinions has a clear proof, and the closest of them is analogy with tamattu'. And Allah knows best.

* *

Third branch: Is the one who is prevented, when he wishes to release himself, required to shave or cut short (the hair), or is nothing of that required of him?

The scholars differed on this. Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, and Muhammad held that there is no shaving or cutting upon him. This is one of the two reports from Imam Ahmad, and it is the apparent meaning of al-Khiraqi's words. The people of this view argued that Allah said: ﴿then [send] what offering is feasible﴾ and did not mention shaving; had it been obligatory, He would have specified it. Abu Hanifa and Muhammad argued for the non-obligation of shaving: shaving is not known to be a rite (nusuk) except after performing the acts, and before that it is a violation (jinayah), so one is not commanded to do it. This is why a slave or a woman, when their master or husband prevents them, are not commanded to shave, by consensus.

There are two reports from al-Shafi'i regarding the shaving of the one who is prevented, based on the disagreement over shaving: is it a rite or a release from a prohibition? A group of scholars, including Malik and his companions, held that the one who is prevented must shave.

The author of this commentary, may Allah forgive him, says: What appears to us to be preponderant by evidence is the view of Malik and his companions regarding the obligation of shaving, due to the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you are prevented, then [send] what offering is feasible. And do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice.﴾

And because it is established in authentic hadiths from him (ﷺ) that "he shaved when the polytheists prevented him in the year of Hudaybiyah while he was in ihram, and he commanded his companions to shave." He said: "O Allah, have mercy on those who shave." They said: "And those who cut short, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "O Allah, have mercy on those who shave." They said: "And those who cut short, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "And those who cut short."

These are clear proofs that shaving is not dropped for the one who is prevented. As for the analogy of those who said that shaving is not obligatory on the rest of the rites from which one is prevented, the apparent drop is evident; for circumambulating the House and running between al-Safa and al-Marwah, for example, are all things the one who is prevented is prevented from and kept from, so they drop from him, because a barrier is placed between him and them.

But shaving is not placed beyond his reach while he is able to do it; so there is no basis for its dropping. There is no doubt that what the texts of the Law point to as preponderant is that shaving is a rite for the one who completes his rite, for the one who misses the Hajj, for the one prevented by an enemy, and for the one prevented by illness.

According to the correct view that shaving is a rite, the one who is prevented releases himself by three things: intention, slaughtering the offering, and shaving. According to the view that shaving is not a rite, he releases himself by intention and slaughtering.

* *

Fourth branch: It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he slaughtered before shaving in the 'Umrah of Hudaybiyah and in the Farewell Hajj. The Qur'an indicates that slaughtering before shaving is in two places. The first is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice﴾.

The second is the words of Allah, the Exalted, in Surah al-Hajj: ﴿that they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of Allah on known days over what He has provided for them of the cattle* [al-Hajj: 28].

So the meaning of His words: ﴿that they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them﴾ (al-Hajj: 34) is mentioning His name at the slaughter of the camels, by consensus. He, the Exalted, said after it, joining with thumma, which denotes sequence: ﴿then let them complete their rites (tafath)﴾ (al-Hajj: 29). Completing the tafath includes, without dispute, removing hair by shaving. This is an explicit text commanding the placing of slaughter before shaving. From the use of tafath for hair and the like, is the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt (Basit):

They shaved their heads, not shaving tafath, and did not strip from them lice and nits.

Some narrated Umayyah's verse as follows (Basit):

Their armpits having been sprinkled, they did not cast off tafath, and removed from them lice and nits.

And from it is another's saying (Wafir):

They completed tafath and vows, then departed toward Najd, and did not wait for Ali.

These texts clearly indicate that shaving comes after slaughtering. However, if the pilgrim or the 'Umrah performer reverses the order and shaves before slaughtering, it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Farewell Hajj that there is no blame in that. The expression of "no blame" indicates by its generality the dropping of both sin and sacrifice together. It was said concerning one who shaved before slaughtering, whether prevented or otherwise, that a sacrifice is due from him. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated through al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Alqamah, who said: "He owes a sacrifice." Ibrahim said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated to me from Ibn Abbas the same. He mentioned this regarding the one who is prevented.

(p-88) Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar: The apparent view is that a sacrifice is not obligatory, for lack of evidence.

The author of this commentary, may Allah forgive him, says: The apparent view is that the evidence for those who said so is the hadiths reporting that when the polytheists prevented him (ﷺ) in the year of Hudaybiyah, he slaughtered before shaving and commanded his companions to do likewise. Among these is what Ahmad, al-Bukhari and Abu Dawud narrated from al-Miswar and Marwan in the account of the 'Umrah of Hudaybiyah and the treaty, that when the Prophet (ﷺ) finished the matter of the document, he said to his companions: "Arise, slaughter, then shave."

Al-Bukhari also narrated from al-Miswar that "the Prophet (ﷺ) slaughtered before shaving and commanded his companions to do likewise." End of quotation. His action and his command indicate that this is what is required of the one who is prevented. And whoever puts shaving before slaughtering has reversed what the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded, and whoever neglects a rite owes a sacrifice.

The author of this commentary, may Allah forgive him, says: What the texts of the authentic Sunnah indicate is that slaughter precedes shaving; but whoever shaves before slaughtering, there is no blame upon him regarding sin or sacrifice. Among this is what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded in their Sahihs from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that "the Prophet (ﷺ) answered one who asked him, having supposed shaving before slaughter, so he slaughtered before shaving, by saying to him: 'Do it, and there is no blame.'"

Among this is what the two Shaykhs also recorded in their Sahihs from Ibn Abbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the slaughter, the shaving, the stoning, and the ordering of them, earlier and later, and he said: 'There is no blame.'"

In a report of al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah: "A man asked him and said: 'I shaved before I slaughtered.' He said: 'Slaughter and there is no blame.' And he said: 'I stoned after the evening came.' He said: 'Do it and there is no blame.'"

In a report of al-Bukhari: "A man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'I visited (the House) before I stoned.' He said: 'There is no blame.' He said: 'I shaved before I slaughtered.' He said: 'There is no blame.'" Hadiths of this kind are numerous. They clearly indicate that whoever shaves before slaughtering incurs neither sin nor expiation (fidyah), because his saying "there is no blame" is an indefinite noun in the context of negation, combined with la and built on the fatha; and an indefinite noun in such a state is an explicit text in generality. So the hadiths are an explicit text in the generality of negation for all kinds of blame, of sin and expiation. And Allah knows best.

It is not evident that the mentioned hadiths are to be applied to one who shaved before slaughter out of ignorance or forgetfulness. Although the context of the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, agreed upon, indicates that the questioner was ignorant, some of those hadiths in the Sahih do not mention forgetfulness or ignorance, so their generality must be retained until a proof indicates restriction to forgetfulness or ignorance. It has also been established in the science of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) that the answer to the questioned, to one who asked, is not governed by the concept of contrary implication (mafhum al-mukhalafah), because restricting the stated words by mention to match the answer to the question does not specifically determine that it serves to exclude the implied meaning from the ruling of the stated meaning. Al-Shinqiti alluded to this in Maraqi al-Su'ud in the discussion of the impediments to considering mafhum al-mukhalafah, with his words, adding to what prevents its consideration:

Or ignorance of the ruling, or the utterance arising in response to the question, or it proceeded in accordance with what predominated.

As will be explained in the discussion of Allah's words: ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ (al-Baqarah: 229). From this you know that the description of lack of awareness mentioned in the question has no implied meaning.

Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar: The question of some of them being conditioned by lack of awareness does not imply that others' questions are so, so as to say that the ruling is restricted to the state of lack of awareness; nor is it permissible to disregard it by attaching deliberate action to it.

Hence it is known that relying on restriction by the description of lack of awareness mentioned in the question of some questioners is not beneficial for the intended aim. End of quotation of the relevant part in his own words.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 198:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no sin upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord﴾. Here he does not specify what this bounty is, the seeking of which during the Hajj is not sinful. In other verses he indicated that it is the profit of trade, as in His saying: ﴿And others travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10], because "travelling through the land" (al-darb fi al-ard) is an expression for journeying for trade, so the meaning of the verse is: they travel seeking the profit of trade. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse through the land and seek of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9], that is, through selling and trading, as evidenced by His saying before it: ﴿And leave off trading﴾ [al-Layl: 9]. That is: when the Friday prayer is over, seek the profit which was forbidden to you at the time of its call (to prayer).

We have already mentioned, in the introduction to this book, that the predominance of a specific meaning being intended in the Qur'an indicates that it is the one meant, since interpreting it according to what is most prevalent is preferable. And there is no disagreement among the scholars that the bounty mentioned in the verse is the profit of trade, as we have mentioned.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 199:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾ [al-Baqarah: 199]. He did not specify here the place from which the departure is commanded, which is expressed by the word (ḥaythu) (p-90), which is a term indicating place, just as (ḥīna) indicates time.

But He clarifies that by His saying: ﴿So when you depart from ʿArafat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198]. The occasion of its revelation was that the Quraysh used to stand on the day of ʿArafah at al-Muzdalifah, saying: "We are the inhabitants of the House of Allah, and it is not fitting for us to leave the Haram, for ʿArafat is outside the Haram, and the general people stand at ʿArafat." So "Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims to depart from where the people depart," and that is ʿArafat, not from al-Muzdalifah as the Quraysh did.

This is the view of the majority of scholars, and Ibn Jarir reported a consensus upon it. Accordingly, the particle (thumma) here denotes sequence in mention, meaning the conjoining of one sentence to another and their ordering in the sequence of mention in general. A parallel to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The freeing of a neck﴾ ﴿or feeding on a day of severe hunger﴾ ﴿an orphan near of kin﴾ ﴿or a needy man in misery﴾ ﴿then he became of those who believed and advised one another to patience and advised one another to compassion﴾ [al-Balad: 13, 14, 15, 16, 17].

And the saying of the poet: [Al-Khafif]

"Indeed, he who ruled, then his father ruled after him, then his grandfather had ruled before that."

Some scholars said: what is meant by His saying ﴿Then depart﴾ is the verse; that is, from Muzdalifah to Mina. Accordingly, what is meant by "the people" is Ibrahim.

Ibn Jarir said regarding this view: Were it not for the consensus of the authorities against it, it would have been the more preponderant.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Adorned for those who disbelieve is the life of this world, and they mock those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 212]. He does not explain here the mockery of these disbelievers toward these believers, but He explains it in another place, that it is laughing at them and winking at them. That is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾ ﴿And when they passed by them, they winked at one another﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 34, 35].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But those who feared Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. He does not explain here the superiority of these believers over these disbelievers, but He explains that in other places, such as His saying: ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾ ﴿upon couches, looking on﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 34, 35].

And His saying: ﴿Are these the ones about whom you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy? [To them it was said], "Enter Paradise; no fear will be upon you, nor will you grieve."﴾ [al-A'raf: 49].

(p-91) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But it may be that you dislike a thing while it is good for you﴾. Here He did not describe this good as abundant, although He described it as abundant in His saying: ﴿And if you dislike them, it may be that you dislike a thing and Allah places in it much good﴾ [An-Nisa': 19].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 217:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will not cease to fight you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217]. He did not clarify here whether they were able to do that or not. However, He clarified in another place that they were not able, and that despair came upon them of turning the believers back from their religion. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Today those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾ — the verse [al-Ma'idah: 3]. And He clarified in other places that He makes the religion of Islam prevail over every religion, as in His saying in "Bara'ah" (Surah al-Tawbah), "al-Saff" and "al-Fath": ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion﴾ [al-Tawbah: 33].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕
