The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab) [Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book]:

(p-225) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever — those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless﴾.

This noble verse indicates that apostasy does not nullify deeds except with the condition of dying in disbelief, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾.

Other verses have come indicating that apostasy nullifies deeds absolutely, even if one returns to Islam; so everything he did before apostasy is nullified by apostasy, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the faith, his deed has become worthless﴾ — the verse [al-Ma'idah: 5].

And His saying: ﴿If you associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be worthless﴾ — the verse [al-Zumar: 65].

And His saying: ﴿And if they had associated others with Allah, what they used to do would have been lost from them﴾ [al-An'am: 88].

The answer to this is that these are among the issues of the conflict between the absolute (mutlaq) and the restricted (muqayyad) texts, so the absolute is interpreted in light of the restricted. Thus the absolute verses are restricted by dying in disbelief. This is what the principles require, and it is the position of Imam al-Shafi'i and those who agreed with him. Malik differed on this question and gave precedence to the verses of unrestricted statement. The saying of al-Shafi'i on this question is more consistent with the principles. And Allah knows best.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Say: In them is great sin﴾. He did not specify here what this great sin is. But He explained it in another verse, that it is the causing of enmity and hatred among them, and the barring from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer. That is His saying: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise between you through intoxicants and gambling, and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91].

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 221:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women﴾ [the verse]. The apparent generality of this includes the People of the Book (kitabiyyat) women. However, He clarified in another verse that the women of the People of the Book are not included in this prohibition, and that is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5]. If it is said: the women of the People of the Book do not fall under the name "polytheists," as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists were not going to depart﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 6],

• and His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1],

• and His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture, nor the polytheists, would like that any good be sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105]. Conjunction (al-'atf) requires difference. The answer is that the People of the Scripture are included in the name "polytheists," as He stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿The Jews say, "Ezra is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." That is their statement from their mouths; they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them. May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded? They have taken their scholars and their monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, the son of Mary. And they were not commanded except to worship one God; there is no deity except Him. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30–31].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [the verse].

This verse, by its apparent meaning, indicates the prohibition of marrying every disbelieving woman. Also His saying, may He be exalted, supports this: ﴿And do not hold on to marriage ties with disbelieving women﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]. But another verse came indicating the permissibility of marrying some disbelieving women, namely the free women and the kitabiyyat, and that is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them; [and lawful for you are] chaste women from among the believing women and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5].

The answer is that this noble verse specifies His saying: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women﴾, i.e., those who are not kitabiyyat, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) related the consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) on this.

As for what is narrated from Umar, that he disapproved of Talhah marrying a Jewish woman and of Hudhayfah marrying a Christian woman (p-226), he only disliked marrying kitabiyyat women lest people become disinclined toward Muslim women, or for other meanings, as Ibn Jarir stated.

**[p. 92]** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when they have purified themselves, then come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾. Here He did not specify this place, the place commanded for intercourse, which is expressed by the word "where." However, He clarified in two verses that what is meant by it is intercourse in the front passage (*al-qubul*):

The first is His saying here: ﴿So come to your tilth (harth)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223]. This is because His saying "come" (*fa'tuhunna*) is a command to approach, meaning sexual intercourse, and His saying "your tilth" (*harthakum*) shows that the approach commanded is only in the place of tilth, meaning the sowing of offspring with the seed. That is the front passage and not the rear, as is clear, because the rear is not a place for sowing children, as is necessarily known.

The second is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So now, have relations with them and seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. This is because what Allah has decreed for you is offspring, according to the view of the majority, and it is the choice of Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari). He transmitted it from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hakam, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim. It is known that seeking offspring is only by intercourse in the front passage. Therefore the front passage is the place commanded for the act of relations, meaning intercourse. So the meaning of the verse is: "So now, have relations with them, and let that relations be in the place of seeking offspring, which is the front passage and not other than it, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿and seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], meaning offspring."

It becomes clear to you from this that the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿how you wish﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223] is that the approach should be in the place of tilth in whatever manner the man wishes, whether the woman is lying on her back, or squatting, or on her side, or otherwise. This is supported by what al-Bukhari and Muslim (*al-Shaykhan*), Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Jews used to say: if a man has intercourse with his wife from behind, the child will be born squint-eyed (*ahwal*). So the verse was revealed: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so come to your tilth how you wish﴾."

From this it is evident that Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, held that the meaning of the verse is: come to them in the front passage in whatever manner you wish, even if it is from behind her.

It is established in the science of hadith that the exegesis of a Companion which is related to the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) has the status of being traced to the Prophet (*hukm al-raf'*), as the author of *Talat al-Anwar* stated in his verse, [Rajaz meter]:

*The exegesis of a Companion that relates to the occasion, its being traced up (to the Prophet) is verified.*

Al-Qurtubi said, in his commentary on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So come to your tilth how you wish﴾, the following text: "As for what the opponent has used as evidence, that His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿how you wish﴾ includes all ways by the rule of its generality, there is no proof in it, since it is specified by what we have mentioned, and by sound, fair, well-known hadiths, which twelve Companions related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, with different wordings, all of which converge on the prohibition of intercourse with women in the rear. Ahmad ibn Hanbal mentioned them in his *Musnad*, and Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi and others.

Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi gathered their chains (*turuq*) in a part he named *Tahrim al-Mahall al-Makruh* (The Prohibition of the Detested Place).

Our shaykh Abu al-'Abbas also has a part on this named *Izhar Idbar Man Ajaza al-Wat' fi al-Adbar* (Exposing the Backsliding of Those Who Permit Intercourse in the Rear). I say: this is the truth that is to be followed, and the correct position on the question.

It is not fitting for a believer in Allah and the Last Day to turn in this matter to the slip of a scholar after it has been authenticated from him, and we have been warned against the slips of scholars. It has been related from Ibn 'Umar the opposite of this, and that the one who does it is an unbeliever, and this is what is befitting of him, may Allah be pleased with him. Likewise Nafi' denied the one who reported that from him, as al-Nasa'i mentioned, and it has preceded."

Malik denied that and considered it grave, and he denied whoever attributed that to him. al-Darimi related in his *Musnad* from Sa'id ibn Yasar Abu al-Hubab, who said: "I said to Ibn 'Umar: what do you say about the slave-girls when I make them *tahmid*?" He said: "What is *tahmid*?" So I mentioned the rear to him. He said: "Does any of the Muslims do that?" And he narrated from Khuzaymah ibn Thabit: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'O people, indeed Allah is not shy of the truth; do not come to women in their *a'jaz* (rear).'" A similar report is from 'Ali ibn Talq. He also narrated from Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever comes to a woman in her rear, Allah will not look at him on the Day of Resurrection."

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related in his *Musnad* from Qatadah, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "That is the lesser sodomy (*al-luti-yyah al-sughra*)," meaning coming to a woman in her rear. It is related from Tawus that he said: "The beginning of the practice of the people of Lut was coming to women in their rears." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "When something is established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it is sufficient without anything else." From al-Qurtubi, verbatim.

Al-Qurtubi also said, the following text: Malik said to Ibn Wahb and 'Ali ibn Ziyad, when they informed him that some people in Egypt were speaking about him that he permits that, and he recoiled from that and hastened to deny the transmitter, saying: "They lied about me, they lied about me, they lied about me." Then he said: "Are you not an Arab people? Did not Allah say: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾? And can tilth be except in the place of growth?" Also verbatim from him.

(p. 94) Among what supports that it is not permissible to come to women in their rears is that Allah, may He be exalted, prohibited the front passage during menstruation because of the filth that occurs there, making clear that this filth is the cause of the prohibition by His saying: ﴿Say: it is a harm, so keep away from women during menstruation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222]. Therefore, by even stronger reasoning, the rear is prohibited because of its filth and its inherent impurity. This is not refuted by the permissibility of intercourse with a woman experiencing *istihadah* (irregular bleeding), because the blood of *istihadah* is not as repulsive as menstrual blood, nor like the impurity of the rear, since it is blood from a bursting vein, so it is like blood from a wound. Also supporting the prohibition of intercourse in the rear is the consensus of scholars that a *ratqa'* (a woman whose passage is closed so that intercourse cannot reach her) is a defective wife who may be returned because of that defect.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "Scholars have not differed on that, except for something related from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz through a route that is not strong, that a *ratqa'* cannot be returned for being closed. But the jurists are all in disagreement with that."

Al-Qurtubi said: "In their consensus on this there is evidence that the rear is not a place for intercourse. If it were a place for intercourse, a woman who cannot be reached in the front passage would not be returned. If it is said: the return of the *ratqa'* may be due to the cause of infertility, so this does not contradict that she may be penetrated in the rear, the answer is that infertility is not a ground for return, and if the cause of returning the *ratqa'* were infertility, then infertility would necessitate return."

Al-Qurtubi related the consensus that infertility is not a ground for return, in his commentary on His saying: ﴿So come to your tilth﴾. When it has been verified from these proofs that intercourse with a woman in her rear is forbidden, know that those who were reported to have permitted it, such as Ibn 'Umar, Abu Sa'id and groups of the earlier and later scholars, must be interpreted as meaning by "intercourse in the rear" intercourse with her in the front passage from the direction of the rear, as the hadith of Jabir explains. And reconciliation (*al-jam'*) is obligatory when it is possible. Ibn Kathir said in his commentary on His saying: ﴿So come to your tilth how you wish﴾, the following text: Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah al-Darimi said in his *Musnad*: "'Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, al-Layth told us, from al-Harith ibn Ya'qub, from Sa'id ibn Yasar Abu al-Hubab, who said: I said to Ibn 'Umar: what do you say about the slave-girls, are they made *tahmid* for?" He said: "What is *tahmid*?" So he mentioned the rear, and he said: "Does any of the Muslims do that?" Likewise Ibn Wahb and Qutaybah related it from al-Layth.

This is a sound chain and a clear explicit statement from him of the prohibition of that. So everything reported from him that is open to interpretation, and that is open, is referred back to this clear (*muhkam*) statement of his, verbatim. You know that His saying: ﴿how you wish﴾ (p. 95) has no evidence in it for intercourse in the rear, because it is ordered with the *fa* of consequence (*al-ta'qibiyyah*) upon His saying: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾. It is known that the rear is not a place of tilth. This is not refuted by the permissibility of intercourse in the folds of the belly, the thighs, the calves, and the like, even though none of these is a place of tilth, because that is called *istimna'* (outercourse), not *jima'* (intercourse). The discussion concerns intercourse, because the approach meant in His saying: ﴿So come to your tilth﴾ is intercourse, and the distinguishing factor exists, because the folds of the belly and the like have no filth in them, whereas the rear has constant filth and inherent impurity.

We have already learned from His saying: ﴿Say: it is a harm, so keep away from women﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222] that intercourse in the place of harm is not permitted.

Some scholars said: the meaning of His saying: ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾ is: from the place which Allah, may He be exalted, commanded you to avoid, because of the harm that occurs there, which is the front passage, and you should not go beyond it to anything else. This view is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and others. According to it, His saying: ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾ is clarified by: ﴿Say: it is a harm, so keep away from women﴾, the verse, because it is known that the place of harm, which is menstruation, is in the front passage. This view ultimately returns in meaning to what we have mentioned. And this view is based on the principle that a prohibition of something is a command to its opposite, because what Allah has forbidden, He has commanded its opposite. That is why the reference in His saying: ﴿Allah has commanded you﴾ to the prohibition in His saying: ﴿and do not approach them until they are purified﴾ is valid. The disagreement about whether a prohibition of something is a command to its opposite is well known in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*), and the author of *Maraqi al-Su'ud* alluded to it in his verse, [Rajaz meter]:

*In the prohibition there is an old disagreement, or that it is a command to concord. And it was said: not definitively, as in the Mukhtasar; and this is, according to al-Subki, an opinion that is not victorious.*

By "old disagreement" he means what was mentioned before this about the disagreement regarding a command to something: is it the very same as a prohibition of its opposite, or does it necessitate it, or is it neither the same nor necessitating it? That is, that disagreement also applies to a prohibition of something: is it the very same as a command to its opposite, or one of its opposites if there are multiple, or does it necessitate that, or is it neither the same nor necessitating it? He added two views concerning the prohibition: the first is that it is a command to the opposite by consensus. The second is that it is definitively not a command to it. He attributed the latter to Ibn al-Hajib in his *Mukhtasar*, and he indicated that al-Subki in *Jam' al-Jawami'* mentioned that he had not seen that view except from Ibn al-Hajib.

(p. 96) Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾ is: from the directions in which it is lawful to approach the woman, and do not approach them from where it is not lawful, such as when they are fasting, or in a state of ihram, or in seclusion (*i'tikaf*).

Abu Razin, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and others besides them said: ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾ means: when they are pure, not menstruating. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 225:

The words of Allah, Exalted:

﴿But Allah will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾

Here he does not explicitly state the meaning of "what your hearts have earned," nor does he mention here what follows from it when one breaks an oath. However, he clarified in Surat al-Ma'idah that what is meant by "what the hearts have earned" is the binding of the oath by intention and determination. He also explained that the obligation in that case, if one breaks the oath, is an expiation (kaffarah), namely: feeding ten needy persons, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. Whoever is unable to do any one of these three, then fasting three days. This is in His saying: ﴿But He will hold you accountable for the oaths you have sworn in earnest. So its expiation is feeding ten needy persons from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. And whoever cannot find [the means], then fasting three days. That is the expiation for your oaths when you have sworn.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 228 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods (qurū')﴾. The apparent meaning of this verse is that it includes all divorced women. However, He clarified in other verses that some divorced women are excluded from this generality, such as pregnant women, whose waiting period is stated to be the delivery of their burden, in His saying: ﴿And for those who carry children, their term is until they give birth to their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. And such as women divorced before consummation, concerning whom it is stated that they have no waiting period at all, in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, then there is for you no waiting period to count concerning them. So provide for them and release them in a fair manner﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49].

As for those who do not menstruate, due to old age or youth, He has clarified that their waiting period is three months, in His saying: ﴿And those who have despaired of menstruation among your women, if you doubt, then their waiting period is three months, and [likewise for] those who have not menstruated﴾ [al-Talaq: 4].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿three qurū'﴾ contains ambiguity (ijmal), because the word qurū' (al-qurʾ) is used linguistically to mean menstruation (al-hayd), and from this is His Messenger's saying (ﷺ): "Leave off prayer during the days of your qurū'." The word qurū' is also used linguistically to mean purity (al-tuhr), and from this is the saying of al-A'sha: [Al-Tawil]

"Do you every day go out on a raid, striving toward its far end with the resolve of your determination,
Leaving behind wealth and high standing among the tribe, for what was lost therein of the qurū' of your women."

It is known that the qurʾ which is lost to the raider from his women is purity, not menstruation. The scholars have differed regarding what is meant by the qurū' in this noble verse: is it the periods of purity or the menstrual periods?

The cause of the disagreement is the homonymy (ishtirak) of qurʾ between purity and menstruation, as we have mentioned. Among those who held that what is meant by qurʾ in the verse is purity are Malik, al-Shafi'i, Umm al-Mu'minin 'A'isha, Zayd ibn Thabit, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, the Seven Jurists (al-Fuqaha' al-Sab'ah), Aban ibn 'Uthman, al-Zuhri, the majority of the jurists of Madina, and this is a narration from Ahmad. Among those who said that the qurū' are menstrual periods were the four Rightly-Guided Caliphs, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Musa, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Abu al-Darda', Ibn 'Abbas, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and a group of the Successors and others, and this is the sound narration from Ahmad.

Each of the two groups argued with the Book and the Sunnah. We have mentioned in the introduction to this book that in such matters we prefer what appears to us to have the stronger evidence. As for those who said the qurū' are menstrual periods, they argued with many proofs, among them His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who have despaired of menstruation among your women, if you doubt, then their waiting period is three months, and [likewise for] those who have not menstruated﴾. They said: the ordering of the waiting period by months upon the absence of menstruation indicates that the original waiting period is by menstruation, and the months are a substitute for the menstrual periods when they are absent. They also argued with His saying: ﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228].

They said: it is the child or the menstruation. They argued with the hadith "Leave off prayer during the days of your qurū'," and said: he (ﷺ) is the explainer of the revelation, and he used the word qurʾ for menstruation, which shows that this is what is meant in the verse. They also argued with the hadith on the slave-woman's waiting period being two menstrual periods, and the hadith on her istibra' being one menstrual period.

As for those who said: the qurū' are periods of purity, they argued with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]. They said: their waiting period for which they are commanded to be divorced is purity, not menstruation, as is the clear sense of the verse. What further clarifies this is His Messenger's saying (ﷺ) in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh): "If it appears to him to divorce her, let him divorce her while she is pure before he touches her, for that is the waiting period as Allah has commanded." They said: the Prophet (ﷺ) clearly stated in this agreed-upon hadith that purity is the waiting period which Allah commanded women to be divorced for, explaining that this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾, and it is a text from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet on the point in dispute.

The one who qualifies it, may Allah forgive him, said: What appears to me is that the evidence of these is this — a decisive matter on the point in dispute — because the axis of the disagreement is whether the qurū' are menstrual periods or periods of purity. This verse and this hadith indicate that they are periods of purity.

Nothing in the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ) opposes this evidence, neither in terms of authenticity nor in terms of explicitness on the point in dispute, because it is an agreed-upon hadith mentioned in the context of explaining the meaning of a verse of the Book of Allah, the Exalted.

The Prophet (ﷺ) clearly stated in it that purity is the waiting period, explaining that this is what Allah, may He be majestic and exalted, intends by His saying: ﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾. So the demonstrative in his saying (ﷺ): "for that is the waiting period" refers to the state of purity in which the divorce occurs, because the meaning of his saying "let him divorce her while she is pure" is: in a state of her being pure. Then he clarified that this state, which is purity, is the waiting period, explicitly stating that this is what Allah intends in His Glorious Book. This is an explicit text that the waiting period is by purity. He used the feminine demonstrative to agree with the feminine predicate. There is no escape from this evidence for one who says they are menstrual periods, except by saying the waiting period is other than the qurū', while the dispute concerns specifically the qurū', as some scholars have said.

This view is refuted by the consensus of the people of the legal usage (al-'urf al-shar'i) and the consensus of the people of the Arabic tongue, that the waiting period of one who observes the waiting period by qurū' is the qurū' themselves, and nothing else added beyond that. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And count the waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], and it is the period of waiting by consensus, and that is what is expressed as "three qurū'", which is the object (ma'mul) of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿they shall wait﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228] in this verse. So it is not valid for anyone to say that upon the divorced woman who observes the waiting period by the qurū' there is something called the waiting period in addition to the three qurū' mentioned in the noble verse, absolutely, as is known.

* *

In al-Qamus: "The waiting period of a woman is the days of her qurū', and the days of her mourning for her husband." This is an explicit statement from it that the waiting period is the qurū' themselves, with nothing added to them. In Lisan al-'Arab: "The waiting period of a woman is the days of her qurū', and her waiting period is also the days of her mourning for her husband, and her abstaining from adornment, whether months or qurū' or the delivery of a child she has conceived from her husband."

This is a conclusive statement of soundness, clarity and explicitness on the point in dispute, such that there is no need for any other discussion with it. It is supported by the indicator of the addition of the ta' in His saying: ﴿three qurū'﴾, since it indicates the masculinity of the counted noun, which is the periods of purity, because it is masculine, whereas the menstrual periods (al-hayḍāt) are feminine.

Some scholars' answer to this is that the word qurʾ is masculine while its referent is feminine, which is the single menstrual period, and that the ta' was brought in observing the word, which is masculine, not the feminine meaning.

It is said in reply: if the word is masculine and its meaning feminine, the ta' is not obligatory with its number; rather, observing the meaning is permissible, so the number is left without the ta', as in the saying of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a al-Makhzumi: [Al-Tawil]

"And my shield, beyond whom I was guarding, was three figures, two young maidens and a woman who has borne children (ma'sir)."

Here he left the word "three" without the ta', considering that the referent of the number is women, although the word "shakhs" that he applied to the female is masculine. And the saying of another: [Al-Tawil]

"Indeed Kilab, this is ten clans, and you are innocent of its ten tribes."

Here the number is without the ta' although "baṭn" is masculine, considering the meaning of "tribe." And likewise the reverse, as in his saying: [Al-Wafir]

"Three persons and three camels, the times have burdened my dependants."

Here he mentioned "thalātha" (feminine number) with "anfus" (feminine in form) being masculine in meaning, since by it are meant male persons; and observing the word is permissible, so it is left without the ta' in the last and the ta' attaches to the first. The attachment of the ta' in such a case is then a mere possibility, and it is not valid to apply it without an indicator that determines it, unlike the number of a noun masculine both in word and meaning, like qurʾ in the sense of purity, where the attaching of the ta' to it is necessary without doubt. What is necessary, which cannot be otherwise, takes precedence over the possible, which could be otherwise and for which no indicator has come, as you see.

If it is said: some scholars have mentioned that the consideration in the gender of the single counted noun is only by the word, and observing the meaning is not permissible except when an indicator points to it, or when that meaning is very frequently intended, and the verse we are discussing has neither of these, Al-Ashmuni said in his commentary on Ibn Malik's verse: [Rajaz]

"Three with the ta' — say it for ten, in counting what its units are masculine,
In the opposite, omit it, etc."

His words are: "The second: the consideration of feminine gender in the singular counted noun, if it is a noun, is by its word. You say: 'thalathat ashkhus' (three persons) intending women, and 'thalath a'yun' (three eyes) intending men, because the word shakhs is masculine and the word 'ayn is feminine. This is so unless the speech is connected to something that strengthens the meaning, or the intention of the meaning is frequent in it. If that is connected to it, observing the meaning is permissible. The first is like his saying: (p-100)

'Three figures, two young maidens and a woman who has borne children,'

and like his saying: 'And indeed Kilab...' the verse. The second is like his saying:

'Three persons and three camels.'"

End of his words.

Al-Sabban said in his gloss on it: "What al-Sharih mentioned refutes what some scholars cited in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿three qurū'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], and ﴿four witnesses﴾ [al-Nur: 4], that the qurū' are periods of purity and not menstruation, and that the testimony of women is not accepted; because ḥayḍ is the plural of ḥayḍa; so if menstruation were intended it would be said thalāth, and if women were intended it would be said bi-arba'a."

The refutation is that what is considered here is the word, and the words qurʾ and shahīd are masculine, so the number is given in its word.

The answer, and God Most High knows best, is that this is contrary to verification. What the induction of the Arabic language indicates is the permissibility of observing the meaning in general. Ibn Hisham affirmed the permissibility of observing the meaning in the word of the number, as al-Suyuti transmitted from him. Indeed the author of al-Tashil and its commentator al-Damamini affirmed that observing the meaning in the singular counted noun is obligatory.

Al-Sabban said in his gloss, the words of which are: "His saying 'then by its word' — its apparent sense is that this is obligatory, and this contradicts what al-Suyuti transmitted from Ibn Hisham and others, that whatever its word is masculine and its meaning feminine, or the reverse, then two options are permissible in it. Ah."

It also contradicts what is in al-Tashil and its commentary by al-Damamini. The wording of al-Tashil deletes the ta' of the three and its sisters if the singular counted noun is feminine in meaning, literally or metaphorically.

Al-Damamini said: "It is derived from it that the consideration in the singular is by meaning, not by word; for this reason it is said: thalathat talahat (three acacia trees)." Then he said in al-Tashil: "Perhaps a masculine is interpreted as feminine, and a feminine as masculine, and the number is brought according to the interpretation." Al-Damamini exemplified the first with such as thalath shukhus, meaning women, and 'ashr abṭun, meaning tribes; and the second with such as thalathat anfus, meaning persons, and tis'at waqā'i', meaning battles. Reflect on this. End of his words.

What al-Tashil and its commentator affirmed, that observing the meaning is obligatory, entails that the qurū' in the verse is necessarily purity, as we have mentioned.

Also in the gloss of al-Sabban: his saying "permissible to observe the meaning" — in the clarification, that (p-101) this is not analogical, and this contradicts what was previously transmitted from Ibn Hisham and others, that whatever its word is masculine and its meaning feminine, or the reverse, two options are permissible in it; i.e., even if there is no indicator favouring the meaning. It also contradicts what was previously transmitted from [al-Tashil] and its commentary, that the consideration is by meaning. Reflect. Ah.

And as for the argument that they are menstruations, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation﴾ [al-Talaq: 4], the verse, it is said in reply: There is nothing in the verse that specifies that the qur' (qur'ū', the term in the verse) means menstruations, because the term aqrā' (plural of qur') is not applied to periods of purity except to periods of purity that are interspersed with menstruation. If menstruation is absent, the designation of periods of purity is absent with it. There is therefore no obstacle to linking the waiting period by months to the absence of menstruation, even though the waiting period is by purity; for the intended purity necessarily entails the presence of menstruation, and when the necessary consequent is negated, the necessitating condition is negated. So the absence of menstruation entails the absence of periods of purity, and it is as if the waiting period by months is also linked to the absence of periods of purity, which is indicated by the absence of menstruation.

As for the argument from the verse: ﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs﴾, it is clearly untenable. For the fact that the qur' means periods of purity does not permit the woman in waiting to conceal menstruation, because the waiting by periods of purity cannot be realised except with menstruation intervening for her. So if she conceals the menstruation, she would be concealing the end of the period of purity; and if she claimed a menstruation, she would not be concealing, since the period of purity has not ended, as is evident.

As for the argument from the hadith, "Leave off prayer during the days of your qur'," it is said in reply: There is absolutely no proof in the hadith for the point in dispute, because it indicates nothing beyond the fact that qur' is applied to menstruation, and this is not disputed.

As for its indicating a prohibition on applying qur' to purity in another place, this is baseless beyond dispute, and there is no disagreement among the scholars who hold that homonymy occurs on this point: that applying a homonym to one of its two meanings in one place is not understood to prohibit applying it to its other meaning in another place.

Do you not see that the word 'ayn is a homonym between, for example, the eye (of sight) and the spring (of water)? Do you say that His applying the word 'ayn to the eye in His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45], the verse, prohibits applying 'ayn in another place to the spring, as in His saying: ﴿therein is a flowing spring﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 12]?

The truth beyond doubt is that a homonym is applied to each of its meanings, or to its meanings, in the context suited to it. The qur' in the hadith "Leave off prayer during the days of your qur'" is suited to menstruation (p-102) and not to purity, because prayer is left off only during the time of menstruation, not the time of purity.

And if applying a homonym to one of its meanings indicated a prohibition on applying it to its other meaning in another place, there would be no homonymy in the language at all, because whatever it is applied to one of them would prohibit its application to the other. This would nullify the very name of homonymy, although we have already cited the explicit statement of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, agreed upon: "The purity is the waiting period." All of this is on the assumption that the hadith "Leave off prayer during the days of your qur'" is authentic, since some scholars have declared it weak and some have declared it sound.

Apparently some of its chains are not below the level of acceptance, but there is no proof in it for the point in dispute.

And even if it did contain proof, it would be rejected by what is stronger than it and more explicit on the point in dispute, namely what we have already cited. Likewise, the waiting period of a slave-woman being two menstruations, on the assumption that it is established from the Prophet ﷺ, does not conflict with what we have already cited, because that is more authentic and more explicit on the point in dispute. Her istibra' (purification-wait) by a single menstruation is a separate question, since the discussion concerns the waiting period (ʿiddah), not istibra'. Some scholars rejected the argument from the verse and the hadith indicating that they are the periods of purity, on the grounds that this entails observing the waiting period by the purity in which the divorce occurred, as the majority who hold that the qur' are periods of purity maintain; it would then follow that the waiting period is two qur' and a fraction of the third. That contradicts what the verse indicates, namely that they are three complete qur'. This is rejected on the grounds that such a thing does not oppose the explicit texts of revelation; the most that can be said is that three qur' is applied to two and part of a third, and its parallel is His saying: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾, where what is meant is two months and a fraction.

As for the claim that this is prohibited in numerical terms, it is answered: The Prophet ﷺ himself stated that the remainder of the purity in which the divorce occurred is a waiting period, clarifying that this is what Allah intends in His Book. And what some of the eminent scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, have mentioned, that the verse and the hadith cited indicate that the qur' are menstruations, is very far from the apparent wording, as you see.

Rather, the wording of the verse and the hadith cited is explicit in its opposite. This is what has become apparent to us in this matter, and Allah Most High knows best, and to Him is the safest attribution of knowledge.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period] if they desire reconciliation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]. The apparent meaning of this noble verse is that the husbands of all divorced women have more right to take them back, with no distinction in this between revocable and other divorces.

Yet He indicated in another place that the one divorced irrevocably has no right of return over her, and that is in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, then there is for you no waiting period [to count] that you could demand from them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49].

This is because divorce before consummation is irrevocable, just as He indicated here that when she has become separated by the completion of the waiting period, there is no right of return over her. This is in His saying: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that﴾; because the reference of "that" in His saying "that" points back to the time of the waiting period, expressed in the verse as ﴿three periods﴾.

Here He stipulated, for the husbands of revocably divorced women to have more right to take them back, that they intend reconciliation through that return, in His saying: ﴿if they desire reconciliation﴾. He did not address the implication of this condition here, but He stated in other places that the husband of a revocably divorced woman who takes her back not with the intention of reconciliation but with the intent to harm her, so that she will ransom herself or the like, his taking her back is unlawful for him. This is indicated by the prohibition in His saying: ﴿And do not keep them, injuring them, to transgress. Whoever does that has wronged himself. And do not take the signs of Allah in jest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231].

So taking back with intent to harm is unlawful by consensus, as the explicit conditional implication in His saying: ﴿And do not keep them, injuring them﴾, the verse, indicates. Its validity in that case is judged by the apparent outward ruling; so if he explicitly declared to the judge that he took her back with intent to harm, he would nullify the return, as we have mentioned. And Allah Most High knows best.

* *

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿(And men have a degree over them)﴾

He did not specify here what this degree is that men have over women, but He alluded to it in another place, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Men are in charge of women by what Allah has given preference to some of them over others and by what they spend from their wealth﴾ [al-Nisa': 34]. Thus He indicated that the man is superior to the woman. This is because maleness is honour and perfection, while femaleness is an innate natural deficiency, and creation seems to agree upon this; for all people adorn the female with kinds of ornament and jewellery, and this is only to compensate for the innate natural deficiency which is femaleness, unlike the male, whose masculine beauty suffices him without jewellery and the like.

Allah Most High has also indicated the woman's innate natural deficiency and weakness in His saying: ﴿Is one who is brought up in ornament, and in disputation is not clear [in expression]?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 18] (p-104), because her upbringing in ornament is evidence of her deficiency, which is intended to be compensated and covered by jewellery, as the poet said:

Ornament is but an adornment against a deficiency, completing beauty when beauty falls short.
But when beauty is abundant, as yours is, it has no need to be embellished.

And because her failure to make her case in disputation when wronged is evidence of innate weakness, as the poet said:

By myself and my family, for whom, when some harm is brought against him, he does not know how to reply; he does not offer the excuse of the innocent, and he remains silent until he is said to be suspicious.

There is no consideration of rare cases among women, because the rare has no ruling.

By His saying: ﴿and by what they spend from their wealth﴾ He indicated that the perfect in his attributes, strength and creation, suits his state of being the guardian over one who is weaker and deficient in creation.

For this wisdom alluded to, his inheritance was made double hers, because whoever is a guardian over another anticipates loss, and whoever is guarded by another anticipates gain; and preferring the one who anticipates loss over the one who anticipates gain is evidently wise.

Just as He indicated the wisdom of the divorce being in the man's hand without the woman's permission by His saying: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾; for whoever knows that his field is unsuitable for cultivation should not be compelled to plough in a field unsuited to cultivation. This meaning is clarified by the fact that the instrument of ploughing is in the man's hand; if he were forced to remain with one who has no need of him until she consents to that, then if she wished to have intercourse with him, his member would not rise or extend to her, and she would be unable to obtain offspring from him, which is the greatest purpose of marriage. Unlike the man, who begets children from her even while she is unwilling, as is self-evident.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾, the verse.

This noble verse indicates by its apparent meaning that every divorced woman observes the waiting period by qur'. And it has come in other verses that some divorced women observe a waiting period other than by qur', such as the elderly and the young, stated in His saying: ﴿And those who have despaired of menstruation... and those who have not menstruated﴾ [al-Talaq: 4], and the pregnant, stated in His saying: ﴿And for those with children, their term is until they give birth to their load﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]; and it has come in another verse that some divorced women have no waiting period at all, namely those divorced before consummation, in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, then there is for you no waiting period [to count] that you could demand from them﴾, the verse [al-Ahzab: 49].

The answer to this is evident: the verse "And divorced women" is general, and the verses cited are more specific than it, so they specify it; thus it is of the general that has been specified.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 229 (part 1 of 7):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Divorce is twice﴾. The apparent meaning of this noble verse is that all divorce is confined to two. However, He, exalted is He, clarified that what is confined to two is the divorce after which revocation (raj'ah) is permitted, not divorce in general. This is shown by His mention of the third pronouncement, after which a husband may not take her back unless she has married another husband. It is the one referred to in His saying: ﴿But if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:230]. According to this view, His saying ﴿or release with kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:229] means non-revocation.

(p. 105) Some scholars said: the third pronouncement is the one mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or release with kindness﴾. This was also narrated as a marfu' report traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

* *

**A note:** Some scholars mentioned that this noble verse, His saying ﴿Divorce is twice﴾, implies that three divorces pronounced in a single utterance take effect. Al-Bukhari indicated this by his chapter heading: "Chapter: On one who permits three divorces, based on the saying of God Almighty: ﴿Divorce is twice; then either retention in kindness or release with kindness﴾."

The apparent intended line of inference for al-Bukhari is what al-Kirmani said: when God said ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:229], we know that in one of the two instances two pronouncements were combined. If combining two pronouncements at once is permissible, then combining three is permissible. Ibn Hajar rejected this, saying it is analogy in the presence of a difference (qiyas ma'a wujud al-farq), and he took the verse as evidence for the opposite.

The author, may God pardon him, said: It is apparent that the argument from the verse is not valid. The intent is not to confine all divorce to two, such that combining two pronouncements in one of the two instances would follow as he mentioned. Rather, the confined divorce means specifically the divorce after which revocation is possible, as we have explained, and as the majority of the scholars of tafsir (exegesis) interpreted the verse. Some scholars said the proof in the verse is that His saying ﴿or release with kindness﴾ is general, covering the pronouncement of three at once. Its lack of clear indication is not hidden. However, the fact that the verse contains no evidence that three divorces in one utterance take effect does not preclude that other proofs establish this. We will mention the proofs for it and the proofs of those who disagreed, and what we consider preponderant on this matter, God willing, along with a full clarification of the essence of the whole discussion at the end of the discourse.

So we say, and in God we seek help: Know that among the evidences of those who hold that three (divorces) are binding together is the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, established in the Sahih, concerning the li'an (mutual imprecation, sworn oaths of accusation and denial between spouses) of 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani and his wife. In it: "When they finished, 'Uwaymir said: I have lied about her, O Messenger of God, if I keep her. So he divorced her three times before the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered him." Ibn Shihab said: "So it became the sunnah of those who perform li'an."

Al-Bukhari narrated this hadith under the chapter heading mentioned earlier. The basis of the proof from it is that he pronounced three in one utterance, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not reject it.

The opponent rejected the argument from this hadith, saying that the separation occurred by the li'an itself, so his pronouncing three did not encounter a valid object (for divorce). This objection was answered: the argument from the hadith is that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not reject his pronouncing three together. Had it been prohibited, he would have rejected it. And if the separation was by the li'an itself, the separation is not indicated by the Qur'an, nor by an explicit sunnah, nor by consensus (ijma'), and scholars differ on this.

Malik and his companions held that the separation occurs by the li'an itself, and it is only realized when both spouses perform li'an together. This is also a narration from Ahmad. Al-Shafi'i and his companions held that the separation occurs by the li'an itself, and takes place when the husband finishes his oaths before the wife's li'an. This is also the view of Sahnun among the companions of Malik.

Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and their followers held that it does not take effect until the judge pronounces it. They relied on the apparent wording of the li'an hadiths. Al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih from Ibn Umar: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) separated a man and a woman who had accused her, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made them swear." He also narrated in his Sahih from Ibn Umar by another route that he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) made a li'an between a man and a woman of the Ansar, and separated them." The rest of the collectors narrated from Ibn Umar. By this you know that the statement of Yahya ibn Ma'in, that the narration with the wording "separated between the two who performed li'an" is an error, refers specifically to the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd mentioned earlier, not in general. The evidence is its establishment in the Sahih from the hadith of Ibn Umar, as you see. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "If he meant the hadith of Sahl, then Sahl is (reliable), otherwise it is rejected." Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari, the text of which is: "It may be taken from this that the statement of Yahya ibn Ma'in and others, declaring the narration with the wording 'he separated between the two who performed li'an' to be erroneous, is meant specifically regarding the hadith of Sahl. Abu Dawud narrated it from the route of Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, from al-Zuhri, from him with this wording, and he said after it: 'No one followed Ibn 'Uyayna in this.' Then he narrated from the route of Ibn 'Uyayna, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Umar: 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) separated the two brothers of Banu al-'Ajlan.'" End of quote. The point of concern is in the wording. We have already mentioned in the hadith of Sahl: "So it became the sunnah of those who perform li'an."

It has been disputed whether this wording is an interpolation (mudraj) from the words of al-Zuhri, making it a mursal (report lacking the companion), which is the view of a group of scholars; or whether it is from the words of Sahl, making it a marfu' and connected (muttasil) report. What supports it being from Sahl's words is what occurred in the hadith of Abu Dawud through the route of 'Iyad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Fihri, from Ibn Shihab, from Sahl, who said: "He divorced her three divorces in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) enforced it, and what was done in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) became a sunnah."

Sahl said: "I was present at this in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and afterward the sunnah continued regarding those who perform li'an that they be separated, and then they never reunite."

Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar: "Its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih."

The author, may God pardon him, said: It is known that what Abu Dawud left without comment is, at the least, of hasan (good) grade in his view. This narration is clear regarding the point of dispute. By it you know that al-Bukhari's argument for the occurrence of three together through the mentioned hadith of Sahl is well placed. This is because one who is acquainted with the subtle indications of al-Bukhari, may God have mercy on him, understands that this wording established in Sunan Abi Dawud matches al-Bukhari's chapter heading, and that he indicated this narration by the heading but did not cite it, because it did not meet his conditions. The clear statement of this distinguished companion in this established narration, "that the Prophet (ﷺ) enforced the divorce of three at once," is refuted by the clarification that his silence and approval (ﷺ) carry no weight, based on the premise that the separation occurs by the li'an itself, as you see.

Uthman al-Batti, and Abu al-Sha'tha' Jabir ibn Zayd al-Basri, one of the companions of Ibn Abbas and among the jurists of the Tabi'un (Successors), held that the separation does not occur until the husband pronounces it. Abu Ubayd held that it occurs by the accusation itself (qadhf). By this you know that the separation occurring by the li'an itself is not a definitive matter, so that the indication of the Prophet's (ﷺ) approval of 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani, regarding pronouncing three at once, established in the Sahih, would not be decisive. Especially since you know that some narrations explicitly state that he (ﷺ) enforced that.

If it is said: there occurred in a hadith of Abu Dawud from Ibn Abbas: "And he ruled that she has no maintenance (qut) and no residence (sukna), because they separate without divorce and without the husband's death."

The answer: this reasoning for not imposing maintenance and residence on the woman who performed li'an, on the ground that there was no divorce or death, may be from Ibn Abbas himself, and it is not traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

This is the apparent view: that Ibn Abbas mentioned the reason for what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ruled regarding the absence of maintenance and residence, and he thought (in his own reasoning) that the reason for it is the absence of divorce and death.

The apparent correct reason for the absence of maintenance and residence is ba'in (irrevocable separation), in its broader meaning which covers its occurrence by divorce or by annulment (fasikh), as shown by the fact that a woman irrevocably divorced has no entitlement to maintenance and residence according to the most sound of the views in terms of evidence.

Thus it is known that the absence of maintenance and residence does not depend on the absence of divorce.

The clearest evidence for this is the sound report from him (ﷺ) of "the hadith of Fatima bint Qays, may God be pleased with her: that her husband divorced her with the last of three pronouncements, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not assign her maintenance or residence." Muslim narrated it in his Sahih, and Imam Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan. It is an explicit, sound text that an irrevocably divorced woman has no maintenance or residence. This hadith is more sound than the hadith of Ibn Abbas mentioned earlier.

The scholars stated explicitly that no sunnah has been established that contradicts this hadith of Fatima. As for what occurred in some narrations from Umar, that he said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say to her: 'She has residence and maintenance.'" Imam Ahmad said: "This is not sound from Umar."

Al-Daraqutni said: "The sunnah is in the hand of Fatima, definitively." Also, that narration from Umar is through the route of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, whose birth was two years after the death of Umar.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: "We bear witness before God, a testimony for which we will be questioned when we meet Him, that it is a lie against Umar and a lie against the Messenger of God (ﷺ). When it is verified that the sunnah is with her and she is the protagonist of the story, know that when she heard Umar's words, 'We will not abandon the Book of God and the sunnah of our Prophet (ﷺ) for the word of a woman, we do not know, perhaps she memorized or forgot,' she said: 'Between me and you is the Book of God.' God said: ﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq 65:1], up to His saying: ﴿You do not know; perhaps God will bring about after that some matter﴾ [al-Talaq 65:1]. So what matter arises after three?" Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ahmad, and Muslim in meaning. Thus it is established that the sunnah is in her hand and the Book of God is with her.

This view, according to the evidence, is the clearest of the views and the most correct. Among the scholars there are opinions regarding the maintenance and residence of the irrevocably divorced woman other than this. Some made both obligatory, some made residence obligatory without maintenance, and some reversed that.

The conclusion is that this hadith of Fatima refutes the reasoning of Ibn Abbas mentioned, and that it is more sound than his hadith. It contains an explicit statement that the falling away of maintenance and residence does not depend on the absence of divorce, but occurs even with an irrevocable divorce. Also, the explicit statement that he (ﷺ) enforced the three together in the mentioned narration is more deserving of consideration than the mentioned statement of Ibn Abbas, because whoever memorized an argument is a proof against whoever did not memorize it. This companion memorized the enforcement of the three, and the affirming (report) takes precedence over the negating one.

If it is said: his (ﷺ) enforcement of the three together from the one who performed li'an, according to the mentioned narration, is not a proof outside of li'an, because in li'an a permanent separation is obligatory. Thus the enforcement of the three reinforces that obligatory matter (p. 109), unlike what occurs outside of li'an.

This is supported by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) became angry at pronouncing three together outside of li'an and said: "Is the Book of God played with while I am among you?!" as narrated by al-Nasa'i from the hadith of Mahmud ibn Labid. The answer is from four aspects. The first: the discussion about the hadith of Mahmud ibn Labid, for it was criticized from two angles. The first: that it is mursal, because it is not established that Mahmud ibn Labid heard from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), although his birth was in his time and his mention among the companions is due to having seen him. Ahmad included him in his Musnad and narrated several hadiths from him, none of which explicitly state hearing.

**Second point:** Al-Nasa'i said, after he cited this hadith: "I do not know of anyone who narrated it other than Makhramah ibn Bukayr, meaning Ibn al-Ashajj, from his father." Makhramah's narration from his father is *wijadah* (a narration taken from a written book without direct hearing). This was said by Ahmad, Ibn Ma'in, and others.

Ibn al-Madini said: "He heard from his father only a little." Ibn Hajar said in *al-Taqrib*: "His narration from his father is *wijadah* from his book, as Ahmad, Ibn Ma'in, and others said, and Ibn al-Madini said: 'He heard from his father only a little.'"

The author, may Allah pardon him, says: As for the first objection, that the hadith is *mursal* (a narration in which a link is missing), it is answered by the fact that it is the *mursal* of a Companion (*mursal al-sahabi*), and the *mursal* narrations of the Companions have the status of connected narrations. Mahmud ibn Labid, mentioned above, narrated most of his reports from the Companions, as Ibn Hajar said in *al-Taqrib* and others.

As for the second objection, that Makhramah's narration from his father is *wijadah* from his book: Muslim included in his *Sahih* several hadiths narrated by Makhramah from his father, and the Muslims are agreed on accepting the hadiths of Muslim unless there is a clear reason that requires rejecting them. Therefore the truth is that the hadith is authentic, but the argument drawn from it is refuted.

**The second aspect:** The hadith of Mahmud does not explicitly state that the Prophet (ﷺ) enforced the three (divorces), nor that he did not enforce them. The hadith of Sahl, according to the narration mentioned there, explicitly states that he enforced them, and the explicit (*mubayyan*) takes precedence over the general or ambiguous (*mujmal*), as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul*). Indeed, some scholars argued for the validity of three divorces pronounced at once with the hadith of Mahmud.

The way they argue from it is that he pronounced three divorces, believing they were binding. Had they not been binding, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have explained that they were not binding, because explanation may not be delayed beyond the time of need.

**The third aspect:** The great imam of the hadith scholars, Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, included the hadith of Sahl under the chapter heading: "Chapter: On one who permitted three divorces." This is evidence that he saw no difference between *li'an* and other cases in using the enforcement of three (divorces) at once as proof.

**The fourth aspect:** It is what will come of the hadiths indicating that three divorces take effect at once, such as the hadith of Ibn Umar and the hadith of al-Hasan ibn Ali, although all of them are subject to criticism. Among those who said that *li'an* is a divorce and not a annulment (*faskh*) were Abu Hanifah, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and Hammad. It is authentically reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, as the hafiz Ibn Hajar transmitted in *Fath al-Bari*, and from al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi: "If he retracts his accusation, his wife is returned to him."

From all of this you know that rejecting the argument from the Prophet's (ﷺ) approval of 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani, as evidence for the effect of three (divorces) at once, on the grounds that separation by *li'an* itself is open to question, is not free from doubt. Even if we grant that separation occurs by *li'an* itself, we do not grant that his (ﷺ) silence contains no evidence. Rather, we say: had it been that it does not occur at once, he would have explained that it does not occur at once, just as he would have explained if the separation were by *li'an* itself, as already mentioned.

\* \*

Among their evidences is the hadith of 'A'ishah, authentic in the *Sahih*, concerning the case of Rifa'ah al-Qurazi and his wife, in which it says: "She said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Rifa'ah divorced me and completely severed my divorce (*fa-batta talaqi*)...'" The hadith. Al-Bukhari included it under the chapter heading mentioned earlier. Her saying "fa-batta talaqi" is apparent evidence that he said to her: "You are divorced irrevocably (*al-battah*)."

The author, may Allah pardon him, says: The argument from this hadith is not conclusive, as it appears to me, because her meaning by her saying "fa-batta talaqi" is: by the occurrence of the third divorce.

This is clarified by the fact that al-Bukhari mentioned in the *Book of Good Manners* from another route that she said: "He divorced me the last of three divorces," and this narration clarifies the meaning of her saying "fa-batta talaqi," and that it was not at one time.

Among their evidences is the hadith of 'A'ishah, authentic in the *Sahih*, which al-Bukhari also included under the same chapter heading: "A man divorced his wife three times, then she married another and he divorced her. The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: 'Is she lawful to the first (husband)?' He said: 'No, until he tastes her sweetness (*'usaylah*) as the first tasted it.'" His saying "three times" is clear that they were gathered together. The argument from this hadith has been objected to on the grounds that it is an abridgment of the story of Rifa'ah. We have mentioned shortly before that some authentic narrations indicate that they were three separate divorces, not gathered together. This objection was answered by saying that someone other than Rifa'ah had with his wife a case like that of Rifa'ah, so there is no obstacle to multiplicity. As for the last hadith being about a different case, this is as the hafiz Ibn Hajar mentioned in his discussion of the story of Rifa'ah, where he said in its text: "This hadith, if it is preserved, the clear implication of its context is that it is a different case, and that each of Rifa'ah al-Qurazi and Rifa'ah al-Nadri had a divorce with a wife of his, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr married each of them and divorced her before he had touched her. So the ruling in their two cases is the same, though the persons differ. By this it becomes clear that the error of one who identified them as one, thinking that Rifa'ah ibn Samaw'al was Rifa'ah ibn Wahb, is evident." Ended; the point of need from it is in his own words.

Among their evidences is what al-Nasa'i transmitted from Mahmud ibn Labid, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was informed about a man who divorced his wife with three divorces all at once, so he rose in anger and said: 'Is the Book of Allah played with while I am among you?!'" We have already mentioned that the way of argument from it is that the one who divorced believed the three gathered together to be binding. Had they not been binding, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have explained that they are not binding, because it is not permissible for him to delay explanation beyond the time of need for it.

Ibn Kathir said about this hadith of Mahmud: "Its chain is good." The hafiz said in *Bulugh al-Maram*: "Its narrators are reliable (*muwaththaqun*)," and he said in *al-Fath*: "Its men are trustworthy (*thiqat*)." If it is said: The Prophet (ﷺ) became angry, and his explicit statement that gathering the divorces together is a play with the Book of Allah indicates that they do not take effect, due to his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever introduces into this matter of ours what is not part of it, it is rejected," and in another narration: "Whoever does an action on which there is not our command, it is rejected." The answer is that his prohibiting it initially does not contradict its taking effect after it is pronounced. This is supported by what will come shortly from Ibn Umar, in his saying to one who asked him: "And if you had divorced her three times, she would have become unlawful to you until she marries a husband other than you, and you would have disobeyed Allah in what He commanded you concerning the divorce of your wife." This is especially so according to al-Hakim's view that it is *marfu'* (traced to the Prophet). This is authentically reported from Ibn Umar in the *Sahih*. It is also supported by what will come, Allah willing, shortly from his *marfu'* hadith in al-Daraqutni, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "She would have separated from you, and it would have been a sin." It is also supported by what will come, Allah willing, from Ibn Abbas with an authentic chain, that he said to one who asked him about three (divorces) pronounced at once: "You did not fear Allah, so He would not have made a way out for you. You disobeyed your Lord, and your wife has become separated from you."

In summary: what befits the one who commits a sin is severity, not leniency by not imposing the ruling. Among their evidences is what al-Daraqutni transmitted from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah! What do you think if I divorced her three times, would it be lawful for me to take her back?' He said: 'No, she would have separated from you, and it would have been a sin.'" In its chain is 'Ata' al-Khurasani, who is disputed. al-Tirmidhi declared him reliable, al-Nasa'i and Abu Hatim said: "There is nothing wrong with him." Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab called him a liar, and many others declared him weak. al-Bukhari said: "Among those who narrated from Malik, none deserves to be abandoned more than him." Shu'bah said: "He was forgetful." Ibn Hibban said: "He was among the best of Allah's servants, but he made many errors and had poor memory; he erred without knowing it. When that became frequent in his narrations, the argument from him was invalidated." Also, the addition that is the basis of the argument in the hadith, namely his saying "What do you think if I divorced her," and so on, is something 'Ata' alone narrated. The memorizers shared with him the original hadith but did not mention this addition. Its chain includes Shu'ayb ibn Zurayq al-Shami, who is weak. 'Abd al-Haqq, in his *Ahkam*, criticized this hadith, saying that its chain includes Mu'alla ibn Mansur, and said: "Ahmad accused him of lying."

The author, may Allah pardon him, says: As for 'Ata' al-Khurasani mentioned, he is among the narrators of Muslim in his *Sahih*. As for Mu'alla ibn Mansur, Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "Reliable, Sunni, a jurist, who was sought for judgeship but refused. Whoever claims that Ahmad accused him of lying is mistaken. The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and the rest of the collectors narrated from him." As for Shu'ayb ibn Zurayq Abu Shaybah al-Shami, Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "Truthful, but he errs." Whoever is like this, his hadith is not to be rejected, especially since his narration is strengthened by what preceded in the hadith of Sahl, and by what al-Bayhaqi transmitted from al-Hasan ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them. He said in *al-Sunan al-Kubra* the following text: "Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Ahmad ibn 'Abdan informed us: Ahmad ibn 'Ubayd al-Saffar told us: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Wasiti told us: Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Razi told us: Salamah ibn al-Fadl told us, from 'Amr ibn Abi Qays, from Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-A'la, from Suwayd ibn Ghaflah, who said: 'Ayshah al-Khath'amiyyah was with al-Hasan ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them. When 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, was killed, she said: "May the caliphate be a comfort to you." He said: "You show gloating at the killing of 'Ali? Go, for you are divorced," meaning three times. He said: She wrapped herself in her garments and sat until she completed her waiting period. He sent to her the remainder of her dowry that was still due to her, and ten thousand as charity. When the messenger came to her, she said: "A little goods from a beloved who is parting." When he heard her words, he wept, then said: "Had I not heard my grandfather, or my father told me that he heard my grandfather say: 'Any man who divorces his wife three times at the (*time of*) *qur'* or three undefined (divorces), she does not become lawful to him until she marries another husband,' I would have taken her back."'"

Similarly it was narrated from 'Amr ibn Shamir, from 'Imran ibn Muslim and Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-A'la, from Suwayd ibn Ghaflah. Ended; his words in full.

The weakness of this chain is that it includes Muhammad ibn Humayd ibn Hayyan al-Razi, of whom Ibn Hajar said in *al-Taqrib*: "A memorizer, weak, and Ibn Ma'in had a good opinion of him." It also includes Salamah ibn al-Fadl al-Abrash, client of the Ansar, judge of Rayy, of whom he said in *al-Taqrib*: "Truthful, but he errs much." It was narrated by another route too, and al-Tabarani narrated something similar from the hadith of Suwayd ibn Ghaflah. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh declared the hadith weak. The hadith of Ibn Umar mentioned is also supported by what is authentically reported in the *Sahih* from Ibn Umar, that he said: "And if you had divorced her three times, she would have become unlawful to you until she marries a husband other than you, and you would have disobeyed Allah in what He commanded you concerning the divorce of your wife." This is especially so according to al-Hakim's view that it is *marfu'*, and if the hadith of Ibn Umar mentioned is established, it is clear in the matter of dispute.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 229 (part 3 of 7):

What some scholars have mentioned, that even if it were authentic it would not be a proof, on the basis that it is interpreted as referring to three [pronouncements] given separately rather than together, is far-fetched. The hadith is clearly about them being given together, because Ibn 'Umar would not ask about three separate [pronouncements], since it would not be hidden from him that they are forbidden, and this is not a point of dispute. Among their evidences is what 'Abd al-Razzaq related in his Musannaf, from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "My grandfather divorced a wife of his a thousand times, so he went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him of that. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Your grandfather did not fear Allah so that He might make a way out for him. Three are for him, and nine hundred and ninety-seven are transgression and injustice. If Allah wills, He will punish him, and if He wills, He will forgive him.'" In another narration: "Your father did not fear Allah, so He did not make a way out for him. She became separated from him by three, contrary to the Sunnah, and nine hundred and ninety-seven sins are upon his neck." In its chain are Yahya ibn al-'Ala', 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Walid, and Ibrahim ibn 'Ubayd Allah, and none of them is relied upon as a proof.

It has also been narrated by some from Sadaqah ibn Abi 'Imran, from Ibrahim ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, from his father, from his grandfather. Among their evidences is what Ibn Majah related from al-Sha'bi, who said: "I said to Fatimah bint Qays: 'Tell me about your divorce.' She said: 'My husband divorced me three times while he was leaving for Yemen, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted that.'"

In the narration of Abu Usamah, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, from Fatimah bint Qays, she said: "O Messenger of Allah, my husband divorced me three times, and I fear that he will break in upon me." So he ordered her, and she moved [elsewhere].

In Muslim, from the narration of Abu Salamah, that Fatimah bint Qays informed him "that Abu Hafs ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi divorced her three times, then set off for Yemen," etc. In it, also from Abu Salamah, she said: "So he divorced me with al-batta (the irrevocable divorce)."

They said: These narrations clearly indicate that the divorce was with three together, especially the hadith of al-Sha'bi, because her saying in it, "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted that," indicates that informing about his permission would only be necessary for three together. The use of this hadith as evidence has been refuted by what is established in some authentic narrations, as Muslim related also from Abu Salamah: that Fatimah informed him that she was under Abu 'Amr ibn Hafs ibn al-Mughirah, and he divorced her with the last of three pronouncements of divorce.

This narration explains the earlier narrations and shows that what is meant by them is that it occurred separately, not at once. Some have answered this objection by saying that the narrations mentioned show that the Companions and the Successors did not distinguish between the phrases of the three-fold irrevocable divorce, meaning the word al-batta, the three together, and the three separated; for in some narrations it is expressed with the phrase "he divorced me three times," in some with "he divorced me al-batta," and in some with the phrase "then he divorced me with the last of three pronouncements." So she did not single out one of these phrases over another, because of her knowledge of the equivalence of the formulations.

And if you knew that some of them are not prohibited, she would have avoided them.

They said: al-Sha'bi said to her, "Tell me about your divorce," i.e., about its manner and circumstances. How can he ask about the manner and accept an answer containing what is, in his view, a generality, without inquiring about it? Abu Salamah narrated from her the three formulations; had there been a difference in his understanding, he would have objected to her on account of the variation in her wording, and sought certainty until he knew from her by which formulation her irrevocable separation occurred. His leaving that aside is evidence of the equivalence of the aforementioned formulations in his view. Thus some eminent scholars have mentioned.

The apparent position is that this hadith contains no proof, because the narrations containing generality have been clarified by the other authentic narration, as is evident, and Allah knows best.

Among their evidences is what Abu Dawud related, and al-Daraqutni, who said: Abu Dawud said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith," and al-Shafi'i, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah, and Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim authenticated it: "From Rukanah ibn 'Abd Allah, that he divorced his wife Suhaymah al-batta, and informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of that. He said: 'By Allah, I intended only one.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'By Allah, did you intend only one?' Rukanah said: 'By Allah, I intended only one.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned her to him, and he divorced her the second time in the time of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and the third time in the time of 'Uthman." This hadith was authenticated by Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim.

Ibn Majah said about it: "I heard Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Muhammad al-Tanafisi say: 'How noble this hadith is!'"

(p-115) Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar: Ibn Kathir said: "Abu Dawud related it through another route, and it has other chains, so it is hasan, if Allah wills." It is explicit on the point in dispute, because the Prophet's (ﷺ) having Rukanah swear that he intended only one by the word al-batta is evidence that if he had intended more than one, it would have taken effect; and the three is more explicit in that in the word al-batta, because al-batta is an allusion (kinayah) while the three is explicit (sarih). And if he could not have divorced more than one, there would be no meaning to his swearing, especially with this hadith being reinforced by the hadiths we have already cited and what we will mention after it, if Allah wills, though all of them are open to some criticism. Moreover, this hadith has been criticized on the ground that its chain contains al-Zubayr ibn Sa'id ibn Sulayman ibn Sa'id ibn Nawfal ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib al-Hashimi.
