Ibn Hajar said of him in al-Taqrib: "Layyin al-hadith (weak in narration); many have declared him weak. It has been said that he is matruk (abandoned)." The truth is what Ibn Hajar said about him, that he is layyin al-hadith.

Al-Tirmidhi mentioned from al-Bukhari that it is mudtarib (inconsistent) in it: it is said "three," and at other times it is said "one." The most authentic version is that he divorced her al-batta, and that "three" was mentioned in it according to the sense.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in al-Tamhid: "They have spoken about this hadith, and we have already mentioned just now the authentication of it by Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim, and that Ibn Kathir said it is hasan, and that it is reinforced by the hadiths mentioned before it, such as the hadith of Ibn 'Umar in al-Daraqutni, the hadith of al-Hasan in al-Bayhaqi, and the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi concerning the li'an of 'Uwaymir and his wife, especially according to the narration 'so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) enforced it,' meaning the three with one formula, as has preceded."

It is also reinforced by what Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i related from Hammad ibn Zayd, who said: "I said to Ayyub: 'Do you know of anyone who said, regarding the matter being in your hand, that it is three, other than al-Hasan?' He said: 'No.' Then he said: 'O Allah, forgive us, except for what Qatadah related to me from Kathir, the freedman of Ibn Samurah, from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Three."' So I met Kathir and asked him, and he did not recognize it. So I returned to Qatadah and informed him, and he said: 'He forgot.'"

Al-Tirmidhi said: "We do not know it except from the hadith of Sulayman ibn Harb, from Hammad ibn Zayd." And it has been criticized from three angles. The first: that al-Bukhari did not recognize it as marfu', and said it is mawquf upon Abu Hurayrah. This is answered by saying: raising it (to the Prophet) is an addition, and the addition of a trustworthy narrator is accepted, and Sulayman ibn Harb narrated it marfu' from Hammad ibn Zayd (p-116), and their eminence is well known.

In Maraqi al-Su'ud he said:
"Raising it, joining it, and adding words are accepted, according to the imam of memorization."

The second: that Kathir forgot it. This is answered by saying that a shaykh's forgetting does not invalidate the narration of one who narrated from him, for it is rare that a narrator retains over a long time everything he narrates; and this is the view of the majority.

Suhayl ibn Abi Salih narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) decided by a witness and an oath," and he forgot it, so he would say: "Rabi'ah narrated to me from me," and no one objected to him. Al-'Iraqi alluded to this in his Alfiyyah with his saying:
"If he intends it without mention, or there is something that indicates forgetting, they have seen...
The ruling is for the one who remembers, according to the majority;
and dropping it has been related from some of them,
like the story of the witness and oath, when
Suhayl, who took it from him, forgot it,
so afterward he narrated it from his Rabi'ah
from himself; he will not lose it."

The third: its weakening due to Kathir, the freedman of Ibn Samurah, as Ibn Hazm said that he is majhul (unknown). This is answered by saying that Ibn Hajar said in al-Taqrib that he is maqbul (acceptable). Among their evidences is what al-Daraqutni related from the hadith of Zadhan, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man who had divorced al-batta, and he became angry and said: 'Do you take the signs of Allah as mockery, or the religion of Allah as mockery or play? Whoever divorces al-batta, we hold him to three, and she is not lawful to him until she marries another husband.'" In its chain is Isma'il ibn Umayyah, whom al-Daraqutni described as "Kufan, weak."

* *

Among their evidences is what al-Daraqutni related from the hadith of Hammad ibn Zayd: 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Suhayb narrated to us, from Anas, who said: I heard Anas ibn Malik say: I heard Mu'adh ibn Jabal say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "O Mu'adh, whoever divorces for innovation, once or twice or three times, we hold him to his innovation." In its chain is Isma'il ibn Umayyah al-Dhari', who is also weak. These hadiths, although none of them is free from some criticism, their multiplicity, the variety of their routes, and the diversity of their sources indicate that they have a basis; and weak narrations, when their sources are diverse, strengthen one another so that together they become fit for use as proof. Especially since some of them have been authenticated by some scholars, such as the hadith of Rukanah's divorce with al-batta, which Ibn Kathir graded hasan; and some of them are sahih, namely the narration that the Prophet (ﷺ) enforced the divorce of 'Uwaymir with three together (p-117), in the collection of Abu Dawud.

You have already come to know the counter-argument to the weakening of the hadith of Ibn 'Umar in al-Daraqutni on the part of 'Ata' al-Khurasani, Mu'alla ibn Mansur, and Shu'ayb ibn Zurayq, and so on, as mentioned earlier:

"Do not contend against a household with one, for two weak ones can overcome a strong one."

Al-Nawawi said in his Sharh Muslim the following text: The majority have argued with the saying of Allah the Exalted: "Whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has certainly wronged himself. You know not; perhaps Allah will bring about after that some matter" (al-Talaq: 1).

They said: its meaning is that the one who divorces may come to regret, and be unable to remedy it because the irrevocable separation has taken place; so if three could not take effect, his divorce would only be revocable and he would not regret. End of quotation; the point at issue is in his own words.

[p. 118] The one who wrote this commentary, may Allah pardon him, said: Among what supports this Qur'anic argument is what Abu Dawud narrated with a sound chain (isnad) through Mujahid, who said: "I was with Ibn 'Abbas when a man came to him and said, 'He divorced his wife three times.' He remained silent until I thought he would return her to him. Then he said: 'One of you goes and mounts the foolishness, then says, "O Ibn 'Abbas, O Ibn 'Abbas!" Allah said: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq: 2], and you have not feared Allah, so I find no way out for you. You have disobeyed your Lord, and your wife has become irrevocably separated from you.'" Abu Dawud also narrated similar corroborating reports from Ibn 'Abbas. This is an interpretation by Ibn 'Abbas of the verse, meaning that ﴿And whoever fears Allah﴾ includes the one who does not combine the divorces in a single pronouncement, for whom Allah makes a way out through reconciliation (raj'ah). Whoever does not fear Allah in this matter, by combining the divorces in a single formula, Allah does not make a way out for him through reconciliation, because irrevocable separation (al-bayunah) occurs with them together. This is the meaning of his statement, which admits of no other meaning. It is very strong in the place of dispute, because it is an interpretation of the Qur'an by him, and he is the interpreter of the Qur'an (turjuman al-Qur'an), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, teach him the interpretation." This view is held by the majority of the Companions and most scholars, including the four Imams. Many have reported a consensus (ijma') upon it. Those who disagree argued with four hadiths.

The first: the hadith of Ibn Ishaq, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, in the collections of Ahmad and Abu Ya'la, which some have declared authentic, that he said: "Rukanah ibn 'Abd Yazid divorced his wife three times in one sitting, and he grieved over her greatly. The Prophet (ﷺ) asked him: 'How did you divorce her?' He said: 'Three times in one sitting.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'That is only one, so take her back if you wish.' So he took her back."

The one who wrote this commentary, may Allah pardon him, said: Using this hadith as evidence is rejected for three reasons.

[p. 118] The first: there is absolutely no proof in it for the point in dispute, even if its authenticity is granted, neither by direct indication (dalalat al-mutabaqah), nor by partial indication (dalalat al-tadammun), nor by necessary implication (dalalat al-iltizam). This is because the wording of the text is that the three divorces occurred in one sitting, and there is no doubt that their occurring in one sitting does not necessarily mean that they occurred in one formula. The claim that, since they occurred in one sitting, they must have been in one formula is utterly baseless, as you see. For their occurrence in one sitting does not indicate their occurrence in one formula, either by transmission, by reason, or by language, as is not hidden from anyone. Rather, the hadith is more evident that they were not in one formula, for if they had been in one formula, he would have said "in one formula" and omitted mention of the sitting. There is no reason to leave out the more specific and express the more general without a cause, as you see.

In sum, this argument is refuted by the objection known among the scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) as "agreeing with the premise" (al-qawl bil-muqtada). It is said: "Grant that they were in one sitting; but from where do you derive that they were in one formula? Understand." You will see the full treatment of this topic, Allah willing, in the discussion of the hadith of Tawus in Muslim.

The second: Dawud ibn al-Husayn, who is the narrator of this hadith from Ikrimah, is not reliable regarding Ikrimah.

Ibn Hajar said in al-Taqrib: "Dawud ibn al-Husayn al-Umawi, their client, Abu Sulayman al-Madani, is reliable except in his narration from Ikrimah, and he was accused of holding the view of the Kharijites." End of quote. If he is unreliable in what he narrates from Ikrimah, then this hadith is from an unreliable narrator. Moreover, we have already noted that even if it were authentic, it would not constitute proof.

The third: what Ibn Hajar mentioned in Fath al-Bari, where he said the following: "Third: Abu Dawud preferred the view that Rukanah had divorced his wife with a final divorce (al-battah), as he narrated it through the family of Rukanah. This is a strong explanation, because it is possible that one of its narrators understood al-battah as three, and so said 'he divorced her three times.' By this point, the argument from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas is blocked." End of quote in his own words.

That is, the hadith of Ibn Ishaq from Dawud ibn al-Husayn mentioned above, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, although we have already noted that the hadith offers no proof at all for the point in dispute. From what we have mentioned, the invalidity of using the hadith of Ibn Ishaq becomes clear.

* *

The second of the four hadiths used by those who make the three divorces count as one is what appears in some narrations of the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, that he divorced his wife during menstruation three times, and it was counted as one. The invalidity of this argument is not hidden, and the sound view is that he divorced her only once, as is found in the authentic narrations in Muslim and others.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh Muslim: "As for the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, the authentic narrations that Muslim and others included state that he divorced her once."

Al-Qurtubi said in his Tafsir: "What is preserved is that Ibn 'Umar divorced his wife once during menstruation."

'Abd Allah said: "His divorcing her during menstruation was once, though he opposed the Sunnah." Likewise said Salih ibn Kaysan, Musa ibn 'Uqbah, Isma'il ibn Umayyah, Layth ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Dhi'b, Ibn Jurayj, Jabir, and Isma'il ibn Ibrahim ibn 'Uqbah, from Nafi', that Ibn 'Umar divorced once, one pronouncement.

Likewise said al-Zuhri, from Salim, from his father, and Yunus ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, and al-Hasan. End of quote in his own words. Thus, the invalidity of using the hadith of Ibn 'Umar is most evident.

* *

The third of their proofs is what Abu Dawud narrated in his Sunan: "Ahmad ibn Salih narrated to us, 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ibn Jurayj informed us, saying: 'Some of the sons of Abu Rafi', client of the Prophet (ﷺ), informed me, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Abd Yazid, Abu Rukanah, and his brothers divorced Umm Rukanah, and he married a woman from Muzaynah. She came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'It avails me nothing except as this hair', a hair she took from her head, 'so separate me from him.' The Prophet (ﷺ) was seized by zeal, so he summoned Rukanah and his brothers, then said to those sitting with him: 'Do you see that this one resembles 'Abd Yazid in such and such ways, and that one in such and such ways?' They said: 'Yes.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Divorce her.' He did so. Then he said: 'Take back your wife, Umm Rukanah.' He said: 'I divorced her three times, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'I know. Take her back.' And he recited: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them for their waiting period and count the waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]."'"

The one who wrote this commentary, may Allah pardon him, said: Using this hadith as evidence is clearly invalid, because Ibn Jurayj said: "Some of the sons of Abu Rafi' informed me," which is a narration from an unknown person who is not known to us. Its invalidity is as you see. There is no doubt that the earlier hadith of Abu Dawud is more deserving of acceptance than this one, whose weakness no one disputes.

It has already been mentioned that in that hadith it is stated that he divorced her with a final divorce (al-battah), and that the Prophet (ﷺ) made him swear that he intended only one. This is a clear proof for the validity of combined divorces, as has already been explained.

* *

The fourth hadith is what Muslim included in his Sahih: "Ishaq ibn Ibrahim and Muhammad ibn Rafi' narrated to us, and the wording is that of Ibn Rafi'. Ishaq said: 'Akhbarana (he informed us),' and Ibn Rafi' said: 'Haddathana (he narrated to us), 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Divorce during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and of Abu Bakr, and for two years of 'Umar's caliphate, was counted as one when a man pronounced three. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab then said: 'The people have hastened in a matter in which they had been given leisure. So if we enforce it upon them,' and he enforced it upon them."' Ishaq ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, Rawh ibn 'Ubadah informed us, Ibn Jurayj informed us; and Ibn Rafi' narrated to us, with the wording being his: 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, Ibn Jurayj informed us, Ibn Tawus informed me, from his father, that Abu al-Sahba' said to Ibn 'Abbas: 'Do you know that three divorces were counted as one during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr, and three in the caliphate of 'Umar?' Ibn 'Abbas said: 'Yes.'"

And Ishaq ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, Sulayman ibn Harb informed us, from Hammad ibn Zayd, from Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, from Ibrahim ibn Maysarah, from Tawus, that Abu al-Sahba' said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Bring some of your nonsense. Was not the triple divorce during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr counted as one?" He said: "It was so. But when it came to the time of 'Umar, people began to rush into divorce, so he enforced it upon them." This is the wording of Muslim in his Sahih.

This last chain was also narrated by Abu Dawud, but he did not name Ibrahim ibn Maysarah, and instead said "from more than one," and the wording of the text is: "Do you not know that when a man divorced his wife three times before consummating the marriage, they counted it as one during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and the early part of 'Umar's caliphate?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Yes. When a man divorced his wife three times before consummating the marriage, they counted it as one during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and the early part of 'Umar's caliphate. But when 'Umar saw that people had rushed into it, he said: 'Enforce them upon them.'"

The majority of scholars have several responses to this hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.

[p. 121]

**First:** The three (divorces) mentioned in it, which used to be counted as one, are not stated in any of the narrations of the Hadith to have been pronounced with a single utterance. The phrase "divorce of three" does not necessarily mean, linguistically, rationally or legally, that they were pronounced in a single utterance. Whoever says to his wife, "You are divorced, you are divorced, you are divorced," three times in one time, his divorce is a divorce of three, because he explicitly pronounced divorce three times. If one who insists that the intended meaning of the Hadith is the pronouncement of three with one word is asked, "From where did you derive that it was with one word? Is there in any wording of the Hadith that it was with one word? Does the application of the term 'three divorces' to divorce pronounced in several words prevent it?" If he says, "No," it is said to him, "Divorce of three" applies only if it is with one word. There is no doubt that this claim of his is not correct. If he admits the truth and says, "It is permissible to apply it to what was pronounced with one word and to what was pronounced with several words, and it is more apparent from the wording," it is said to him, "Then your insistence that it was with one word has no basis, and if it is not determined in the Hadith that the three were with one word, the argument from it falls entirely with respect to the point of dispute." Among what indicates that the phrase "divorce of three" in this Hadith does not necessarily mean that it was with one word is that the Imam Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Nasa'i, despite his eminence, knowledge and acute understanding, did not understand from this Hadith anything except that the intended "divorce of three" in it is: "You are divorced, you are divorced, you are divorced," with the divorces separated, because the word "three" is more apparent in pronouncing divorce three times. For this reason, in his *Sunan*, he entitled the narration of Abu Dawud mentioned in this Hadith, saying: "Chapter: The divorce of three separated before consummation with the wife." Then he said: Abu Dawud Sulayman ibn Sayf informed us, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, that Abu al-Sahba' came to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and said: "O son of 'Abbas, do you not know that the three (divorces) were, in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr and the early part of the caliphate of 'Umar, reckoned as one?" He said: "Yes." So you see that this eminent Imam explicitly stated that the divorce of three in this Hadith is not with one word, but with separate words. What confirms the correctness of what al-Nasa'i, may Allah have mercy on him, understood from the Hadith is what Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned in *Zad al-Ma'ad* in refuting those who argued for the occurrence of three divorces at once from the Hadith of 'A'isha: "That a man divorced his wife three times, and she married (another)..." — the Hadith. He said therein the following text: "But where in the Hadith is it that he divorced three with one utterance? Rather, the Hadith is a proof for us, for it is not said, 'He did that three times and said three times,' except of one who did and said it time after time. This is what is understood in the languages of nations, Arab and non-Arab, just as it is said, 'He slandered him three times, insulted him three times, and greeted him three times.'" End of quotation from him verbatim.

[p. 122]

This is a clear proof for the correctness of what Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Nasa'i, may Allah have mercy on him, understood from the Hadith, because the word "three" in all its narrations is more apparent in indicating three divorces occurring time after time, as Ibn al-Qayyim clarified in the Hadith of 'A'isha mentioned just above.

Among those who said that the intended meaning of "three" in the Hadith of Tawus mentioned is the three separated by words such as "You are divorced, you are divorced, you are divorced," is Ibn Suraj. He said: "It seems that it was narrated concerning the repetition of the wording, such as saying: 'You are divorced, you are divorced, you are divorced.' At first, people were of sound intention, so it was accepted from them that they intended emphasis. But when people multiplied in the time of 'Umar, and deception and the like multiplied among them, which prevented accepting the claim of one who claims emphasis, 'Umar took the wording as an apparent repetition and enforced it upon them." This was said by Ibn Hajar in *Fath al-Bari*, and he said that this answer was approved by al-Qurtubi, and he strengthened it with the saying of 'Umar: "People have hastened in a matter in which they had leisure."

Al-Nawawi said in his *Sharh Muslim* the following text: "As for the Hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, the people differed in its answer and interpretation. The most correct is that its meaning is that at the beginning, if a man said to her, 'You are divorced, you are divorced, you are divorced,' and did not intend emphasis or resumption, it was ruled as one divorce, because they rarely intended resumption by that. So it was taken according to the prevalent case, which is the intention of emphasis. But when it was the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and people's use of this formula increased, and the intention of resumption by it became prevalent among them, it was taken, when unqualified, as three, acting upon the prevalent meaning that came first to understanding in that era."

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: This view is free of difficulty, because the state may change when the intention changes, since "actions are by intentions" and "every person will have what he intended." The apparent wording indicates this, as we have mentioned.

In any case, the claim of certainty that the meaning of the Hadith of Tawus is that the three were with one word is a claim devoid of evidence, as you have seen. So let him who has dared to attribute that to the Prophet ﷺ fear Allah, especially since there is nothing in any of the narrations of the Hadith of Tawus stating that the three mentioned were with one word, and this has not been determined from the language, nor from the Shari'ah, nor from reason, as you see.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: What indicates that the three mentioned are not with one word is what preceded in the Hadith of Ibn Ishaq from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, narrated by Ahmad and Abu Ya'la: "He divorced his wife three times in one sitting," and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "How did you divorce her?" [p. 123] He said: "Three times in one sitting." For the expression "sitting" implies that they were not with one word, since if the word were one, he would have said "with one word" and would not have needed to mention the sitting, for there is no reason to mention the more general description and omit the more specific one without a reason. As is apparent in the second answer concerning the Hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, the meaning of the Hadith is that the divorce pronounced in the time of 'Umar as three used to occur before that as one, because they did not use three at all, or used it rarely. But in the time of 'Umar, their use of it increased.

The meaning of his saying "so he enforced it upon them," according to this view, is that he applied to it the ruling of the occurrence of divorce as it was applied before. Ibn al-'Arabi preferred this interpretation and attributed it to Abu Zur'a al-Razi. Likewise, al-Bayhaqi narrated it with a sound chain to Abu Zur'a, who said: "The meaning of this Hadith, in my view, is: 'You are the ones who divorce three; they used to divorce one.'" Al-Nawawi said: "Accordingly, the report would be about a difference in people's custom specifically, not about a change of the ruling in a single matter." This answer was quoted by al-Qurtubi in his commentary on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿The divorce is twice﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], from the verifier, the judge Abu al-Walid al-Baji, the judge 'Abd al-Wahhab, and al-Kiya al-Tabari.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: The strained character of this answer is not hidden, even if some eminent scholars have held it.

* * *

**The third answer:** Concerning the Hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is the statement that it is abrogated (*mansukh*), and that some of the Companions did not become aware of the abrogation (*naskh*) except in the time of 'Umar. Al-Bayhaqi narrated in *al-Sunan al-Kubra*, in the chapter on whoever makes the three one, from Imam al-Shafi'i the following text: Al-Shafi'i said: "If the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's saying is that the three were counted as one in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, i.e., that it was by the command of the Prophet ﷺ, then what seems likely, and Allah knows best, is that Ibn 'Abbas knew that there was something that was abrogated. If it is said: 'What indicates what you described?' It is said: It is not likely that Ibn 'Abbas would narrate something from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and then oppose it with something he did not know had come from the Prophet ﷺ, on which there was disagreement." The Shaykh (al-Bayhaqi) said: "The narration of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas has already passed in the chapter on abrogation, and it contains confirmation of the correctness of this interpretation." Al-Shafi'i said: "If it is said: 'Perhaps this is something narrated from 'Umar, and Ibn 'Abbas spoke by the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him,' it is said: We know that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, opposed 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning temporary marriage (*nikah al-mut'ah*), concerning the sale of a dinar for two dinars, concerning the sale of the mothers of children (*umm al-walad*), and other matters. So how would he agree with him in something that is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ in which 'Umar opposed it?" End of quotation. The point of need from al-Bayhaqi verbatim.

The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari* the following text: "The third answer is the claim of abrogation. Al-Bayhaqi narrated from al-Shafi'i that he said: 'It seems that Ibn 'Abbas knew of something that abrogated that.'" Al-Bayhaqi said: "It is strengthened by what Abu Dawud narrated through the route of Yazid al-Nahwi, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: 'A man, if he divorced his wife, had more right to her return, and if he divorced her three times, that was abrogated.'" The chapter under which Abu Dawud mentioned the aforementioned Hadith is his saying: "Chapter: The abrogation of return after the three divorces."

Ibn Kathir said in his commentary on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿The divorce is twice﴾ and the verse, after citing the aforementioned Hadith of Abu Dawud, the following text: "It was also narrated by al-Nasa'i from Zakariyya ibn Yahya, from Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn with it. And Ibn Abi Hatim said: Harun ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abdah, that is, Ibn Sulayman, narrated to us, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, from his father, that a man said to his wife: 'I will never divorce you, nor will I ever shelter you.' She said: 'And how is that?' He said: 'I will divorce you, and when your term approaches its end, I will take you back.' So she came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and mentioned that to him, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿The divorce is twice﴾. He said: 'So the people began the divorce anew, whoever had divorced and whoever had not divorced.'" It was also narrated by Abu Bakr ibn Mardawayh through the route of Muhammad ibn Sulayman, from Ya'la ibn Shabib, client of al-Zubayr, from Hisham, from his father, from 'A'isha, and he mentioned it with something similar to what preceded. Al-Tirmidhi narrated it from Qutayba, from Ya'la ibn Shabib with it, then he narrated it from Abu Kurayb, from Ibn Idris, from Hisham, from his father, as a mursal report, and said: "This is more correct." Al-Hakim narrated it in his *Mustadrak* through the route of Ya'qub ibn Humayd ibn Kulayb, from Ya'la ibn Shabib with it, and said: "Its chain is sound."

Then Ibn Mardawayh said: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, from his father, from 'A'isha, who said: "There was no set time for divorce. A man would divorce his wife and then take her back, as long as the waiting period had not ended. There was some dispute between a man from the Ansar and his family, of the kind that happens among people, and he said: 'By Allah, I will leave you neither a widow nor a wife,' so he began to divorce her, and when the waiting period was about to end, he would take her back. He did this repeatedly, so Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿The divorce is twice; then either retention in an acceptable manner or release with good treatment﴾, so Allah set the divorce at three, with no return after the third, until she marries another husband." Similarly, it was narrated from Qatada as a mursal report, and mentioned by al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Jarir in the same way, and he chose that this is the explanation of this verse. End of quotation from Ibn Kathir verbatim.

And in these narrations there is clear evidence for the abrogation of the *muraja'ah* (the husband's right to take back his wife, *ruj'ah*) after the three pronouncements. Al-Mazari's denial of abrogation (may Allah have mercy on him) is refuted by what al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari*. When he cited al-Mazari's rejection of abrogation on several grounds, he said after it, and this is his exact wording: "I say: al-Nawawi transmitted this section in *Sharh Muslim* and endorsed it, but it is open to objection in several respects.

First: the one who claimed that the ruling was abrogated did not say that 'Umar was the one who abrogated it, such that what he mentioned would follow. Rather he said what has preceded: 'It seems that he knew something of it had been abrogated', i.e., he became aware of an abrogating text for the ruling that he had narrated as a *marfu'* (attributed to the Prophet). That is why he issued a ruling contrary to it. Al-Mazari himself conceded in the course of his discussion that their consensus indicates an abrogating text, and this is what those who claimed abrogation intended.

Second: his denial of departing from the apparent meaning is strange, for whoever tries to reconcile through interpretation necessarily departs from the apparent meaning.

Third: his censure of those who said 'the meaning is that the abrogation became apparent' is also strange, for by its becoming apparent is meant its spreading. Ibn 'Abbas's statement that it was practised in the time of Abu Bakr is to be understood as referring to those who practised it without the abrogation having reached them, so what he mentioned about their consensus on an error does not follow." End of quotation from *Fath al-Bari* in its own words, the point at issue. There is no difficulty in this, because many of the Companions became aware of many rulings they had not known. This occurred in the caliphates of Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman. Abu Bakr did not know the Prophet's (ﷺ) judgement concerning the inheritance of the grandmother until al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba and Muhammad ibn Maslama informed him. 'Umar had no knowledge of the Prophet's (ﷺ) judgement concerning the blood-money for a fetus until the two just mentioned informed him. He had no knowledge of the Prophet's (ﷺ) taking the *jizya* from the Magians of Hajar until 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf informed him, nor of the threefold seeking of permission until Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri informed him. 'Uthman had no knowledge that the Prophet (ﷺ) had made residence obligatory for the widow during the waiting period until Furay'a bint Malik informed him.

Al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib and Fatima al-Zahra' (may Allah be pleased with them both) had no knowledge that the Prophet (ﷺ) had said: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from," until they sought their inheritance from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Examples of this are very numerous indeed.

The clearest proof that removes the difficulty regarding the claim of abrogation mentioned is the occurrence of a similar case, and the admission of the dissenter to it in the matter of temporary marriage (*nikah al-mut'a*). Muslim narrated from Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him): "The temporary marriage of women was practised in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and the early part of 'Umar's caliphate. Then 'Umar forbade it to us, and we desisted," and this is exactly like what occurred regarding the triple divorce in one go. How alike the night is to the day!

Ṭawīl meter:
*Unless she is it, or he is it, then he is her brother, whose mother nursed him with her own milk.*

It is strange that a fair-minded person should accept the possibility of abrogation in one of the two cases while claiming its impossibility in the other, although Muslim narrated in both of them, from an eminent Companion, that this practice was carried on in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and the early part of 'Umar's caliphate, in a matter concerning private parts, and then 'Umar changed it.

As for whoever permits the abrogation of temporary marriage but deems the abrogation of making the three (pronouncements) one impossible, it is said to him: "Why does your camel pull while mine does not pull?" If it is said: "The abrogation of temporary marriage is established by a text," we reply: "You have seen the narrations preceding regarding the abrogation of taking back after three (pronouncements)." Among those who firmly held that the making of three into one was abrogated is Imam Abu Dawud (may Allah, the Exalted, have mercy on him), who held that making them one applied only at the time when a man could take his wife back after three or more pronouncements. He said in his *Sunan*: "Chapter: The abrogation of the taking back after the three pronouncements." Then he related with his chain the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "*And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three menstrual periods. And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs*" (2:228), the verse. "That was because a man, when he divorced his wife, had more right to take her back, even if he had divorced her three times, and this was abrogated," and he said: "*Divorce is twice*" (2:229), the verse. Al-Nasa'i transmitted something similar, and in its chain is 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Waqid, of whom Ibn Hajar said in *al-Taqrib*: "Truthful, but makes errors."

Malik narrated in the *Muwatta'* from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, from his father, that he said: "A man, when he divorced his wife and then took her back before her waiting period ended, that was permitted to him, even if he had divorced her a thousand times. A man deliberately divorced his wife, and when she was about to complete her waiting period he took her back, then said: 'I will neither shelter you nor divorce you.' So Allah revealed: '*Divorce is twice; then either retain in an acceptable manner or release with good treatment*' (2:229). From that day on the people began divorce afresh, whether they had divorced or not."

This is supported by the fact that none of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) denied 'Umar the pronouncing of three at once, despite their great number, their knowledge and their scrupulousness. It is further supported by the fact that a very large number of the eminent and learned Companions are authentically reported to have held this view, such as Ibn 'Abbas, 'Umar, Ibn 'Umar, and countless others.

(p-127) As for the abrogating text that abrogated the taking back after three, some scholars said it is the words of Allah, the Exalted: "*Divorce is twice*," as was shown explicitly in the narrations preceding. There is no rational or customary obstacle to many people being unaware of such an abrogating text until the caliphate of 'Umar, especially since the Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly declared its abrogation and its prohibition until the Day of Resurrection on the day of the Conquest, and also during the Farewell Pilgrimage, as is found in a narration in Muslim.

And although the Qur'an indicates the prohibition of anyone other than a wife or a concubine by His words: "*And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess*" (23:5-6), it is known that a woman with whom one has contracted temporary marriage is neither a wife nor a concubine, as will be clarified, Allah willing, in *Surat al-Nisa'* in discussing His words: "*So for whatever you have enjoyed of them*" (4:24), the verse.

Those who said there was abrogation interpreted 'Umar's words, "The people have hastened in a matter in which they had a respite," to mean that the respite lay in their being deliberate in divorce, so that they would not pronounce the three at one time. The meaning of their hastening is that they came to pronounce them with one utterance, according to the view that this is the meaning of the hadith, although we have already mentioned that it is not necessarily its meaning. His enforcing it upon them is then what is necessary, and it does not contradict his words "so had we enforced it upon them", meaning, we held them to the consequence of what they had said. A parallel is Jabir's statement in Muslim regarding temporary marriage: "'Umar then forbade us from it." The apparent meaning of each of these two is that it was 'Umar's own *ijtihad*, and abrogation is established in both of them together, as you have seen. The respite is not in the abrogated matter; it is in not hastening to pronounce the three at once. On the first view, the three which used to be counted as one are: "You are divorced, you are divorced, you are divorced." The apparent reading of his enforcing it upon them is that, since their intention changed from emphasis to new pronouncement, as already explained, there is no difficulty in that.

As for the claim that 'Umar knew "that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to make three pronouncements in one utterance into one," and then deliberately opposed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and made them three, and no one among the Companions denied it, its improbability is not hidden. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

The fourth response concerns the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): Tawus's narration from Ibn 'Abbas contradicts what the memorizers among his students related from him. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, 'Amr ibn Dinar, Malik ibn al-Harith, Muhammad ibn Iyas ibn al-Bukayr, and Mu'awiya ibn Abi 'Ayyash al-Ansari all related from him the binding force of three at once, as transmitted by al-Bayhaqi in *al-Sunan al-Kubra* and al-Qurtubi and others.

(p-128) Al-Bayhaqi said in *al-Sunan al-Kubra*: "Al-Bukhari did not include this hadith, because of the opposition of these people to Tawus's narration from Ibn 'Abbas."

Al-Athram said: "I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (Ahmad ibn Hanbal) about the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: 'The triple divorce was, in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them), a single divorce,' how do you repel it?" He said: "By the narration of the people from Ibn 'Abbas in many ways contrary to it." Ibn Mansur transmitted similarly from him, as Ibn al-Qayyim said.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him) says: This is the leader of the hadith scholars and the master of the Muslims in his age, through whom Allah redressed Islam after its foundations had nearly crumbled and its beliefs had been altered: Abu 'Abd Allah Ahmad ibn Hanbal (may Allah, the Exalted, have mercy on him). He said to al-Athram and Ibn Mansur that he deliberately set aside the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, because he held that it could not be used as proof for the binding force of three in one utterance, given the memorizers' narrations from Ibn 'Abbas that contradict it. And this imam, Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari, the very same, is reported by the memorizer al-Bayhaqi to have deliberately left out this hadith for the same reason that led Imam Ahmad to leave it. There is no doubt that they both left it only for a reason that necessitated this.

If it is said: "Tawus's narration has the status of a *marfu'* report, while the narration of the group mentioned is a *mawquf* report on Ibn 'Abbas, and a *marfu'* report is not countered by a *mawquf*."

The answer is that when a Companion acts contrary to what was transmitted, scholars hold two views, and these are two narrations from Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him). The first: the hadith is not used as proof, because the one who knows it best is its transmitter, and he abandoned acting on it, and he is a trustworthy and knowledgeable person. On this narration there is no difficulty.

On the other narration, which is the well-known one among scholars, the consideration is the transmitter's narration, not his opinion. Yet his narration is not given precedence unless its meaning is explicit, or apparent in it to a degree that weakens the probability of its opposite. But if it admits of another meaning with strong probability, then the transmitter's contradicting what he narrated shows that this probable meaning which he set aside is not the meaning of what he narrated. We have already stated that the phrase "triple divorce" in the said hadith of Tawus strongly admits of the reading that the pronouncements were separate, as al-Nasa'i affirmed and al-Nawawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Surayj confirmed as sound. The conclusion is that Ibn 'Abbas's abandonment of making three pronouncements in one utterance into one indicates that the meaning of the transmitted hadith is not (p-129) that they were in one utterance, as you will see explained in al-Qurtubi's words in *al-Mufhim* in the response that follows this.

Know that it is not established from Ibn 'Abbas that he ruled, regarding three in one utterance, that they count as one. What Abu Dawud transmitted from him through Hammad ibn Zayd, from Ayyub, from 'Ikrima, that Ibn 'Abbas said: "If he says, 'You are divorced three times' in one utterance, it is one," is countered by what Abu Dawud himself transmitted through Isma'il ibn Ibrahim from Ayyub, from 'Ikrima, that this was 'Ikrima's own statement and not Ibn 'Abbas's. The narration of Isma'il ibn Ibrahim is preferred over that of Hammad, because the memorizers agree with Isma'il that Ibn 'Abbas held them to be three, not one.

* *

The fifth response is the claim that the hadith is weak. Among those who attempted to weaken it were Ibn al-'Arabi the Maliki, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, and al-Qurtubi.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 229 (part 7 of 7):

Ibn al-'Arabi al-Maliki said: "In the latter times, some people slipped and said that triple divorce pronounced in a single utterance does not take effect, and they treated it as a single divorce. They attributed this to the early predecessors (al-salaf al-awwal), reporting it from 'Ali, al-Zubayr, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. They ascribed it to al-Hajjaj ibn Artah, who was of low standing and obscure rank, and they related a hadith for this which has no basis. Some people among the seekers of knowledge went astray, following innovated desires regarding it, and they said: 'His statement, "You are divorced three times," is a lie, because he did not divorce three times, just as if he had said, "I divorced three times" while he had divorced only once, and just as if he had said, "I swear three times," which would be only one oath.'

"I have traveled through the lands and met every truthful scholar of Islam and of the schools of law, yet I have not heard any report on this issue, nor have I found any trace of it, except among the Shi'a, who consider temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah) permissible and do not regard divorce as taking effect. For this reason Ibn Sukkara al-Hashimi said about them:

'O you who deem temporary marriage in his religion lawful, even without a dowry,
And who does not regard ninety divorces as separating from him the lady of the curtained chamber,
From here your offspring have become goodly, so seize it, O sons of the nature (al-fitra).'

"The scholars of Islam and the people who bind and loose in legal matters (ahl al-hall wa-l-'aqd) have agreed that triple divorce in a single utterance, although it is forbidden according to some of them and an innovation according to others, is binding. Where are these wretched people from the scholar of religion and the flag of Islam, Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari? He stated in his Sahih (p-130): 'Chapter: On the permissibility of triple divorce,' citing His saying: ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ [2:229].

"He also mentioned the hadith of li'an: 'So he divorced her three times before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not object to him.' The Prophet (ﷺ) does not approve of falsehood. Moreover, [the husband] combined what had been permitted to him for separation, so the Sharia obligated him to its ruling. What they attributed to the Companions is pure falsehood, having no basis in any book and no narration from anyone.

"Malik included in his Muwatta' a report from 'Ali that the forbidden (al-haram) is three binding (divorces) in one utterance. This is in its meaning, so how much more so when one explicitly pronounces it. As for the hadith of al-Hajjaj ibn Artah, it is not accepted in the religion, nor by any of the imams. If it is said: 'But in Sahih Muslim, from Ibn 'Abbas,' and he mentioned the hadith of Abu al-Sahba' which is mentioned there, we say: 'There is no connection (to this issue) in it from five aspects.'

"The first: It is a hadith whose authenticity is disputed, so how can it be preferred over the consensus (ijma') of the Ummah? No disagreement on this issue is known except from a people who fell below the rank of the Successors (al-tabi'un), and the two noble eras had already passed with agreement on the binding of three. If they narrate that from any of them, then do not accept from them except what they accept from you: the transmission of a just person from a just person. And you will never find this issue attributed to any of the predecessors.

"The second: This hadith was not narrated except from Ibn 'Abbas, and from him it was not narrated except through Tawus. How can what only one Companion narrated, and which only one person narrated from that Companion, be accepted? How could it have been hidden from all the Companions, and they remained silent about it, except Ibn 'Abbas? And how could it have been hidden from the companions of Ibn 'Abbas, except Tawus?" End of Ibn al-'Arabi's words relevant to the purpose.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "The narration of Tawus is a mistake and an error, which none of the jurists of the cities in the Hijaz, al-Sham, Iraq, the East, or the West have relied upon. It has also been said that Abu al-Sahba' is not known among the clients (mawali) of Ibn 'Abbas."

The author, may Allah forgive him, says: "Such (criticism) does not establish the weakening of this hadith, because the imams such as Ma'mar, Ibn Jurayj and others narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and he is an imam, from Tawus, from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibrahim ibn Maysara, who is trustworthy and retentive (thiqah hafiz), also narrated it from Tawus. The Companion being the sole narrator does not harm (the hadith), even if only one person narrated from him at all, as al-'Iraqi indicated in his Alfiyya with his saying:

'In the Sahih, both (Shaykhs) brought (the hadith of) al-Musayyab,
And al-Ju'fi brought (the hadith) of Ibn Taghlib.'

(p-131) He means: the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated the hadith of al-Musayyab ibn Hazn, and no one narrated from him except his son Sa'id. Al-Bukhari also narrated the hadith of 'Amr ibn Taghlib al-Namari, also called al-'Abdi, and no one narrated from him except al-Hasan al-Basri. This is his intended meaning. Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned that 'Amr ibn Taghlib was also narrated from by al-Hakam ibn al-A'raj, as stated by Ibn Hajar, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others.

"The conclusion is that the hadith of Tawus is established in Sahih Muslim with a sound chain, and whatever is like this cannot be weakened except by a clear matter. Yes, one may say: when a report (khabar al-ahad) concerns something for which the motives to transmit it were strong, yet only one person or the like transmitted it, this indicates that it is not authentic. The reasoning is that the strength of the motives entails that its transmission would be widespread and well known; if it is not well known, this indicates it did not happen, because the absence of the necessary implies the absence of what necessitates it. This is an established principle in the fundamentals of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), which he indicated in Maraqi al-Su'ud with his saying, coordinating it with what is judged to be of no authenticity:

'And a solitary report (khabar al-ahad) in the Sunni (tradition),
Where the motives to transmit it were (such that it should be) mass-transmitted, we see that if he had said it, it would have been established.'

"Several of the usulis have definitively affirmed this. The author of Jam' al-Jawami' said, coordinating it with what is definitively judged to be non-authentic: 'And what is transmitted as a solitary report in matters where the motives to transmit it are strong, is (judged) against (its authenticity), contrary to the Rafidah.' End of his words verbatim.

"His meaning is that among what is definitively judged to be non-authentic is a report transmitted solitarily despite the strong motives to transmit it."

Ibn al-Hajib said in his Mukhtasar al-Usuli, as a question: "If one person alone reports something for which the motives to transmit it are strong, and a great multitude has also shared in it, as when one person alone reports the killing of a preacher on the pulpit in a city, then he is definitively a liar, contrary to the Shi'a." End of the relevant part of his words verbatim. There are objections to this issue and answers to them known in the fundamentals.

The author, may Allah forgive him, says: "There is no doubt that, according to the view that the meaning of the aforementioned hadith of Tawus is that triple divorce pronounced in a single utterance was counted as one during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and the early part of 'Umar's caliphate, and then 'Umar changed what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims had practiced during the time of Abu Bakr, and most or all of the Companions knew this, then the motives to transmit what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims after him practiced were strong to a degree that cannot be denied. Because if this change introduced by 'Umar had been rejected, then the silence of all the Companions about it, and the fact that not a single word of it was transmitted except from Ibn 'Abbas, clearly indicates one of two matters:

"One: that the hadith of Tawus which he narrated from Ibn 'Abbas does not mean that they were (counted) as one utterance, but rather as three utterances at one time, as we have mentioned, and as al-Nasa'i affirmed definitively, and al-Nawawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Surayj declared sound. In that case there is no problem, because 'Umar's change of the ruling was based on a change of their intention, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended.' So whoever says, 'You are divorced, you are divorced, you are divorced,' intending emphasis, it is one; and if he intends a fresh start with each one, it is three. Variation in the implications of one wording due to variation in the intentions of those who utter it is not problematic, because of his saying (ﷺ): 'Every person will have only what he intended.'

"Two: that the hadith is not judged authentic, because it was transmitted solitarily despite the strong motives to transmit it. The first (explanation) is better and lighter than the second. Al-Qurtubi said in al-Mufhim, in discussing the aforementioned hadith of Tawus: 'The apparent context of it implies, concerning all of them, that most of them held this view, and the custom in such matters is that the ruling becomes widespread and spreads; how then could one person alone transmit it from another person alone?' He said: 'This aspect requires refraining from acting on its apparent meaning, if it does not require certainty of its falsehood.' End of his words, as transmitted by Ibn Hajar in Fath al-Bari from him, and it is very strong according to what is established in the fundamentals, as you see."

* *

"The sixth answer: Regarding the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), it is to interpret the word 'three' in the hadith as meaning 'the complete divorce (al-battah),' as we have mentioned concerning the hadith of Rukanah, which is also from the transmission of Ibn 'Abbas. The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari after mentioning this answer, and his exact words are: 'It is strong, and it is supported by al-Bukhari's inclusion in this chapter of the reports in which there is 'the complete (al-battah)' and the hadiths in which there is an explicit statement of 'three.' It seems he is pointing to there being no difference between them, and that when 'the complete' is used without qualification, it is understood as three, unless the one who divorces intended one, in which case it is accepted. So some of its narrators understood the word 'the complete' as meaning three, because the equivalence between them was well known, so they narrated it with the word 'three.' What is actually meant is the word 'the complete,' and in the earliest era they used to accept from someone who said, 'I intended one by "the complete,"' but when the time of 'Umar came, he enforced three in the apparent ruling.' End of his words from Fath al-Bari verbatim, and it has a point of view, as is not hidden."

As for what each of those who say that three (divorces) bind at once, and those who say they do not bind, mention among theoretical matters in order to validate their own school, we have not prolonged the discussion with it, because the apparent matter is that all of that falls away. And if this issue cannot be established from the angle of transmission, then it cannot be established from the angle of reason either. And the analogy of "You are divorced three times" to the oaths of li'an, in that if one swears them with a single wording it is not valid, is an analogy in the presence of a distinguishing factor (qiyas ma'a wujud al-fariq). This is because whoever limits himself to one of the four testimonies mentioned in the verse of li'an, the scholars have unanimously agreed that it is like not having given any of them at all. In contrast, with the three divorces, whoever limits himself to one of them, it is counted by consensus (ijma'), and separation is achieved by it upon the completion of the waiting period, by consensus.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 231:**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, then either retain them in kindness or release them in kindness﴾ — the verse... The apparent meaning of His statement, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿when they reach their term﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236] is the actual completion of their waiting period ('iddah). However, He clarified in another place that there is no return (raj'ah) except during the waiting period specifically, and that is in His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228]; for the demonstrative in His statement "that" refers to the period of the waiting period, expressed by "three periods" in His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three menstrual periods﴾ — the verse [al-Baqarah: 228]. It becomes clear from that verse that the meaning of ﴿they reach their term﴾ is: they have nearly completed the waiting period and are about to reach its end.

* *

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not retain them to harm them, to transgress﴾ — the verse. In this noble verse He explicitly forbade retaining a woman in order to harm her, for the purpose of transgressing against her by taking back what he gave her; for if the harm against her is prolonged, she ransoms herself from him, seeking safety from his harm. And He stated in another place that if she commits a clear immorality, it is permissible for him to restrain her (ḍal') until she ransoms herself from him, and that is in His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not restrain them in order to take away part of what you have given them, unless they commit a clear immorality﴾ [an-Nisa': 19]. The scholars differed over the meaning of "clear immorality" (al-fāḥishah al-mubayyinah).

A group of them said it is adultery (zina), and another people said it is disobedience (nushuz), rebellion, and foul speech. The apparent meaning is that the verse encompasses all of these, as Ibn Jarir chose.

Ibn Kathir said: "It is good. So if she commits adultery, or harms him with her tongue, or shows disobedience, then it is permissible to make her life hard for him, so that she ransoms herself from him with what he gave her, based on the generality of the verse that we mentioned."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 233:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you intend to seek wet-nurses for your children, there is no blame upon you﴾, and so on, to the end of the verse. In this noble verse He mentions that if a man wishes to seek a wet-nurse for his child other than the child's mother, there is no blame upon him in that, provided he pays the fixed wage stipulated in the contract. He does not state here the reason that makes this permissible, but he explains it in Surah at-Talaq with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you disagree, then another woman shall nurse [the child] on his behalf﴾ [at-Talaq: 6]. What is meant by their disagreement is: the man's refusal to pay what the woman asks, and the woman's refusal to accept nursing for the payment the man offers and is content with.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 234:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind—they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾. The apparent meaning of this noble verse is that every widow observes a waiting period of four months and ten days. However, He explained in another place that this applies only when she is not pregnant. If she is pregnant, her waiting period is the delivery of her child, as in His saying: ﴿And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth to their load﴾ [at-Talaq: 4]. What further clarifies this is what is established in the agreed-upon hadith (hadith muttafaq 'alayh) concerning the permission the Prophet (ﷺ) gave to Subay'ah al-Aslamiyyah to remarry after giving birth to her child, a few days after her husband's death. That the waiting period of a pregnant widow is the delivery of her child is the truth, as is established from him (ﷺ), contrary to those who said: "She observes the waiting period of the longer of the two terms." This is narrated from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas. And Allah knows best.

Two points of clarification

The first: these two verses, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind—they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾, and His saying: ﴿And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth to their load﴾, come under the category of conflict between two general statements that are each general in one respect (ta'arud al-a'mmayn min wajh). What is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) is weighing one against the other, and the stronger of the two specifies the generality of the weaker, as he (the author of al-Marāqi) stated in his verse: [Rajaz meter] "And if a generality from one aspect appears, then weighing is absolutely binding to be considered."

The authentic Sunnah has made clear that the generality of ﴿And for those who are pregnant﴾ specifies the generality of ﴿Those of you who die﴾ (the verse). Although a group of the usulis mentioned that indefinite plurals (al-juma' al-munakkarah) have no generality, and accordingly there is no generality in the verse of al-Baqarah, because His saying ﴿and leave wives behind﴾ is an indefinite plural and so does not generalize, unlike His saying ﴿And for those who are pregnant﴾, which is a construct (idafah) to a definite noun with the article "al-", and what is in construct to a definite noun with the article is among the forms of generality, as he stated in Maraqi al-Su'ud, coordinating it with the forms of generality: [Rajaz meter] "...and what is definite with 'al-' has been found, or in construct to a definite, when specificity is established, it negates..."

The second: the resumptive pronoun linking the clause to the relative pronoun is omitted, due to the context indicating it, i.e.: "Those who die among you and leave wives behind—they shall wait after them four months and ten days," like the Arabs' saying: "Ghee is two manas for a dirham," meaning: two manas of it for a dirham.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind—they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days﴾.

This verse apparently appears to conflict with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind—a bequest for their wives, provision until the year, without eviction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 240]. The answer is clear: the former (verse 234) abrogates this one (verse 240), even though it comes before it in the Mushaf, because it was revealed later than it. There is no verse in the Qur'an that comes first in the Mushaf and abrogates a verse after it in the Mushaf except in two places: one is this place; the second is the verse: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50], which is first in the Mushaf and abrogates His saying: ﴿Women are not lawful to you after this﴾ [al-Ahzab: 52], because although it precedes it in the Mushaf, it is later in revelation. This is according to the view of abrogation (al-naskh), and the detailed treatment of this matter will come, Allah willing, in surah al-Ahzab.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 2, Verse 241:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for divorced women is a provision (mata') according to what is reasonable, a duty upon the God-fearing﴾. The apparent meaning of this noble verse is that the provision (mut'ah, a consolation gift) is a right for every divorced woman upon her God-fearing former husband, whether she was divorced before consummation or not, and whether a dowry (mahr, bridal gift) was specified for her or not. This generality is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the worldly life and its adornment, then come, I will provide for you and release you with a fair release﴾ [al-Ahzab: 28], together with His saying: ﴿Indeed there is for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21]. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that a ruling addressed specifically to the Prophet ﷺ extends to the whole community unless there is evidence of its restriction to him, as he stated in *Mara'iq al-Su'ud* with his verse:

*Whatever the Prophet was addressed with, its generalization is in the Sunni school,*

and this is the view of the three Imams, in contrast to al-Shafi'i, who held that it is restricted to him ﷺ unless there is evidence of its generality, as we have explained in another place.

Knowing this, be aware that the wives of the Prophet had dowries fixed for them and had been consummated with. It may be understood from another passage that the provision is specifically for the divorced woman before consummation and when a dowry has been fixed for her together, because the woman divorced after consummation is entitled to the full dowry, and the woman divorced before consummation but after a dowry was fixed is entitled to half the dowry. The woman divorced before both is entitled to nothing, so the provision is for her alone, to compensate for her loss. This is in His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them an obligation, but provide for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236]. Then He said: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them and you have specified for them an obligation, then half of what you specified﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. So this verse is clear about this distinction, and its reasoning is evident and rational.

He, may He be exalted, has mentioned in another place what indicates the command to give provision to the woman divorced before consummation, even if a dowry was fixed for her. This is in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, you have no right to count against them any waiting period you could calculate; so provide for them and release them with a fair release﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49], because the apparent generality of this verse includes both the woman for whom a dowry was fixed and others. A group of scholars took according to each of the three verses, and the more cautious course is to take the generality. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that a text indicating a command takes precedence over a text indicating permissibility. He stated this in *Mara'iq al-Su'ud* with his verse:

*Transmitting, affirming, and commanding after prohibitions, then this latter one [is over] permissibility...* 

(p-152)

Its meaning, his saying "then this latter one is over permissibility," is that a text indicating a command takes precedence over a text indicating permissibility, for caution in exiting the obligation of the demand.

The verified position is that the amount of the provision has no fixed limit in the law, due to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means﴾. If they agree on a specific amount, the matter is clear. If they disagree, the judge exercises ijtihad (independent reasoning) in determining the case (tahqiq al-manat), and fixes the amount in light of His saying: ﴿The wealthy according to his means﴾, and so on. This is the apparent view. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿And provide for them﴾ and His saying ﴿And for divorced women is a provision﴾ [al-Baqarah: 241] requires that the provision be obligatory in general, in contrast to Malik and those who agreed with him that the provision is not obligatory at all. Some Maliki scholars used as evidence that it is not obligatory His saying: ﴿a duty upon the doers of good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236], and His saying: ﴿a duty upon the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 241]. They said: if it were obligatory, it would be a duty upon everyone; and also, if it were obligatory, He would have specified the required amount for it.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: This argument for its non-obligation does not hold, as far as is apparent, because His saying ﴿upon the doers of good﴾ and ﴿upon the God-fearing﴾ is an emphasis on the obligation, and no one may say, "I am not God-fearing," for example, since God-fearing is obligatory upon all people.

Al-Qurtubi said in his commentary on His saying: ﴿And provide for them﴾, the verse, the following text: "His saying ﴿upon the God-fearing﴾ is an emphasis on its obligation, because each person is obliged to fear Allah regarding association with Him and His disobediences, and He has said in the Qur'an: ﴿Guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [2]. As for their saying, 'if it were obligatory, He would have specified the required amount for it,' its falsehood is clear. The maintenance of wives and relatives is obligatory, yet the required amount was not specified for it, and this kind of application of the general principle (tahqiq al-manat) is agreed upon in all the religious laws, as is well known."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 243:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes, being thousands, fearing death? Then Allah said to them, "Die," and then He brought them back to life.﴾ The purpose of this noble verse is to encourage the believers to fight by informing them that fleeing from death does not save one. When a person knows that fleeing from death or killing will not save him, facing a champion in single combat and advancing onto the battlefield become easy for him. God, exalted is He, has indicated that this is what He intends by the verse when He followed it with His words: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ (2:244), and He stated explicitly what He had alluded to here in His words: ﴿Say, "Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing, and then you will not be given enjoyment except for a little."﴾ (33:16). This is the greatest verse for encouraging fighting, because it makes clear that fleeing from killing does not save one from it. Even if one were assumed to be saved from it, one is dead soon after, as Qu'nub ibn Umm Sahib said [Mutaqarib metre]:

If you meet in a moment of bravery, do not let the thought of advancing alarm you.
For whoever fears death, it will surely find him wherever he is.
And if its causes pass you by, your utmost is only to grow old.

Zuhayr said [Tawil metre]:

I have seen death like a blind camel: whoever it strikes, it kills; whoever it misses, lives long until he grows old.

Abu al-Tayyib said [Khafif metre]:

And if there is no escape from death, then cowardice is a disgrace.

And whoever said it well said [Basit metre]:

In cowardice is shame, and in boldness is nobility, yet a man in cowardice does not escape from fate.

This is the meaning of the verses cited. It is also derived from this verse that it is not permissible to flee from plague if it occurs in a land where you are. It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he forbade fleeing from plague and forbade coming to a land where it is present if you are outside of it.

Note

The expression "Have you not considered" (alam tara) and similar phrasings do not occur in the Qur'an, when preceded by "alam," with a direct object other than through the preposition "ila" (to). Some scholars thought this was obligatory, but the verified view is that it is not obligatory, and that the verb may be transitive directly without the preposition, as the statement of Imru' al-Qays attests [Tawil metre]:

Have you not seen me, whenever I came at night, finding its fragrance, even if you had not perfumed yourself?

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 245:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan so that He may multiply it for him many times over?﴾ He did not specify here the measure of these many multiples. However, He specified it in another place, that they reach seven hundred times and more than that (p-154). That is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whom He wills.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 251:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom, and taught him of what He willed﴾. He does not specify here anything of what He taught him. But He has explained in other places that among what He taught him was the craft of making coats of mail (durū', sing. dir', the armour), as in His saying: ﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you, to protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Anbiya: 80], to the end of the verse, and His saying: ﴿And We made iron soft for him, [saying]: Make full coats of mail and measure well the links﴾ [Saba: 10-11].

The words of the Most High: ﴿And indeed you are among the messengers﴾. The phrase "indeed you are among the messengers" is understood, from its emphasis here through "inna" (indeed) and the lam (emphatic particle), to indicate that the disbelievers deny his messengerhood, as is established in the science of *ma'ani* (the science of meaning and rhetoric). He has explicitly stated this implied meaning in His words: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger."﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43].

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 253:**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Those messengers — some of them We caused to excel others. Among them are those to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some of them in rank.﴾ Here he did not specify who among them Allah spoke to. But He did make clear that Musa (peace be upon him and our Prophet) is among them, by His saying: ﴿And Allah spoke to Musa directly.﴾ [An-Nisa: 164], and His saying: ﴿I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 144].

Ibn Kathir said: "﴿Among them are those to whom Allah spoke﴾ means Musa and Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon them both. Likewise Adam, as is reported in the hadith narrated in *Sahih Ibn Hibban* from Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him)."

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: The speaking of Allah to Adam mentioned in *Sahih Ibn Hibban* is explained by His saying: ﴿And We said: "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden."﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 35], and similar verses. For it is apparent that this was without an intermediary angel. And it appears from this verse that Hawwa' was forbidden from the tree through his speech, so he was a messenger to her in that matter.

Al-Qurtubi said, in his tafsir of His saying: ﴿Among them are those to whom Allah spoke﴾, the following text: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about Adam: 'Was he a sent prophet?' He said: 'Yes, a prophet who was spoken to.'" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Some people have interpreted that the speaking to Adam was in the Garden. On this view, the distinction of Musa remains." [End of quotation.]

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said, in his tafsir of His saying: ﴿Then, if guidance comes to you from Me﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 38], in Surah al-Baqarah, the following text: "Because Adam was the prophet (ﷺ) during his life, after he was sent down to the earth, and the messenger from Allah, may His praise be exalted, to his offspring. So it is not permissible that the one meant by His saying ﴿if guidance comes to you from Me﴾ should be him, i.e., the Messenger (ﷺ), but rather it means messengers." [End of quotation.] The point of evidence from his words, and in them and in the earlier statement of Ibn Kathir from *Sahih Ibn Hibban*, is the explicit affirmation that Adam was a messenger. This is problematic in light of what is established in the hadith of intercession (agreed upon as authentic), that Nuh (peace be upon him and our Prophet) was the first of the messengers. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Nuh and the prophets after him.﴾ [An-Nisa: 163]. The apparent reconciliation of these is only by two ways:

The first: Adam was sent to his wife and offspring in the Garden, and Nuh was the first messenger sent on the earth. This reconciliation is supported by what is established in the *Two Sahihs* and others, where he (ﷺ) says: "But go to Nuh, for he is the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth," the hadith. His words "to the people of the earth": if it were not intended to exclude a messenger sent to other than the people of the earth, that statement would be superfluous. Rather, what is understood from the implication of its opposite is what we have mentioned. This is also reinforced by the words of Ibn 'Atiyyah, whose statement al-Qurtubi quoted earlier.

The second: Adam was sent to his offspring while they were upon the *fitrah* (natural disposition), and no disbelief had yet come from them, so they obeyed him. Nuh was the first messenger sent to a disbelieving people, forbidding them from associating partners with Allah, and commanding them to devote worship to Him alone. This view is supported by His saying: ﴿And mankind was not but one nation﴾ — the verse [Yunus: 19] — i.e., upon the upright religion, until the people of Nuh disbelieved. And His saying: ﴿Mankind was one nation, then Allah sent the prophets﴾ — the verse [Al-Baqarah: 213]. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and raised some of them in rank﴾, He indicated in other places that among them is Muhammad (ﷺ), such as His saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [Al-Isra: 79], or His saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind﴾ — the verse [Saba': 28],

• and His saying: ﴿I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾ [Al-A'raf: 158],

• and His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [25]. He also indicated in other places that among them is Ibrahim,

• such as His saying: ﴿And Allah took Ibrahim as an intimate friend﴾ [An-Nisa: 125],

• and His saying: ﴿Indeed, I will make you a leader for mankind﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 124],

and other verses besides these.

He indicated in another place that among them is Dawud, namely His saying: ﴿And We have certainly caused some of the prophets to exceed others, and to Dawud We gave the Zabur﴾ [17]. He indicated in another place that among them is Idris, namely His saying: ﴿And We raised him to a high station﴾ [Maryam: 57]. And He indicated here that among them is 'Isa, by His saying: ﴿And We gave 'Isa, son of Maryam, the clear signs﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 87].

\* \*

**Note (tanbih)**

In this noble verse, I mean His saying: ﴿Those messengers — some of them We caused to excel others﴾ — the verse, there is a well-known strong difficulty. Its basis is that it is established in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, agreed upon, that he (ﷺ) said: "Do not give me preference over Musa, for the people will be struck senseless on the Day of Resurrection, and I will be the first to regain consciousness, and behold, Musa will be holding onto the pillar of the Throne. So I do not know whether he regained consciousness before me or was among those whom Allah excepted." It is also established in the hadith of Abu Sa'id, agreed upon: "Do not make distinctions among the prophets, for the people will be struck senseless on the Day of Resurrection," the hadith. In another narration: "Do not prefer one over another among the prophets of Allah." And in another narration: "Do not choose me over the prophets."

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of this verse, the following text: "This verse is problematic, and the hadiths are firmly established that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do not make distinctions among the prophets, and do not prefer one over another among the prophets of Allah.'
