As for what al-Bayhaqī — may Allah have mercy on him — mentioned, that what he previously presented regarding the prohibition of Abu al-Dardāʾ and ʿUmar to Muʿāwiyah, it is his saying: "Abu Zakariyyā ibn Abi Isḥāq, Abu Bakr ibn al-Ḥasan and others informed us, saying: Abu al-ʿAbbās al-Aṣamm narrated to us; al-Rabīʿ informed us; al-Shāfiʿī informed us; Mālik informed us. And ʿAlī ibn Aḥmad ibn ʿAbdān informed us; Aḥmad ibn ʿUbayd al-Ṣaffār informed us; Ismāʿīl ibn Isḥāq narrated to us; ʿAbd Allah, meaning al-Qaʿnabī, narrated to us, from Mālik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār: that Muʿāwiyah ibn Abi Sufyān sold a vessel of gold or silver for more than its weight. Abu al-Dardāʾ said to him: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbid the like of this except equal for equal.' Muʿāwiyah said: 'I do not see any harm in this.' Abu al-Dardāʾ said to him: 'Who will excuse me regarding Muʿāwiyah? I inform him of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he informs me of his opinion. I will not live with you in a land where you are.' Then Abu al-Dardāʾ came to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, and mentioned that to him. ʿUmar wrote to Muʿāwiyah that he should not sell that except equal for equal and weight for weight." Al-Rabīʿ did not mention from al-Shāfiʿī the coming of Abu al-Dardāʾ to ʿUmar, though al-Shāfiʿī mentioned it in the narration of al-Muzanī. End of quotation from him in his words.

Similar to this, Muslim narrated in his Ṣaḥīḥ from the hadith of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, may Allah be pleased with him, through the narration of Abu al-Ashʿath, who said: "We went on a military campaign, and Muʿāwiyah was over the people. We gained many spoils, and among what we gained were vessels of silver. Muʿāwiyah ordered a man to sell them in the people's allotments (ʿuṭiyyāt), so the people rushed to that. The news reached ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, so he stood and said: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbid the sale of gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat, barley for barley, dates for dates, and salt for salt, except equal for equal, hand to hand. Whoever gives more or asks for more has engaged in ribā.' So the people returned what they had taken. The news reached Muʿāwiyah, so he stood to deliver a sermon and said: 'Look! What is the matter with men who narrate hadiths from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ which we used to witness and accompany him in, yet we did not hear them from him?' Then ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit stood and repeated the story, then said: 'We will certainly narrate what we heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, even if Muʿāwiyah dislikes it' — or he said: 'even if he is displeased. I do not care that I would not accompany him in his army on a dark night.'" Ḥammād said: "This or something similar." End of quotation.

This is the text of the Hadith in Muslim's *Sahih*, and these authentic texts indicate that the craftsmanship applied to gold or silver has no effect and does not permit an excess in exchange equal to the value of the craftsmanship, as we have mentioned. This is the correct position, about which there is no doubt. Malik ibn Anas, may Allah have mercy on him, permitted a traveler to give gold to the minting house (*dar al-darb*), together with the fee for its shaping, and to take in return ornaments equal in weight to the currency without the fee, because of the necessity of travel. Khalil ibn Ishaq indicated this in his *Mukhtasar* with his statement: "Unlike bullion that a traveler gives to the minting house, along with its fee, in order to take back its weight."

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him, says: The apparent meaning of the authentic texts of the Sunnah is that this is not permitted, even because of the necessity of travel. Ibn Rushd also inferred its impermissibility, and the statement of the author of the *Mukhtasar* refers to this: "And the more apparent (ruling) is its opposite," meaning: even if the need for it becomes severe, except for a harm that makes carrion permissible. This is how the commentators of the *Mukhtasar* established it.

**The Fifth Branch:** People have differed concerning the paper notes that are used in dealings: does riba apply between them and the two precious metals? Some hold that they are a document (*sanad*), and that what is sold is the silver which the document represents. Therefore selling them is prohibited even hand to hand and equal for equal, and selling them for gold is also prohibited even hand to hand, because it is an exchange of present gold or present silver for absent silver; what is present is only a document for it, so it is prohibited for lack of immediate exchange (*munajazah*), due to the absence of one of the two currencies. Others hold that none of this applies to them, considering them to be like trade goods (*urud al-tijara*). Many of the later scholars held that they are like trade goods, so excess and deferment are permitted between them and silver and gold. Among those who issued this legal opinion that they are like trade goods was the well-known scholar 'Ulaysh al-Misri, author of *al-Nawazil* and the *Sharh Mukhtasar Khalil*, and many of the later Maliki scholars (p-182) followed him in this opinion.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him, says: What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that they are not like trade goods; rather they are a document for silver, and what is sold is the silver which they represent. Whoever reads what is written on them understands the validity of this. Accordingly, it is not permitted to sell them for gold or silver, even hand to hand, because of the lack of immediate exchange due to the absence of the silver whose document has been paid, since they are neither property (*mutamawwalah*) nor beneficial in themselves at all. If it is said that there is no difference between the paper notes and iron coins, because each of them is not property in itself, although it circulates according to what the ruler has made it for dealing, the answer is in three aspects:

First: When we establish that today's iron coins have no benefit at all, and that their reality is a document for silver, what prevents us from prohibiting riba in them together with currency? The texts are explicit in prohibiting it between the two currencies, and there is no consensus (*ijma'*) preventing the application of the texts to their apparent meanings. Rather, Malik's position is that iron coins may not be exchanged for either of the two currencies on credit (*nasi'a*). So paying dirhams for coins, or the reverse, is prohibited in his view.

As for what has been reported from some scholars indicating that there is no riba between the two currencies and iron coins, it is to be understood as referring to the fact that the iron from which those coins are made has the known benefits of iron, which are alluded to in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is great might and benefits for mankind﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. If those coins were gathered and placed in the fire, there would be made from them what is made from iron of useful things. Even if they were like our present coins, granting that they have no benefit at all, they would not have said that exchange is permitted, because what is a document is undoubtedly not what is sold; what is sold is what the document represents, not the document itself. Therefore the early generation did not differ that what is sold in the sale of *sukuk* (written tickets), which Muslim mentioned in the *Sahih* and elsewhere, is the provision written on them, not the *sukuk* themselves, which are papers that are documents for provisions.

Second: There is a general difference between them, namely that iron coins are customarily used, past and present, only for small trifling items, so nothing of significance is bought with them, unlike paper notes. This shows that the notes are closer to silver than coins are.

Third: Even if we assume that both possibilities are equally likely, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt." He also said: "Whoever leaves doubtful matters has cleared himself regarding his religion and his honor." And he said: (p-183) "Sin is that which wavers in the soul," and the Hadith continues. The poet said:

*Whoever is cautious in matters of religion, fleeing from doubt to certainty.*

We have mentioned repeatedly that what indicates prohibition takes precedence over what indicates permission, because abandoning what is permitted is easier than committing what is forbidden, especially the prohibition of riba, concerning which Allah, the Exalted, declared that its perpetrator is at war with Allah, and it is authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he cursed it.

Among the types of riba is that about which scholars have differed concerning its prohibition, such as when a sale appears outwardly permissible, but it may be intended as a means to reach forbidden riba through the permissible form apparent on the surface. For example, if someone sells a commodity for a price deferred to a term, then buys that same commodity back for a lower price in cash, or for a nearer term than the first, or for a higher price for a more distant term. The outward appearance of the two contracts is permissible, because it is a sale of a commodity for dirhams deferred to a term in each of them, and there is no prohibition in this. But it may be that the intention of the two contracting parties is to hand over dirhams and take back more dirhams for a term, while the commodity leaving the hand and returning to it is disregarded. So the matter comes down to handing over dirhams and taking more of them for a term, which is exactly forbidden riba. Such a transaction is prohibited according to Malik, Ahmad, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifa, and al-Hasan ibn Salih. It is also reported from al-Sha'bi, al-Hakam, and Hammad, as in *al-Istidhkar*. Al-Shafi'i permitted it.

Those who prohibit it rely on what al-Bayhaqi and al-Daraqutni narrated from 'A'isha, that she denounced this to Zayd ibn Arqam and said: "Inform Zayd that he has invalidated his jihad with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) unless he repents."

Al-Shafi'i said: Zayd ibn Arqam opposes 'A'isha. When two Companions differ on a matter, we prefer the one whose view agrees with analogy (*qiyas*), and analogy here agrees with Zayd, because they are two contracts, each of which is valid in itself.

Al-Shafi'i also said: Even if this were established from 'A'isha, she only objected to deferment until the stipend (*'ata'*), because it is an unknown term, and a sale to an unknown term is not permitted. Some scholars objected to him, saying that the Hadith is authentically transmitted from 'A'isha, and that Ibn Abi Shayba mentioned in his *Musannaf* that the Mothers of the Believers used to buy on credit until the stipend. And Allah knows best. Also, 'A'isha did not claim that jihad is invalidated by opposing her opinion; rather, she claimed it on the basis of something she had learned from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The sale we have mentioned as prohibited is what scholars mean by *bay' al-'inah*, which the Malikis call *buyu' al-ajal* (sales of terms). I have set its rule in my long poem on the branches of Malik's school with my words:

[Rajaz meter]
*The sales of terms, when the term or the price is like their two counterparts, are lawful*
*And if the price is other than the first, and the term differs from the original term*
*Then look at the one who gave first: has he returned more, or has he returned less?*
*If he has returned more than what he gave, that is a loan with a benefit.*
*And if it is like his thing, or less, than the thing he gave earlier, it is lawful.* (p-184)

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and He increases charities﴾, etc. In this noble verse He mentioned that He, the Exalted, ﴿increases charities﴾. He explained in another place that this increase is the multiplication of reward, and that it requires sincerity of intention for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, as in His words: ﴿And whatever you give in zakat seeking the Face of Allah — those are the ones who receive multiplied (reward)﴾ [al-Rum: 39].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 282:

The words of the Most High: ﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down﴾. The apparent meaning of this noble verse is that writing down a debt is obligatory, because a command from Allah indicates obligation. However, He indicated that it is a command of guidance (irshad), not of obligation, by His words: ﴿And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken into possession﴾ and the rest of the verse, because a pledge (rahn) is not obligatory by consensus (ijma'), and it is a substitute for writing when writing is impossible in the verse. So if writing were obligatory, its substitute would be obligatory too. He also explicitly stated that it is not obligatory by His words: ﴿But if one of you entrusts another, let the one who is entrusted fulfil his trust﴾ and the rest of the verse. Therefore, the correct view is that the command in ﴿write it﴾ is for recommendation (nadb) and guidance, because the creditor may forgive the debt and leave it, by consensus. So the recommendation to write it down is only for the sake of caution for people. This is what al-Qurtubi said.

Some said: "If you call witnesses, it is prudent; if you trust one another, there is ease and latitude," Ibn 'Atiyyah said. This view is the sound one, as al-Qurtubi also said.

Al-Sha'bi said: They used to think that His words ﴿But if one of you entrusts another﴾ abrogate (naskh) His command to write. Ibn Juraij related something similar, Ibn Zayd said it, and it was narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. Al-Rabi' held that writing was obligatory by these words, then Allah lightened it by His words: ﴿But if one of you entrusts another﴾. A group held to the apparent command in His words "write it," and they said: writing down a debt is an obligatory duty by this verse, whether it is a sale or a loan, lest forgetfulness or denial occur. This is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari in his Tafsir.

Ibn Juraij said: Whoever borrows should write, and whoever sells should call witnesses. End of quotation from al-Qurtubi. He will have further explanation later, if Allah wills, shortly.

Note:

Some scholars took from His words: ﴿And if you are on a journey﴾ and the rest of the verse that a pledge is only lawful during a journey, as Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Dawud said. But the correct view is that it is permissible while at home (al-hadar).

It is established in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) from 'A'isha that he (ﷺ) died while his armour was pledged to a Jew for thirty measures of barley. And in the two Sahihs it is stated that it was an iron armour.

Al-Bukhari, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah related from Anas that he (ﷺ) pledged an armour to a Jew in Madinah and took barley from him for his family. Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah related from Ibn 'Abbas something like the hadith of 'A'isha. Thus the sound hadith indicates that His words ﴿And if you are on a journey﴾ carry no implicit contrary meaning (mafhum al-mukhalafa), because it refers to the usual situation. The usual case is that a scribe is not unavailable at home, and is usually unavailable only on a journey. Adhering to the usual case is one of the obstacles to treating an implicit contrary meaning as valid, as we have mentioned in this book many times. And knowledge is with Allah the Most High.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And call witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾. The apparent meaning of this command is also obligation, so whoever sells must call witnesses. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Umar, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Jabir ibn Zayd, Mujahid, Dawud ibn 'Ali and his son Abu Bakr, 'Ata' and Ibrahim said this, as al-Qurtubi related. Al-Tabari, in the strongest terms, defended this view and stated that whoever does not call witnesses opposes the Book of Allah. But the majority of scholars hold that calling witnesses for a sale and for writing a debt is a recommended matter, not obligatory, and His words ﴿But if one of you entrusts another﴾ and the rest of the verse indicate this.

Ibn al-'Arabi the Maliki said: This is the view of the majority (al-kafffa). He said: It is the sound view, and no one who held obligation has been reported except al-Dahhak. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) sold and wrote, and the text of his document was: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. This is what al-'Adda' ibn Khalid ibn Hawdhah bought from Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He bought from him a male or female slave, with no disease, no concealed defect, and no wickedness. A sale of a Muslim to a Muslim." He sold without calling witnesses, and he bought and pledged his armour to a Jew without calling witnesses. Had calling witnesses been obligatory, it would have been obligatory along with the pledge, to avoid dispute. End of quotation.

Al-Qurtubi said after quoting the words of Ibn al-'Arabi, the following: I say: We have mentioned the obligation from others besides al-Dahhak. The hadith of al-'Adda' was reported by al-Daraqutni and Abu Dawud. His Islam came after the conquest (of Makkah) and Hunayn, and he is the one who said: "We fought with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Hunayn, and Allah did not grant us victory." Then he became Muslim and his Islam was good. Abu 'Umar mentioned this and mentioned this hadith.

At its end he said: al-Asma'i said: I asked Sa'id ibn Abi 'Urwah about the "concealed defect" (ghā'ilah), and he said: running away, theft, and adultery. I asked him about "wickedness" (khubthah), and he said: selling to the people of a covenant with the Muslims.

Imam Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyyah said: Obligation in this matter is uncertain. As for documents, it is difficult and burdensome. As for what is frequent, a merchant may intend to win favour by not calling witnesses, and it may be a custom in some lands, and one may feel shy before a scholar or an honoured elderly man, so one does not call witnesses against him. All of that falls under trust (i'timan), and the command to call witnesses remains a recommendation, because of the benefit it contains in most cases, as long as no excuse arises that prevents it, as we mentioned. Al-Mahdawi, al-Nahhas and Makki related from a people that they said: ﴿And call witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾ is abrogated (mansukh) by His words: ﴿But if one of you entrusts another﴾. Al-Nahhas traced this to Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and that he recited: ﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down﴾, up to His words: ﴿But if one of you entrusts another, let the one who is entrusted fulfil his trust﴾. He said: This verse abrogated what came before it.

Al-Nahhas said: This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Hakam and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

Al-Tabari said: This has no meaning, because this is a different ruling from the first; it is the ruling of one who does not find a scribe.

* *

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken into possession. But if one of you entrusts another, let the one who is entrusted fulfil his trust﴾, meaning, he does not demand a pledge from him. Al-Tabari said: If it were permissible that this be abrogating the first, it would be permissible that His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And if you are ill or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾ [al-Nisa': 43] abrogate His words: ﴿O you who believe, when you rise to prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and it would be permissible that His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Then whoever does not find [the means], then fasting two consecutive months﴾ [al-Nisa': 92] abrogate His words: ﴿Then the freeing of a slave﴾.

Some scholars said that His words: ﴿But if one of you entrusts another﴾ did not become clear, by the latest revelation, as abrogating the beginning of the verse which contains the command to call witnesses. Rather, both came together. It is not permissible for the abrogating and the abrogated to come together at one and the same time. He said: It has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas that when he was told that the verse on debt was abrogated, he said: No, by Allah, the verse on debt is firm (muhkamah) and contains no abrogation. He said: Calling witnesses was made only for peace of mind, because Allah, the Most High, made several ways to secure a debt: among them writing, among them the pledge, and among them witnesses. And there is no disagreement among the scholars of the regions that the pledge is legislated as a recommendation and not as an obligation. So from this the same is known about calling witnesses. People have continued to trade at home and on journeys, on land and at sea, on plains and in mountains, without calling witnesses, and people knew of this without objection. Had calling witnesses been obligatory, they would not have left off objecting to the one who omitted it.

I say: All of this is a good argument, and better than it is what came in clear Sunnah about omitting witnesses. It is what al-Daraqutni related from Tariq ibn 'Abd Allah al-Muharibi, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We set out in a caravan from al-Rabadhah and the south of al-Rabadhah until we camped near Madinah, and with us was a litter of ours. While we were sitting, a man came to us wearing two white garments. He greeted us and we returned his greeting. He said: 'Where are the people from?' We said: From al-Rabadhah and the south of al-Rabadhah. He said: 'With you is a red camel?' We said: Yes. He said: 'Will you sell me this camel of yours?' We said: Yes. He said: 'For how much?' We said: For such and such measures of dates. He did not ask us for any reduction, and said: 'I have taken it.' Then he took hold of the camel's head until he entered Madinah, and he disappeared from us. We blamed one another and said: You have given your camel to someone you do not know. The litter-woman said: Do not blame one another. I have seen the face of a man who would not betray you. I have never seen a face more like the moon on the night of the full moon. When it was evening, a man came to us and said: 'Peace be upon you. I am the messenger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to you, and he has commanded you to eat from this until you are full, and to measure out until you have received your full measure.' He said: So we ate until we were full, and we measured out until we had received our full measure." And al-Zuhri mentioned the hadith from 'Umarah ibn Khuzaymah that his paternal uncle, who was one of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), told him: "The Prophet (ﷺ) bought a horse from a Bedouin..." the hadith, in which: the Bedouin began to say: "Come, a witness who will testify that I sold it to you." Khuzaymah ibn Thabit said: "I testify that you sold it." The Prophet (ﷺ) turned to Khuzaymah and said: "On what basis do you testify?" He said: "By your confirmation, O Messenger of Allah." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made Khuzaymah's testimony equal to the testimony of two men. Related by al-Nasa'i and others. End of quotation from al-Qurtubi in his wording.

The author, may Allah pardon him, said: In what we have quoted there is clear evidence that calling witnesses and writing are recommended, not obligatory duties, as Ibn Jarir and others said. And Allah, the Most High, did not specify in this verse, that is His words, Majestic and Exalted: ﴿And call witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾, the condition of uprightness (adalah) in the witnesses, but He specified it in other places, such as His words: ﴿from among those whom you approve as witnesses﴾, and His words: ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that the absolute (mutlaq) is understood in light of the restricted (muqayyad), as we have explained in other places.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 284:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whether you show what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will bring you to account for it﴾, the verse.

This verse indicates, by its apparent meaning, that a person is held accountable for whisperings (waswasah) and passing thoughts of the heart, even though he has no power to repel them. Other verses have come indicating that a person is not charged except with what he can bear, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and His saying: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16].

The answer is that the verse ﴿And if you show what is within yourselves or conceal it﴾ is abrogated (mansukhah) by His saying, ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾.
